(Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears kicked off their 2026 preseason slate with an impressive 34-10 victory at Soldier Field. Although Saturday’s game will be their lone preseason contest at home, the stakes will continue to rise when they head to Cincinnati to take on the Bengals during a midweek joint practice and then on Saturday evening for their Week 2 game. Before we turn the page on the Bears’ preseason opener, we’ll take a look back at the five things that stood out the most on Saturday afternoon in a special edition of our Five Bears Takes. 1. The receiver depth might be better than advertised, even without any of their “roster locks” playing a snap on Saturday. There’s no denying that the subtraction of DJ Moore is going to be a move that will at least take away from the top-end of their depth chart. That being said, a healthy Rome Odunze, combined with a Year 2 breakout from Luther Burden III, could be more than enough to help take this offense to the next level. Add in the veteran presence of Kalif Raymond, and another year of experience for Jahdae Walker, and all of a sudden, the Top 4 of their depth chart is all but set in stone. That’s not even counting third-round pick Zavion Thomas, who, assuming he’s healthy, will take another roster spot as well. That is why, as the team headed into training camp, I questioned whether it really needed to use six roster spots at receiver. It’s been a long time since fans have been able to look at the roster and clearly see a group of players that will be good enough to make the roster, yet still be either cut or traded due to an overabundance of talent. Receiver, maybe more than any other position, feels like a prime candidate for exactly that, and Saturday afternoon’s game did nothing to dissuade anyone’s feelings on this subject. Former CFL’er Kaden Davis led the offense with 88 receiving yards on four receptions. That included a 44-yarder that caught everyone’s eye. Moving down the list, veterans Ray-Ray McCloud (three catches for 63 yards), Maurice Alexander (three catches for 42 yards, and a touchdown), and Scotty Miller (three catches for 37 yards) all stood out at various points during the game. Assuming all goes well on the health front, the final spot on the depth chart could come down to that trio of veterans who all stood out in the first game. Special teams value will play a big role, but it’s worth noting that all three players bring plenty of experience in that department. Buckle in, Bears fans, the race for the sixth and final spot promises to heat up over the next two weeks. 2. Speaking of the offense, it’s a good thing that Ozzy Trapilo is being activated off PUP, because neither Kiran Amegadjie nor Jedrick Wills Jr. looked ready to be a serious contestant for the Week 1 starting job. If you had Trapilo being activated on PUP before Kyler Gordon, Shemar Turner, or Elijah Hicks, congratulations, and I hope you bought a lottery ticket (or 12). For the rest of us (mere mortals), the news of Trapilo not only being activated but practicing on Sunday came as a shock, to say the least. After all, the former second-round pick is just seven months removed from an injury that typically costs players anywhere from 10-12 months in rehab and recovery. For all the bad injury luck the team has experienced so far this camp, getting Trapilo back into the mix is one of the best outcomes anyone could ask for, even though it’s likely that he wouldn’t be expected to start right away as the regular season approaches. A big reason is Amegadjie’s lack of development and the fact that Wills doesn’t look remotely healthy enough to play a full game. Neither “development” nor the fact that Wills doesn’t look remotely healthy enough to play a full game is overly surprising, but the Wills’ gamble was one that many, including me, would have expected to pan out a bit better. Now, it’s possible that as he continues to get back into football shape, he’ll round into form, but with Braxton Jones, Trapilo and Theo Benedet all with an ability to start and play left tackle, the chances of either Amegadjie or Wills making the team don’t look great. It’s clear that Trapilo is still the team’s long-term hope at left tackle, and being on the 53-man roster heading into Week 1 would only boost his chances of “earning” the starting job early in the season. For now, we’ll be left to marvel at how impressive a comeback it’s been and hope that when all is said and done, he shows meaningful contributions to this roster in 2026. 3. While the questions at defensive end remain, it’s easy to feel better about the depth that they’ve built on the interior, starting with sixth-round rookie Jordan van den Berg and veteran James Lynch. Now, that’s not to say that the Bears will get into the season and magically have a top-end defensive tackle room. That said, there’s enough youthful upside between Gervon Dexter Sr. and van den Berg to go along with a quality veteran presence in the form of Grady Jarrett, Neville Gallimore, and Lynch. On Saturday night, Lynch played on the edge more than he did on the interior, which shouldn’t come as a surprise considering his tweener size. Even so, he finished the game with multiple pressures, a quarterback hit, and a batted pass. More importantly, he was all over the place and provided one of the more steady presences on the defensive line, regardless of the level of competition he was facing. Van den Berg was also impressive, even if his numbers showed just one tackle and one quarterback hit. He got a pressure on 20% of his pass-rushing snaps and finished with an 83.3 pass-rushing grade per Pro Football Focus. The biggest key heading into the season will be how healthy (and productive) the top three names on the depth chart can be. With that in mind, having developmental depth in the form of van den Berg, on top of potentially a veteran to round out this group in the form of Lynch or even Kentavius Street, could be enough to help provide better depth and more overall upside to a group that truly needs it if they expect the defense to improve in 2026. 4. Although there was plenty to like about the defense’s performance on Saturday, some veteran additions might be needed in the coming weeks. Veteran defensive end Marcus Davenport is first up. Still, fans should have their eyes set on better. The continued ambiguity surrounding nickelback Kyler Gordon is reaching new levels of frustration for fans and the organization alike. Couple that with the news that Coby Bryant likely won’t be back until December at the earliest, and this is all starting to feel like Dejavu all over again. Couple that with the complete lack of improvements (on paper) along the defensive line, and it’s fair to wonder what the defense’s ceiling is heading into the regular season. More importantly, is there a high enough ceiling with this group for the Bears to be considered “Super Bowl contenders” for 2026? I’ll tell you one thing: adding Davenport isn’t going to move the needle, not one iota. Improvements along the defensive line are always going to be hard to come by, especially this late in the process. Outside of 31-year-old veteran defensive tackle Vita Vea, is there one impact player worth making a move for before Week 1? Unless someone like Josh Sweat becomes available, it’s unlikely. Which means fans might want to shift their focus to the secondary. While Beanie Bishop’s two-interception performance on Saturday was fun, bringing in a proven veteran or two in the secondary might make the most sense in the short term. The name that keeps standing out on the free agent market is Kenny Moore. Allen values versatility…

title: The two most interesting PFF grades from the Chicago Bears’ Week 1 preseason win
summary: As far as preseason openers go, that Chicago Bears win over the Cleveland Browns was pretty…boring. (Which isn’t bad, especially on an injury front.) None of the stars, like Caleb Williams, played a snap, leaving the backups to show their stuff and make their case to stick on the 53-man roster or practice squad down […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 10: Theo Benedet #79 of the Chicago Bears runs across the field during an NFC Wild Card Playoff game against the Green Bay Packers at Soldier Field on January 10, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images As far as preseason openers go, that Chicago Bears win over the Cleveland Browns was pretty…boring. (Which isn’t bad, especially on an injury front.) None of the stars, like Caleb Williams, played a snap, leaving the backups to show their stuff and make their case to stick on the 53-man roster or practice squad down the line. Splash plays like running back Salvon Ahmed’s slaloming touchdown run and cornerback Beanie Bishop Jr.’s two INTs certainly won the day. But as far as players who might actually matter to the Chicago Bears this season or in the future, there were a couple of performances that may have flown under the radar that we should be watching, one each on offense and defense. Theo Benedet (72.8) It was good to see rookie center Logan Jones get out there for some game reps this week with the presumed starters sitting out, and he generally looked fine. But the backup offensive lineman who helped himself the most in Week 1 was unquestionably Benedet. Getting the start at right tackle, Benedet earned the sixth-best offensive grade of the game for the Bears, including the second-best among all Chicago’s offensive linemen. Even more importantly, Benedet posted a clean pass-pro stat line for the game—no pressures of any kind allowed. By contrast, veteran free-agent signee Jedrick Wills (58.2) and starting left tackle Kiran Amegadjie (44.8), who gave up three pressures, didn’t pass the smell test when it came to improving their stock. The news that Ozzy Trapilo is, somehow, unbelievably, returning to practice for the Bears not even months after rupturing his patellar tendon—I mean, seriously, what?!—could change the math for Chicago’s left tackle position. If he’s even remotely prepared to start, you can potentially say goodbye to Braxton Jones, who had been starting in his place, or, at the very least, Wills and Amegadjie if you’re not ready to put Trapilo on the field right away. But Benedet, the former undrafted free agent, keeps earning a role on this team. Jordan van den Berg (69.1) You get the feeling that the sixth-round rookie out of Georgia Tech is a bit of a bull in a china shop right now. But boy, does that bull have some impressive traits. The uncanny athleticism and raw physicality that made van den Berg one of the most athletic defensive tackle prospects ever to come out of the draft showed up on Saturday, as he racked up three pressures, including a quarterback hit. His violent swipe to the inside to get a lick on Shedeur Sanders (just stay higher next time)—was one of the best reps of the day from an interior defender. It’s not going to be enough to vault him into significant snaps off the bat, especially given his need to play with more discipline. But if he keeps flashing like this, he’s going to get his handful of snaps a game on pass-rushing downs to push the pocket. The Bears needed all the help they could get in that regard last season, so every little bit helps. At the very least, we saw a guy with the tools to be a solid player. Now, it’s just about coaching him up.

title: Chicago Bears Question of the Day: Will Kyler Gordon ever be the same?
summary: Go ahead — let it out. I know that a lot of you have been looking for a place to vent. Use this, down below. Kyler Gordon’s injury issues are getting more confusing and frustrating with each passing day. And Bears fans are calling him out. A few days ago, Adam Hoge of CHGO had […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 29: Kyler Gordon #6 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Solider Field on September 29, 2024 in Chicago, IL. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Go ahead — let it out. I know that a lot of you have been looking for a place to vent. Use this, down below. Kyler Gordon’s injury issues are getting more confusing and frustrating with each passing day. And Bears fans are calling him out. A few days ago, Adam Hoge of CHGO had this to say when on the Spiegel and Holmes show: . @AdamHoge : "This Kyler Gordon situation has veered into Nate Davis territory. There were valid reasons why he wasn't on the field, and then it eventually just got to the point where everybody is a little fed up the guy's not out there. That's the vibe you get in the building." pic.twitter.com/Ii3qyY2RZK — 104.3 The Score (@thescorechicago) August 12, 2026 Nate Davis is one guy that you never want to be compared to when dealing with an injury issue. The issue with Nate Davis was not so much that he was injured, but more that there was a sentiment that he gave up on the team after receiving a large payday in free agency. Gordon, the beneficiary of a 3 year, $40 million deal in April of 2025 was viewed as a major part of the Bears defense moving forward, after posting 5 INTs, 17 PDs, 1.5 sacks, and 9 TFLs in his first three seasons. His versatility at playing in coverage and making plays behind the LOS were particularly interesting. And then the 2025 season came. Kyler Gordon entered the season dealing with soft tissue injuries in his calf that started his season on the PUP list. After being activated for weeks 6 and 7, Gordon didn’t look himself, playing a little over half of the defensive snaps. He was ruled out again until week 13 where a similar story materialized. It was noted that he was dealing with a variety of soft tissue issues, including his groin, calf, and hamstring. He was then sidelined until the playoffs. Gordon’s play in the postseason was solid, but still looked a step off as he struggled in coverage. However, many saw this as a sign that Gordon would be primed to return fully healthy for the 2026 campaign. Gordon’s status was once again in question when it was noted he was sitting out some offseason workouts; then later, our collective fears were confirmed when he was once again placed on the PUP list ahead of training camp. Now, with the miraculous return of a player like Ozzy Trapilo, who is back in action after only 7 months removed from a ruptured patellar tendon, many are questioning Kyler Gordon’s commitment to the team and ability to stay healthy. Will Kyler Gordon ever be the same? I suppose this presumes a certain baseline condition that Kyler had early in his career. Even in his first three seasons, he was not immune to injury setbacks, averaging 14 games played per season, never tallying more than 15 any given year. Even if that is the baseline expectation for Gordon, it’s hard to imagine he will be able to replicate that, especially with a head coach in Ben Johnson who seems frustrated by him. In June of this year, Ben noted that he and Kyler are “still getting to know each other” and that “trust is a huge thing” when speaking to availability: Ben Johnson and Kyler Gordon still getting to know each other: ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/NsG1Ka1qQm — CHGO Bears (@CHGO_Bears) June 3, 2026 In July, Ben’s message to Gordon was trite — “get healthy” Here's the Ben Johnson quote on Kyler Gordon. Short and maybe not so sweet. Via @ChicagoBears pic.twitter.com/9V4WzhxlwI — Brendan Sugrue (@BrendanSugrue) July 28, 2026 Most recently, this past Saturday while giving updates on a variety of injured Bears, Ben’s frustration with Kyler seemed at an all-time high, noting his status as “Unknown.” Given all of this, it’s getting increasingly difficult to trust that Gordon will be the player the Bears hoped he would be when they signed him to his contract 18 months ago. At this point, he is going to have to earn back trust before any of us can extend more in his direction. Now it’s your turn! Do you think Kyler Gordon will ever be the same? Sound off in the comments.

Parker Conley was van den Berg’s football coach for all […]
full_text: Chicago Bears rookie defensive tackle Jordan van den Berg has been a training camp sensation so far, and he flashed in the preseason opener too, so for her latest Making Monsters podcast, Taylor Doll wanted to learn more about him and his introduction to football. Parker Conley was van den Berg’s football coach for all 3 years of his high school career at Providence Christian Academy in Lilburn, Georgia, and Coach Conley was excited to talk about one of his former players. We’ve heard van den Berg discuss his enjoyment of being violent on the football field, but there’s also this. “He’s one of the most incredible people I’ve ever met, and every time I talk to him, it still feels like it’s a high school kid talking to this coach,” Conley said. “Just incredibly respectful. He is just such a kind-hearted individual that cares about others. Loves his family, loves his friends, extremely loyal, and can turn it on, and I think that’s a beautiful thing for a football player to be able to have that, you know, that incredible work ethic and respect of his peers, because of who he is as a person and then to have the same thing as a violent competitor or strong football player. All he knows is putting in work, and like I said, it’s 100%. It doesn’t matter if it’s him in the weight room, or if it’s him in meetings, he is putting every aspect of his being into it.” Make sure you check out her show in either of the embeds below for her discussion with Coach Conley! title: Bengals News (8/19): Josh Newton is turning the corner
summary: One preseason game is in the books. The Bengals defeated the Lions at home by a score of 16-14. What did we learn? We learned that some players are still knocking the dust off, and some look like they’re ready to go. We got to see most of the starters, and we got to see […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals practice during the 2026 preseason on Tuesday August 18, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co One preseason game is in the books. The Bengals defeated the Lions at home by a score of 16-14. What did we learn? We learned that some players are still knocking the dust off, and some look like they’re ready to go. We got to see most of the starters, and we got to see a lot of the guys whose spots on the roster aren’t etched in stone. They play their second of three preseason games on Saturday, also at home, against the Chicago Bears. Practice resumed this week in preparation for the practice game. Here’s what’s going on Wednesday morning. By all accounts, cornerback Josh Newton hasn’t had a good camp. In fact, it’s gotten to the point where some are questioning whether or not he has a spot on the 53-man roster. He had a good day on Tuesday , intercepting one pass and breaking up another on a third-and-long pass attempt to Charlie Jones. “Man-to-man backside, we like to run a lot of digs in our offense backside when it is 3 by 1 (receivers on a side). I was in front and had the leverage. Anytime your man-to-man backside three by one, you’re hot,” he said, per bengals.com beat writer Geoff Hobson. John Sheeran makes a strong case for the Bengals to add running back Khalil Herbert , who was just released by the San Francisco 49ers. Sheeran mentions the Bengals traded for Herbert in 2024 when Zack Moss’ injury thinned out the depth at the position. He also mentions that the depth behind Chase Brown and Samaje Perine isn’t as strong as it should be. This Bengals Youngster Is Primed for Huge Season in 2026 Despite Recent Hiccup “Cincinnati invested heavily in its defensive front this offseason, including signing Boye Mafe, trading for Dexter Lawrence and drafting Cashius Howell. So Stewart can’t afford another poor season or he risks being discarded. I think he’ll rise to the challenge and prove to be a versatile and important contributor to one of the NFL’s most improved teams this year.” ‘I Feel Really Confident’ – Bengals LT Orlando Brown Jr. Talks Bad Rep Vs. Lions, Camp Performance Overall “I feel really confident,” Brown said. “Normally at this time I would feel a lot more rusty than I have. But at this point, I feel pretty good.” Paul Dehner Jr. takes a look at three positions that could still be considered “positions of need” as the Bengals motor through the preseason. On the defensive side of the ball, he lists linebacker and cornerback as the two positions that are lacking some depth. Then on the offensive side of the ball he lists offensive tackle. After Orlando Brown Jr. and Amarius Mims, the Bengals have a lot of hopes wrapped up in Cody Ford. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals don’t typically do much wheeling and dealing, but we have seen them be a bit more aggressive in that regard in the Zac Taylor era. We could see them pull something similar off as they reportedly have asked about Green Bay Packers corner Carrington Valentine, according to Easton Butler. The Pittsburgh Steelers and Miami Dolphins have also reportedly called about Valentine’s availability. The 6-foot, 189-pound Valentine would instantly improve the depth at the boundary corner position. DJ Turner and Dax Hill are locked in as starters, but Hill himself is already dealing with a hamstring issue. The only names behind them are DJ Ivey and rookie Tacario Davis, neither of whom is very experienced in getting NFL snaps on defense. As for what the Bengals could offer, it could simply resemble a trade that helped fuel their last Super Bowl run. They traded center Billy Price for the New York Giants defensive tackle B.J. Hill. You simply need to look where the Bengals are deepest, and it is wide receiver and defensive tackle. Names like Andrei Iosivas, T.J. Slaton (who was a Packer prior to joining the Bengals last year), or even Kris Jenkins Jr. could be brought up. All of them either have expiring contracts and are already on the roster bubble or have young guys showing promise behind them. It could also be as simple as a conditional pick, but if Green Bay can get a depth piece as well in the trade, then it makes more sense for both sides than simply getting a pick later on down the line. Who do you think gets traded if the Bengals are able to complete the trade for Valentine? Teams have been calling the Packers about the availability of CB Carrington Valentine. The 3 teams that have called are the Pittsburgh Steelers, Miami Dolphins, and Cincinnati Bengals. title: The Bengals are giving Landon Robinson a chance to play on offense
summary: Not many teams in the NFL utilize the fullback position as they did 20 years ago, but let’s imagine the Cincinnati Bengals manage to utilize one this season. It’s actually conceivable, and it comes in the form of a seventh-round draft pick. Landon Robinson was seemingly on the Bengals’ radar from the Senior Bowl. Sure […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals defensive tackle Landon Robinson (96) reacts after a play in the first half against the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Not many teams in the NFL utilize the fullback position as they did 20 years ago, but let’s imagine the Cincinnati Bengals manage to utilize one this season. It’s actually conceivable, and it comes in the form of a seventh-round draft pick. Landon Robinson was seemingly on the Bengals’ radar from the Senior Bowl. Sure enough, the Bengals drafted the defensive tackle from Navy and an Ohio native in the seventh round this past April. Robinson shined in the preseason opener last Thursday, showing a ferocity to get into the offensive backfield and disrupt the flow of the play the opposing offense is trying to run. However, the Bengals have a deep defensive line, so they may find another way to keep Robinson on the 53-man roster: Giving him reps at fullback. 5. We got our first look at rookie DT Landon Robinson as a short yardage fullback. His block on Demetrius Knight (#44) helped pave the way for a Samaje Perine TD. “Coach Pitcher came to me and said, ‘Hey Landon, have you ever played fullback?’” said Robinson. “I was able to sit… pic.twitter.com/KsHSbUa8xN — Dan Hoard (@Dan_Hoard) August 18, 2026 Robinson at fullback? Before you quickly dismiss this notion, remember that Domata Peko came in multiple times and acted as a fullback in goal-line situations. A guy like Robinson can play a similar role. “Coach Pitcher came to me and said, ‘Hey Landon, have you ever played fullback?’” said Robinson. “I was able to sit in on a couple of offensive meetings, and he installed the goal-line package. “The quickness I use at D-line kind of translates to fullback. Low center of gravity and boom! I think it worked out pretty well.” Even being a blocker for Chase Brown or Samaje Perine down near the goal line can provide great value for the Bengals. Versatility is a great asset for any seventh-round pick trying to make the 53-man roster, and it looks like Robinson is showing just that in training camp.

title: Standout offensive rookie performances for Bengals vs. Lions
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals’ first offensive selection during the 2026 NFL Draft, Connor Lew, was inactive vs. the Detroit Lions. After tearing his left ACL during October of 2025, the Bengals are being cautious in easing him back into full contact on a regular basis. He has been getting some first- and second-team action in camp, […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals ’ first offensive selection during the 2026 NFL Draft, Connor Lew, was inactive vs. the Detroit Lions. After tearing his left ACL during October of 2025, the Bengals are being cautious in easing him back into full contact on a regular basis. He has been getting some first- and second-team action in camp, but the next step will be to see if he plays in one of the final two preseason games. Colbie Young was also a fourth-round draft selection for the Bengals. He has made quite the impression so far during camp. That continued with a couple of catches versus Detroit. He finished the game with two receptions for 28 yards. He could have had a third catch, but it was knocked away on a contested catch opportunity. Young could push Andrei Iosivas for snaps at the third receiver position throughout the season. His size, strength in his hands, and ability to generally win those contested catch situations are all standout traits. Brian Parker II was a sixth-round draft selection for the Bengals this year. He played mostly right tackle during his time at Duke. For the Bengals, he has moved almost exclusively to the interior so far in camp. The majority of his snaps against the Lions came at left guard, with a handful at center late in the game. I thought Parker looked really good, especially in pass protection. He has such a calm presence for a young lineman. He doesn’t panic, and he trusts his technique. He also has the athleticism to recover when it is needed. Brian Parker played mostly left guard last night, with some late playing time at center. It wouldn’t surprise me if he gets snaps at a couple other spots this preseason. pic.twitter.com/2kPf4auhLZ — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 14, 2026 Jack Endries showed up in the first preseason game after having a rather quiet camp beforehand. He finished the game with three catches for 25 yards. He also caught the Bengals’ lone touchdown of the game from Joe Flacco. Endries has been working on his blocking, both at Texas and now with the Bengals. While there is still work to be done, he has the chance to become a solid all-around tight end for this team. Jack Endries with the strong debut. Tight End continues to be one of the more interesting roster battles. I am finding a way to keep Endries in any scenario. pic.twitter.com/aH4zxYUZBR — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 16, 2026 I will toss in one more rookie performance, this one coming from an undrafted free agent. While only playing in nine snaps during the first preseason game, Corey Robinson II made the most of it. He looked athletic and played through the whistle. For an offensive lineman, that is exactly what you want to see out there. Robinson is likely a practice squad candidate to start the season, but certainly a player who may stick around if he continues to develop. Corey Robinson II looked good in limited snaps on Thursday against the Lions. pic.twitter.com/yqgjkVGUXz — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) August 16, 2026

title: Bengals Tuesday Trenches: Who’s safe, and who’s on the bubble?
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals’ first preseason game is in the books. They defeated the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium by a score of 16-14. Evan McPherson was money, and we got a good look at the starters. I’m not going to share my takes—they played on Thursday night, and anything I’m going to say has already […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals cornerback Tacario Davis (20) breaks up a pass intended for wide receiver Colbie Young (86) during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Cincinnati Bengals’ first preseason game is in the books. They defeated the Detroit Lions at Paycor Stadium by a score of 16-14. Evan McPherson was money, and we got a good look at the starters. I’m not going to share my takes—they played on Thursday night, and anything I’m going to say has already been said by better minds than mine. Instead, let’s take a look at who I think is definitely safe on the 53-man roster, and who still needs to fight for their right to wear stripes during the regular season. Offense Locks: 1 – WR Ja’Marr Chase 5 – WR Tee Higgins 9 – QB Joe Burrow 15 – WR Charlie Jones 16 – QB Joe Flacco 25 – HB Tahj Brooks 30 – HB Chase Brown 34 – HB Samaje Perine 60 – OT Cody Ford 63 – G Dylan Fairchild 64 – C Ted Karras 65 – C Connor Lew 66 – G Dalton Risner 71 – OT Amarius Mims 75 – OT Orlando Brown Jr. 80 – WR Andrei Iosivas 83 – TE Erick All Jr. 84 – TE Jack Endries 88 – TE Mike Gesicki 89 – TE Drew Sample Notes: This is pretty cut and dry, in my opinion. The Joe’s will be the quarterbacks. Chase, Higgins and Iosivas are locks, and I think Jones’ abilities as a return specialist add him to that list. Then we have the entire starting offensive line, but the only backups I’m willing to say are locks right now are Ford and Lew. Then at tight end, we have Gesicki and Sample, who are unique to their roster (the first as a pass catcher, and the latter as a blocker). All and Endries, I think, are the only other two locks at the position. Bubble Players: 4 – QB Sean Clifford 11 – QB Josh Johnson 12 – WR Ke’Shawn Williams 14 – WR Jordan Moore 17 – WR Noah Thomas 18 – WR Xavier Johnson 19 – WR Kendric Pryor 24 – HB Jamal Haynes 31 – HB Kentrel Bullock 32 – HB Gary Brightwell 36 – HB Kendall Milton 48 – TE Josh Kattus 59 – G Liam Brown 61 – G Brian Parker II 69 – C Jacob Bayer 73 – OT Javon Foster 74 – G Jalen Rivers 76 – OT Christian Jones 77 – G Corey Robinson II 79 – OT Andrew Coker 81 – WR Dohnte Meyers 82 – WR Mitch Tinsley 85 – TE Cam Grandy 86 – WR Colbie Young 87 – TE Tanner Hudson Notes: Some of these guys will definitely make the team, but I can’t confidently say any of them are 100% certain locks right now. At wide receiver, there are three guys, Meyers, Tinsley, and Young, fighting for the last two roster spots at that position. Along the offensive line, it’s hard to say how the backup line could take shape. Remember, they signed Risner really late in August. Who knows what players could be cut from other teams that the front office could see as a better fit than anyone on this list. Then at tight end, the big surprising name possibly here is Hudson because he’s been on the roster and has contributed pretty regularly over the last few seasons. The thing that’s different this season is All’s health. I’m not sure there’s room enough for five tight ends on this roster. Defense Locks: 0 – CB DJ Turner 6 – S Bryan Cook 20 – CB Tacario Davis 23 – CB Dax Hill 26 – CB Ja’Sir Taylor 27 – S Jordan Battle 29 – S Kyle Dugger 35 – CB Jalen Davis 38 – CB DJ Ivey 42 – LB Oren Burks 43 – LB Joe Giles-Harris 44 – LB Demetrius Knight Jr 49 – LB Barrett Carter 52 – DE Cedric Johnson 53 – DE Boye Mafe 55 – DE Cashius Howell 90 – DT Kris Jenkins Jr. 92 – DT BJ Hill 93 – DT Jonathan Allen 94 – DE Shemar Stewart 96 – DT Landon Robinson 97 – DT Dexter Lawrence II 98 – DT T.J. Slaton Jr. 99 – DE Myles Murphy Notes: The defensive line depth in 2026 is incredible compared to what it was in 2025. Lawrence and Allen are starting this year, and last year’s starters are this year’s backups. Having said all that, I think the defensive line has a lot of locks. Jenkins has flashed, and I really like what we’ve been able to see from rookie Landon Robinson. At linebacker, I think the foursome of Carter, Knight, Giles-Harris, and Burks are locks. I’m not sure if they’ll keep a fifth linebacker, but these four are in. Then in the secondary, the safety position has locks with Cook, Battle, and Dugger, but that fourth (and fifth?) spot is still up for grabs. The same goes for a couple of the backup cornerback positions. I think Ivey is a lock, as is Taylor, but beyond that, there are some openings. Bubble Players: 21 – CB Bralyn Lux 22 – CB Ceyair Wright 28 – CB Josh Newton 33 – S Daijahn Anthony 37 – S PJ Jules 39 – S Russ Yeast 40 – CB Jalen Kimber 45 – LB Liam Anderson 47 – LB Swayze Bozeman 50 – LB Shaka Heyward 51 – DE Isaiah Foskey 52 – DE Cedric Johnson 56 – DE Antwaun Powell-Ryland 57 – LB Eric Gentry 58 – LB Jack Dingle 68 – DT Jordan Jefferson 91 – DT McKinnley Jackson 95 – DT Howard Cross III Notes: Jackson, a former third-round pick, struggled to make the active roster throughout the year last season, and with all the depth on the line added this offseason, he’s probably going to be looking for a new home. What happens with Johnson depends on what happens with Stewart’s knee injury, but I’m not willing to call him a roster lock yet. At linebacker, it all comes down to whether or not they keep a fifth. Similarly, I wonder if the Bengals could possibly keep seven cornerbacks. Then at safety, I think that spot goes to either Anthony or Jules, whoever has the better camp. It’s also possible they could keep both, going for five safeties, but neither are locks like Cook, Battle or Dugger. The Bengals practice more privately this week as they prepare for their Preseason Week 2 game against the Bears at home. We’ll likely get another look at the starters, maybe more of them, and more tape on some of the guys whose positions aren’t etched in stone. full_text: Jan 15, 2023; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase (1) and quarterback Joe Burrow (9) warm up before an NFL wild-card playoff football game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Cincinnati Bengals during a wild card game at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kareem Elgazzar-USA TODAY Sports For its most recent Future Power Rankings , ESPN asked its panel of experts—Louis Riddick, Aaron Schatz, Ben Solak, and Seth Walder—to give grades for every NFL team’s QB situation, non-QB roster, front office, and coaching staff based on how good they’ll all be from 2027 to 2029. The results may surprise you slightly. The most promising future belongs to the Super Bowl champ Seattle Seahawks. The least promising future belongs to the Arizona Cardinals. The Cincinnati Bengals, meanwhile, fall just about in the middle at 17. The experts gave the Bengals high scores for QB (5th best) and overall roster (11th best), but considered them subpar in terms of coaching (23rd) and the front office (28th). Solak wrote that the Bengals have hope thanks to a healthier defense and offensive line, which have “reinvigorated” quarterback Joe Burrow. Riddick’s concern is that the Bengals’ defense won’t necessarily perform the way the team anticipated when they traded the 10th overall pick in the Draft for Dexter Lawrence. If it doesn’t, he predicts that “there could be major changes in Cincinnati on and off the field.” Schatz noted that Cincinnati has the NFL’s largest free agent class in terms of snaps for 2027, with DJ Turner, Dax Hill, Jordan Battle, Chase Brown, Samaje Perine, Ted Karras, and Dalton Risner all due new contracts. Finally, Walder’s bold prediction is that Erick All Jr. will finish in the top five in receiving yards for tight ends in one of the seasons from 2027 to 2029. Meanwhile, the Pittsburgh Steelers are predicted to have the 30th most promising future in the league, the Cleveland Browns the 28th, and the Baltimore Ravens the 9th. title: Browns: Dylan Sampson is ‘electric with the ball.’ Even with this flaw.
summary: The Cleveland Browns have had some familiar names showcasing their talents in the passing game coming out of the backfield.  From Bobby Mitchell (a team-high 45 receptions and six touchdowns in 1960) through Greg Pruitt (No. 20 on the franchise’s all-time list for receptions) and Calvin Hill (six receiving touchdowns in 1978 and 1980), Earnest […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 10: Dylan Sampson #22 of the Cleveland Browns catches a pass during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 10, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have had some familiar names showcasing their talents in the passing game coming out of the backfield. From Bobby Mitchell (a team-high 45 receptions and six touchdowns in 1960) through Greg Pruitt (No. 20 on the franchise’s all-time list for receptions) and Calvin Hill (six receiving touchdowns in 1978 and 1980), Earnest Byner (No. 15 on the franchise’s all-time list for receptions), and Duke Johnson (a team-record for running backs with 74 receptions in 2017), the Browns have found ways to incorporate running backs into the passing game successfully. The latest player looking to join that group is second-year running back Dylan Sampson, who was third on the team with 33 receptions and a team-long 66-yard reception. Dylan Sampson goes for 43 yards 😤 CLEvsCHI on @nflnetwork Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/Km6FWPu6wD — NFL (@NFL) August 15, 2026 Sampson flashed his ability in Saturday’s preseason game against the Chicago Bears when he ripped off a 43-yard catch-and-run, which is the type of play the coaches want to see from him, according to head coach Todd Monken : “Well, he’s electric with the ball in his hands. So how do we get (the ball) to him? I think, over time, he’s going to be a guy that’s a tough matchup … when he gets matched up on a linebacker, it will be an advantage for us. I think he has that in him. So, there’s a lot there to like, now as we get to practice and get into games.” If there is one thing holding Sampson back, it may be his pass-blocking ability. Last season, both Sampson (Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of 23) and Quinshon Judkins (PFF grade of 19.1) struggled in that area, and it is something that Monken is waiting to see improvement from in Sampson : “Can he hold up in protection? That’s the biggest thing. Because it’s one thing to say you’re a matchup. It’s another to say, OK, how am I going to hold up when I’ve got to protect a blitzing linebacker, a safety off the edge? (Baltimore safety) Kyle Hamilton comes off the edge, and we need you to really stick him. That’s where it’ll come down to.” While that could be seen as a detriment, Monken views it as yet another opportunity to coach up his players to get the best out of them : “Well, our job is to find out what our players do really well, what do they lead at? They made it to the NFL because of a trait that they had. Now, how do we develop and round out their skill set? That’s what coaching and development are about. “So, how are we able to get players with an elite skill set to do what they do best without being so tendency-oriented that that’s all you do when they’re in? Does that make sense? How do you get them in your rotation and utilize them in a way that allows you to function at a really high level? And that’s what I really like about Samp. I think he’s going to be an explosive player. You just got to get him in space.” Sampson, along with rookie wide receiver KC Concepcion, gives Monken some opportunities to exploit the defense and help out the league’s worst quarterback room in the process. With any luck, that long catch-and-run from Sampson won’t be the last time he makes a defense look foolish this season.

title: 10 options for the new “Face of the Browns”
summary: Anytime you see a network plug an upcoming NFL game, they always display a featured player as part of the enticement to get viewers. Usually, it is the quarterback since that is normally the most recognized face on their team. Teams like the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills are an easy sale with the […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - DECEMBER 28: Harold Fannin Jr. #44 and Shedeur Sanders #12 of the Cleveland Browns react after a touchdown pass during the first quarter of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Huntington Bank Field on December 28, 2025 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Anytime you see a network plug an upcoming NFL game, they always display a featured player as part of the enticement to get viewers. Usually, it is the quarterback since that is normally the most recognized face on their team. Teams like the Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills are an easy sale with the photos of Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, respectively. RELATED: BROWNS QB BATTLE UPDATE Sometimes, the networks will show a trio of guys so that they can feature other players who usually are the ones who score points. But for an upcoming Cleveland Browns telecast, that was always All-World EDGE rusher Myles Garrett, a defensive athlete. Yes, defenders have been featured before, but for any Browns enticement, it has been Garrett since he came into the league in 2017 as the first overall selection in the NFL Draft. And as Browns fans, we all know he was involved in a trade to the Los Angeles Rams this offseason. Which means the “Face of the Browns” is empty. Who should replace him? Let’s examine some candidates. QB Deshaun Watson Well, certainly the quarterback for the franchise should be considered. However, Watson hasn’t been named the starting quarterback for the 2026 season. Yet. Or at all. But if he does win the starting QB position, which is currently expected, he will need to find that former self when he was an absolute stud while at Clemson and in his first four seasons in the NFL with the Houston Texans. He earned three consecutive Pro Bowls and threw for 4,823 yards with 33 touchdowns to just 7 interceptions in 2020 on a team that only won four games. Since coming to Cleveland, Watson has only played in 19 games and has missed 33 due to suspensions and various injuries. His play has been below average and has yet to show the talent he displayed with the Texans when he was a Top-5 signal-caller in this league. In order to become “The Face” of the Browns, he will need to ball out and play at a Pro Bowl level all season. Then again, the franchise just might decide that his reputation off the field would be just too much for their fanbase. Browns’ fans either like Deshaun or despise him. None of them love him. And never will, even if he took Cleveland to the promised land. The Cleveland Browns need to name Shedeur Sanders their starting QB. This Shedeur Sanders’ play from training camp shows 3 things: 1. His command of the offense at the line of scrimmage and cerebral part of his game 2. His calmness under pressure 3. He’s won the locker room pic.twitter.com/zzmJGNskSU — Robert Griffin III (@RGIII) August 4, 2026 QB Shedeur Sanders Another quarterback whose fanbase either absolutely loves him, is frustrated by him, or is a hater. He too is in the running for the starting job this year. His naysayers state he needs more development and only started in college because his dad was the head coach. His teams never won a conference title and only played in one bowl game, in which they were blown out. Sanders’ followers adore him and believe he is the next superstar QB in the league, a cross between Michael Vick, Tom Brady, and Johnny Unitas all rolled into one player. He will need a great showing in the final two preseason games while being inserted into Cleveland’s first-team offense against the opponent’s first-team defense. If he is indeed this superstar in waiting, perhaps becoming “The Face” of the franchise is feasible. But for now, he has to win the starting job, then play at an elite level. WR Jerry Jeudy Everyone loves the guys who catch passes and score touchdowns. These players can perform electric plays and, of course, advance the scoreboard. In college, Jeudy was all of this: National Champion, All-American, two-time First Team All-SEC, and won the Biletnikoff Award. His professional career has been a roller coaster. He came to the Browns in a trade and then proceeded to gain 1,229 yards on 90 receptions with a staggering 145 targets, plus earned a Pro Bowl nod. But then last year, his production was cut in half; he scored only a pair of TDs, his average receiving yards per game dipped to 36.8 yards, plus he tied for the league lead in dropped passes with 10. He had 13 drops the year before and 41 for his career. If Jeudy had had a great season last year in consecutive seasons, he just might have become the default new face of the Browns. As it is now, he is playing in his contract year and will need to have an excellent year in order to be considered for a new deal. RB Quinshon Judkins Now, we’re talking. The new Browns head coach called Judkins a bull, and he definitely runs like one. The issue with Judkins is that he is only in his second season with Cleveland and missed games last year due to a holdout and injuries. If Q were to bust out to say, 1,400 yards rushing, with numerous goal-line touchdowns, then he would certainly be in the running. And in Monken’s new offense, it does feature the run. But all of that needs to happen first. View this post on Instagram TE Harold Fannin, Jr. It is conceivable for a tight end to gather the limelight. Look at Travis Kelce with the Chiefs, Trey McBride of the Arizona Cardinals, and George Kittle with the San Francisco 49ers. They show their tight ends frequently as featured players. And Fannin is more of a large receiver than a traditional tight end. He has the background to become a league leader, as he led the nation in receiving yards (1,555) and receptions (117) in his senior year of college. His numbers were decent as a rookie, with 107 targets, 72 receptions for 731 yards, 32 first-down conversions, and six touchdowns. But Kelce has had six seasons where he gained over 1,000-yards. He owns 11 Pro Bowls. Like Judkins, Fannin has only been in the league one year and will need to get a ton of production as a sophomore, and then let’s talk. The WR Twins If rookie receivers KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston bust out and dominate games, we can see, at some point in their rookie year, the franchise as well as the TV networks featuring them. However, this isn’t college. NFL cornerbacks are great on every team the Browns will face. In an 11-game college schedule, both of these rookies may have faced four cornerbacks who were exceptional. That left a lot of contests for stat padding. Put a pin in it and let’s discuss this before next season. LG Zion Johnson If Joe Thomas can be “The Face,” then another offensive lineman can become the icon as well, right? But why Johnson? He is replacing LG Joel Bitonio. His mission this year is to not have to be compared repeatedly to one of the greatest Browns’ linemen in franchise history. Plus, with the five new offensive linemen, he is the only one who hasn’t been injured and missed any practice or playing time. Doesn’t durability get any votes? LB Carson Schwesinger The rookie linebacker certainly has plenty of cred going into his second season. Being named to the “NFL All-Rookie Team” and winning a league award such as the “NFL Defensive Player of the Year” is a terrific beginning to his career. This just might be our man. “The Face” has been a defender for quite some time, and perhaps Schwesinger can just slide into the position. Then again, perhaps a wait-and-see agenda needs to come first. There have been a lot of really great rookie campaigns followed by mediocre play in NFL history. In 1981, the New Orleans Saints selected RB George Rogers of South Carolina with the first overall draft pick. He ran for 1,674 yards, averaged 104.6 yards per game, was named “NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year,” voted First Team All-Pro, and earned a Pro Bowl. Four years later, he was traded for a fifth, seventh, and 11th-round draft picks and played just three…

title: Browns starting offensive line all but set; is it the right starting 5?
summary: Significant changes were made this offseason to revamp the Cleveland Browns’ offensive line and put out a better product on the field. With several competitions happening in training camp and the preseason, it will be interesting to see where these positions net out starting in Week 1 against the Jacksonville Jaguars.  Left Tackle: Spencer Fano […]
full_text: Significant changes were made this offseason to revamp the Cleveland Browns’ offensive line and put out a better product on the field. With several competitions happening in training camp and the preseason, it will be interesting to see where these positions net out starting in Week 1 against the Jacksonville Jaguars . Left Tackle: Spencer Fano The ninth pick in the draft is the obvious answer at left tackle. It won’t be a perfect situation as the transition to the NFL can be challenging, but Fano is the obvious starter at the position. Left Guard: Zion Johnson Johnson comes into this season with four years of experience under his belt with the Los Angeles Chargers. He is virtually a lock to start at the position and will bring some much-needed experience to the offensive line. Center: Elgton Jenkins Jenkins has experience at a range of positions across the offensive line, but given where the Browns need the most help right now, he will likely start at Center. His versatility is a major asset for the team, giving them the flexibility to move him around and fill different positions as needed. Right Guard: Teven Jenkins Jenkins is the choice that makes the most sense at right guard. He played in Cleveland in 2026, so given his history with the organization, it makes sense to have him start the year. KT Leveston is the other option right now. Right Tackle: Tytus Howard Howard joined the Browns in a trade with the Houston Texans and is a fairly easy choice to start at right tackle. He is another player who brings valuable experience and reliability to the position. Let me know what you think in the comments – Who should be the Browns’ starting 5 on the offensive line? title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 26
summary: It is Day 26 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: Dallas Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott (4) during the NFC wild-card NFL football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Seattle Seahawks in Arlington, Texas, Saturday, Jan. 5, 2019. (Photo by Tom Hauck/Getty Images) | Getty Images It is Day 26 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Here we go for Day 26 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, when we revisit the playoff victory that gave the Cowboys’ young core something tangible to believe in. Dallas leaned on Ezekiel Elliott, a physical defensive performance and Dak Prescott’s late determination to defeat the Seattle Seahawks in the Wild Card Round. Saturday, January 5, 2019 AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 24, Seattle Seahawks 22 In the 2019 season, the Cowboys had recovered from a 3-5 start to finish 10-6, win the NFC East and earn a home playoff game. Seattle had beaten Dallas 24-13 earlier in the season, but this rematch looked very different. The Cowboys were more settled offensively following the arrival of Amari Cooper, while their young defense had developed into one of the team’s greatest strengths. Dallas opened the scoring with Brett Maher’s 39-yard field goal. Seattle answered during the second quarter with Sebastian Janikowski field goals from 27 and 42 yards, moving ahead 6-3. The Cowboys reclaimed the lead shortly before halftime when Prescott found Michael Gallup for an 11-yard touchdown, completing a 75-yard drive and sending Dallas into the break ahead 10-6. The Seahawks moved back in front during the third quarter. Russell Wilson scored on a four-yard option run before Mike Davis converted the two-point attempt, giving Seattle a 14-10 advantage. The Cowboys responded early in the fourth when Elliott powered across the goal line from one yard out, putting Dallas back ahead 17-14. Dallas had a chance to create separation after Tavon Austin’s 51-yard punt return, but Prescott’s pass for Noah Brown was intercepted by K.J. Wright in the end zone. Instead of allowing the mistake to change the game, the Cowboys’ defense forced another stop and gave Prescott an opportunity to finish the job. The defining moment came on third-and-14 from Seattle’s 17-yard line. Prescott escaped through the middle, lowered his shoulder and flipped over a defender before being brought down at the one. He scored on a quarterback keeper on the following play, completing an 11-play drive that consumed more than five minutes and put Dallas ahead 24-14 with 2:08 remaining. Seattle refused to disappear. Wilson completed a 53-yard pass to Tyler Lockett before finding J.D. McKissic for a seven-yard touchdown. Chris Carson ran in the two-point conversion, reducing Dallas’ lead to 24-22 with 1:18 left. Seattle then attempted an unusual onside drop kick, but Cole Beasley secured it and allowed the Cowboys to run out the clock. This game belongs on the countdown because it represented the first postseason breakthrough for the Prescott-and-Elliott core. Dallas had developed a young roster capable of winning through defense, rushing efficiency and quarterback toughness. Prescott’s fearless third-down run became the lasting image of a victory that gave the group credibility and renewed belief that it could compete deep into January. #Cowboys vs #Seahawks 2018 Wildcard Round Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 24, Seattle Seahawks 22 #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/aqJfNmw8WJ — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) August 18, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game Elliott accumulated 169 yards from scrimmage on 30 touches, including 137 rushing yards against a Seattle defence built to make opponents play physically. title: Cowboys RB battle: Malik Davis is doing what he always does
summary: The Dallas Cowboys first preseason game at the Seattle Seahawks made it clear who this offseason’s “pet cat” at wide receiver is, with Camden Brown hauling in two acrobatic touchdowns, but didn’t nearly provide the same clarity about the direction this team will go in the backfield beyond returning veteran starter Javonte Williams. Jaydon Blue […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys first preseason game at the Seattle Seahawks made it clear who this offseason’s “pet cat” at wide receiver is, with Camden Brown hauling in two acrobatic touchdowns, but didn’t nearly provide the same clarity about the direction this team will go in the backfield beyond returning veteran starter Javonte Williams. Jaydon Blue led the team in carries with eight but had the fewest rushing yards out of the RB group. Malik Davis and Israel Abanikanda both had seven carries, the former for a team-high 39 yards and latter for 36. Phil Mafah tried to get in on the action as well with his four carries, but then exited due to injury. Dallas was off on Sunday when they returned to Oxnard, and then got back to work on Monday ahead of another joint practice/scrimmage opportunity against old friend Kellen Moore and the New Orleans Saints. In their first practice since the preseason win, it was reported that, seemingly based on what happened in that game, the Cowboys were going to adjust the depth chart accordingly and distribute reps differently. Some shaking up is coming to the Cowboys depth chart in today’s practice, per HC Brian Schottenheimer: “We’ve made some adjustments. We’re creating competition, and you guys will see some of those today. All of the guys have been informed of why we’re making those decisions.… pic.twitter.com/dqYx5GQw1o — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 17, 2026 Even well before an announcement like this was made by head coach Brian Schottenheimer, the reps and competition at running back has been closely monitored. The team is not looking for a new starter here with Javonte Williams back as the steady hand after a career year in 2025, and in the bigger picture are still positioned to have all 11 of last year’s offensive starters back in those roles. This makes the playing time behind Williams in a RB2 or RB3 role one of the very few areas the Cowboys could have a new wrinkle in personnel on offense going into 2026. The fan-favorite player to see this playing time has been the year-two draft pick Blue, because on any given snap he has big-play potential that can create more game-breaking plays for this explosive offense. The best thing Blue did in this department against the Seahawks was take one of two screen pass attempts for 13 yards on the drive that ended in a field goal. Not only were Blue’s rushing attempts a bit disappointing in Seattle though, unfortunately he also didn’t have a chance to continue getting valuable reps at Monday’s practice as he was out of team drills with a shoulder injury. This positioned Malik Davis to do something he seemingly always finds a way to do since joining the team in 2022 and bouncing back and forth ever since. Take full advantage of the chance to get on the field, just like he did in the preseason test, and practice Monday as the primary backup to Williams. Some observations on how reps were split today in Cowboys camp: – Joe Milton QB2 – Malik Davis was the first running back to rotate in after Javonte Williams. Blue did not participate in the team period (shoulder) while Mafah (ribs) and Abanikanda (ribs) were limited – Devin… https://t.co/DEw71RAivD — Nick Harris (@NickHarrisFWST) August 17, 2026 Davis also benefited from both Mafah and Abanikanda being limited, but to say injuries in total were the only reason Davis saw these reps would also not be fair. The idea of a running back duo that complements each other with different skills is a fun one that fans still want to see manifest itself, but proven results trump all, and the Cowboys are seeing for the second year in a row of this offense that physical running between the tackles is still their best approach at the position. Davis does this well, with plus burst and decisiveness at the line of scrimmage to make something out of nothing on many of his carries. This was a strength of Mafah’s as well earlier in camp, a real year-two development for the 2025 seventh-round pick to feel good about, but just for the moment the arrow is pointing down on Mafah as camp grinds on and the Clemson product has to fight his way back into the mix. The burst, the speed, the vision! Malik Davis is RB2 pic.twitter.com/tpvzZY8qTP — Shane ☃️ (@MakeItR4yne) August 17, 2026 Projecting further down the line just for fun at the moment, let’s say Williams and Davis are the 1-2 punch at running back going into week one at the Giants. This duo may not light up the fantasy football score sheets or have a lot of casual fans fired up about what the Cowboys can bring out of the backfield, but it stands to be effective anyway. The Dallas defense showed glimpses against the Seahawks of being the type of defense built to protect leads, a notion that got even more true after the team formally signed Von Miller on Monday as well. Besides the obvious of scoring points, the next best thing an offense can do to complement this type of defense (one that pitched a three and a half quarter shutout on Saturday) is control the clock and tempo of a game with their rushing attack. Running between the tackles also gets a whole lot easier once defenses have to respect the perimeter threats of George Pickens, CeeDee Lamb, and Ryan Flournoy, and right now the Cowboys depth at RB is sorting itself out when it comes to which players do this best, and most consistently. Having Williams is a great start in this department for the Cowboys, and if things keep going how they are in the RB competition beyond him, they’ll be looking up even more as Davis continues to capitalize on opportunity, and hopefully Mafah and Abanikanda get healthy. The Cowboys offense will be out to prove against the Saints they’re in a better overall place than when Kellen Moore left them as the Saints come marching in on Tuesday, making this an even bigger day than Monday to keep an eye on what happens at the running back position.
author: Sean Martin

title: Predicting Cowboys’ OLB depth chart after Von Miller addition
summary: Von Miller, a Desoto native and Texas A&M legend, is now living out his dream to play for his hometown team, the Dallas Cowboys, after signing a one-year, $5.5 million deal that could max out to $7.5 million if built-in incentives are met. While adding Von Miller to the mix isn’t the “substantive” trade many […]
full_text: Von Miller, a Desoto native and Texas A&M legend, is now living out his dream to play for his hometown team, the Dallas Cowboys, after signing a one-year, $5.5 million deal that could max out to $7.5 million if built-in incentives are met. Source: Von Miller’s deal with the Cowboys is for one year, $5.5 million. With contract incentives, it has a maximum value of $7.5 million — Jon Machota (@jonmachota) August 17, 2026 While adding Von Miller to the mix isn’t the “substantive” trade many of us have been anticipating to upgrade the pass rush, his addition helps. The 37-year-old proved last year he still has plenty left in the tank with a nine QB sack season in 2025 and that kind of production is something the Cowboys can definitely use more of. Miller brings a wealth of experience and production with him to Dallas as well as a résumé that will make him a first ballot future Hall of Famer in the not-too-distant future. 2x Super Bowl champion 7x All-Pro 8x Pro Bowler 203 games 138.5 sacks 27 forced fumbles 9 fumble recoveries Dallas ! Let’s make this one Special ! 😈 pic.twitter.com/STWZiqBLij — Von Miller (@VonMiller) August 17, 2026 Von Miller certainly seems to be excited about playing for the Cowboys this year and we should as well. He may not be the player he once was, but he helps stabilize the position and upgrades things from a depth standpoint. The only question now is how many OLBs Dallas will carry on the roster and who makes the cut? The guess here is the Dallas Cowboys will carry six OLBs on the active 53-man roster this season with a couple more on the practice squad to be called up when/if needed. As things stand right now, we have Rashan Gary and Donovan Ezeiruaku as the starter’s with Malachi Lawrence and now Von Miller as the primary backups. That leaves two spots up for grabs. Outside the top four, we have James Houston securing a roster spot as the fifth OLB on the depth chart right now. He’s played well since signing with the Cowboys as a free agent last year and provides special teams value as well, playing 37.19% of Dallas’ special teams snaps last year. With his spot likely secured, that leaves one undecided. The Cowboys other current options to claim the final OLB roster spot are Sam Williams, a former 2022 second-round pick, and Marist Liufau, a third-round pick in 2024. Tyrus Wheat and Isiah Land are also hoping to crash the party. Williams is more of a prototypical OLB by NFL standards, but Liufau has the potential position flex to play off-ball or outside LB. Between the two, the better special teams player could win out. Both Williams and Liufau have proven their special teams value with the Cowboys over the years. The former played 29.55% of the special teams snaps last year while the latter played 74.59%. Based on this and No. 35’s position flex, we predict Liufau as the edge over Williams to round out Dallas’ OLB position this year, leaving No. 54 then as Dallas’ best trade candidate. Final OLB depth chart prediction Rashan Gary Donovan Ezeiruaku Malachi Lawrence Von Miller James Houston Marist Liufau Hit the comments and let us know your OLB depth chart after the Von Miller signing.

title: Cowboys secondary already looks nothing like last year
summary: Yes, it’s just one preseason game. Yes, most of the players on the field against the Seahawks on Sunday won’t make the 53-man roster. Yes, individual preseason stats mean next to nothing when the regular season rolls around. But you can’t just ignore what happens in these preseason games either. One interesting stat that popped […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - AUGUST 15: Ameer Speed #39 of the Dallas Cowboys high fives Caelen Carson #21 during the first quarter during the NFL preseason game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on August 15, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jack Compton/Getty Images) | Getty Images Yes, it’s just one preseason game. Yes, most of the players on the field against the Seahawks on Sunday won’t make the 53-man roster. Yes, individual preseason stats mean next to nothing when the regular season rolls around. But you can’t just ignore what happens in these preseason games either. One interesting stat that popped after the game ( per Bobby Belt) was the fact that the Cowboys had 19 missed tackles in last year’s preseason opener. On Sunday, Next Gen Stats charted the Cowboys with zero missed tackles. Will that carry over into the regular season? Who knows. But is it indicative of an improved defensive performance? Probably. The same applies to defensive passer rating, which is a good proxy for the performance of the pass defense. On Sunday, the Cowboys allowed a defensive passer rating of just 88.8. That’s almost 12 points lower than what they allowed in last year’s preseason opener, but more importantly, it’s lower than what the team allowed in all but one of its regular-season games last year. The Cowboys allowed a 109.6 defensive passer rating in 2025, the worst mark in the league. Sunday’s 88.8 rating is almost 21 points lower than last year’s average and would have ranked the Cowboys 13th in the league last season. And the difference wasn’t limited to one player. Here’s what the Seahawks passing game looked like by pass direction and distance: The Seahawks weren’t exactly attacking the Cowboys vertically. Drew Lock and Jalen Milroe didn’t test the Cowboys secondary deep very often, and when they did, they weren’t particularly successful. That obviously comes with a massive caveat: we’re dealing with a very small sample size here, and neither Seattle nor Dallas played most of their established starters. Still, the lack of explosive passing plays shows up in the individual defensive passer ratings as well. And it wasn’t just the cornerbacks. Where last year’s Cowboys safeties averaged a 134.6 DPR, the five safeties who played against Seattle were targeted just once — an incompletion — producing a combined DPR of 39.6.
