title: It’s time for the Packers to let Jordan Love rip it
summary: After years of maintaining a balanced offensive attack, it’s time for the Green Bay Packers and Matt LaFleur’s offensive staff to let Jordan Love air it out in 2026. Over the last two seasons, the Packers have operated one of the more run-focused offenses in football. Last season, they ranked fifth in the NFL with […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 12: Head coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers talks with Jordan Love #10 during a timeout in the fourth quarter in the game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Lambeau Field on October 12, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images After years of maintaining a balanced offensive attack, it’s time for the Green Bay Packers and Matt LaFleur’s offensive staff to let Jordan Love air it out in 2026. Over the last two seasons, the Packers have operated one of the more run-focused offenses in football. Last season, they ranked fifth in the NFL with a run called on 50.2 percent of offensive plays, down slightly from third in the league in 2024 at 52.3 percent. A young, developing quarterback combined with the arrival of Josh Jacobs likely played factors in that decision making process. After all, Jacobs was two years removed from leading the NFL in rushing before arriving in Green Bay, and he has taken on a heavy workload with 30 total touchdowns in his two years with the Packers. However, Jacobs started to show signs of wear and tear this past season, and despite ranking fifth in rush rate, the Packers ranked just 22nd in rushing DVOA . That efficiency isn’t likely to bounce back in 2026, either. While MarShawn Lloyd is on track for his first healthy season as a backup, Jacobs is now a 28-year-old running back with over 1,800 professional carries, not to mention a potential suspension coming before the start of the regular season that would deal a major blow to Green Bay’s rushing attack. Even if the Packers were expecting Jacobs to be ready for a bounce-back season, that shouldn’t take away from the fact that Love is ready to take charge and start ramping up Green Bay’s passing volume. Love solidified himself as a big-play hunter with surprising efficiency in 2025, posting his best season in three years as a starter with a 101.2 passer rating, 23 touchdowns, and just six interceptions. In fact, Love was behind only Drake Maye among quarterbacks with 0.29 EPA per play (min. 200 pass attempts). A reminder that Jordan Love is good at football. pic.twitter.com/fXo1qeVfq7 — Tyler Brooke (@TylerDBrooke) August 18, 2026 Love’s supporting cast of weapons should also give him a significant boost, provided that all of them can stay healthy. Tucker Kraft looked like the best tight end in the NFL last season before a torn ACL, but is expected to be ready to go for Week 1. Meanwhile, Christian Watson established himself as a legitimate WR1 after returning from a torn ACL last season, and Jayden Reed should be back fully healthy to take control of the slot role in the offense. Even Matthew Golden is looking to make a huge leap forward in Year 2 now that the WR room has become significantly less crowded due to the departures of Romeo Doubs and Dontayvion Wicks. While the number of weapons has decreased in this offense, Love mentioned in training camp that the clearly defined roles for their starting receivers should help with timing and chemistry heading into 2026. A week into camp, Jordan Love believes working mostly with Christian Watson, Jayden Reed and Matthew Golden has accelerated their timing. Something he couldn’t do a year ago with WR depth. “You build trust and understanding of where guys are going to be and how things time up.” pic.twitter.com/07108wucHh — Ryan Wood (@ByRyanWood) August 6, 2026 That timing and chemistry has already been flashing in training camp, but it especially did so during Family Night. The Jordan Love and Matthew Golden connection is going feed families. #Packers pic.twitter.com/CvMysIf0jS — Kyle Malzhan (@KyleMalzhan) August 8, 2026 There are still questions about Green Bay’s offense, particularly on the offensive line. However, if Jordan Morgan can hold down the left tackle spot and the guard spots can get figured out, this offense has a chance to take a big leap forward in 2026. But that doesn’t happen unless the Packers let Love air it out and put the league on notice that he’s one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL.
author: Tyler Brooke

title: Which Packers players could play surprisingly big roles in 2026?
summary: Every year, NFL teams need to rely on unheralded depth players to fill in at big moments. Sometimes, these players need to step up all season long due to early injuries — just think about the 2010 Packers going running back-by-committee, seeing Desmond Bishop take over a starting linebacker spot, or getting 8 starts and […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 10: Josh Whyle #81 of the Green Bay Packers looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lambeau Field on November 10, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Every year, NFL teams need to rely on unheralded depth players to fill in at big moments. Sometimes, these players need to step up all season long due to early injuries — just think about the 2010 Packers going running back-by-committee, seeing Desmond Bishop take over a starting linebacker spot, or getting 8 starts and 4 sacks out of undrafted rookie Frank Zombo. Other times, it’s just a fill-in here and there in big moments, like in 2018 when a gassed Jimmy Graham came off the field for the Packers in Seattle and an unknown Robert Tonyan hauled in a 54-yard touchdown in his place. Those opportunities can be jumping-off points for these players as they look to grab hold of bigger roles moving forward. In either case, injuries or rest will force the Packers to lean on their depth and put surprising names in play in big situations. With a look ahead to the 2026 regular season, here are three players whose names are a ways down the depth chart who Packers fans should know now in preparation for them making a big impact later on this fall. Josh Whyle The Packers’ tight end room feels about as deep as the kiddie pool right now. Tucker Kraft is the unquestioned starter and, thanks to his return to 11-on-11 drills on Sunday, he’s well on track to being the starter in week one, which is still three-and-a-half weeks away. But behind him, Luke Musgrave remains on the PUP list with a mysterious neck injury, making Whyle the top backup at the position. Throughout his Packers tenure, Whyle has played mostly the H position, the “move” tight end that ends up on the wing or in the backfield. However, circumstances will require him to play a bit more in line than he has become accustomed to. Musgrave’s injury is a big part of that — he has typically been Kraft’s backup at the Y — but Kraft also acknowledged after Sunday’s practice that he’ll be on a bit of a restricted snap count. That means that Whyle is the next man up, unless Musgrave surprisingly returns before the start of the regular season and is ready to go. Whyle has generally been running with the starting offense all summer anyway, so he has had plenty of time to get in sync with Jordan Love and company. He’s also no stranger to at least a moderate role on an offense, having been on the field for nearly 350 offensive snaps for the Titans in 2024. (That season, he caught 28 passes for 248 yards and a touchdown.) If Kraft will be held to something like two-thirds of offensive snaps, rather than his usual 90 percent, that could be an extra 20 snaps per game or so that would need to go to someone else, and Whyle is clearly the next man up. Kitan Oladapo Johnathan Baldwin’s injury in training camp put the Packers in quite a bind. Javon Bullard is entrenched as the team’s starting nickel back, but Baldwin was running as his backup through the first two weeks of camp. Now, that role appears to be falling to Oladapo. Like Bullard, Oladapo is a safety by trade. Unlike Bullard, he had never really played in the slot before being drafted by the Packers, and in fact only ever started getting a few reps there last year in the dime package. A bigger, physical safety, Oladapo has good-but-not-great movement skills; contrast that with Bullard, who put up an elite time in the short shuttle drill (3.97 seconds) in pre-draft testing. These are two very different types of players at that spot, and the concern arises about what the team would do there if Bullard has to miss any time with an injury. To make Oladapo’s importance even greater, he is likely the next man up at both safety positions as well. This Packers team will likely put Xavier McKinney, Evan Williams, and Javon Bullard all on the field for at least half of their defensive snaps this season; if any one of them gets banged up, Oladapo should be the next man up. Donovan Jennings Plenty of electrons have been used posting about the Packers’ machinations on the offensive line. Aaron Banks is in and out of the lineup with injuries; Anthony Belton can’t seem to settle in at one position; right guard is up for grabs in a battle that likely involves Jacob Monk and Jager Burton as well. But while all of those names are making headlines, Jennings is quietly waiting in the wings for a depth role on this team. The Packers originally signed Jennings as an undrafted free agent out of South Florida in 2024, and he spent the entirety of his rookie year on the team’s practice squad. Last year, he stuck around on the 53-man roster as the team’s 10th offensive lineman, but he only appeared in two games, totaling 13 snaps (6 on offense, 7 on special teams). Such has been the career trajectory of many a Packers offensive lineman, however. Players like Yosh Nijman and Lucas Patrick followed a similar path over their first two years, only to become multi-year starters. Jennings might not be in the thick of the battle for a starting job in 2026, but he lined up at right guard with the #2 line last Thursday in Pittsburgh and projects as a potential backup all across the interior of the line. Don’t be surprised if the Packers need to lean on him to close out a couple of games or even make a few spot starts in 2026 should injuries strike.
author: Evan "Tex" Western

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 1: Jordan Love
summary: The Packers lost to the Steelers in their first preseason by the score of something-to-something. It’s preseason. The final score does not matter. There are two main things I truly care about when it comes to preseason:1. Were there any injuries?2. How did the players look on an individual basis? Point 2 is a little […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 13: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers throws against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the first half at Acrisure Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers lost to the Steelers in their first preseason by the score of something-to-something. It’s preseason. The final score does not matter. There are two main things I truly care about when it comes to preseason: 1. Were there any injuries? 2. How did the players look on an individual basis? Point 2 is a little more complicated than that (finding individual performance in a team game isn’t always cut-and-dry), but those are the main focal points. So we’re going to do a few mini-posts on individual players from the preseason. We’re starting with an easy one: Jordan Love. It’s easy because, as a starter, Love didn’t really get a lot of playing time. He got 5 dropbacks in the passing game, going 3/5 for 18 yards. The main goal at this point is basically to get the ball out quickly, and he did that. Let’s just roll through the dropbacks real quick, shall we? Dropback 1 Three-step out-breaker to Christian Watson. Love was money on these last year to the point where it felt like the entire offense was built out of these at times. The timing/placement here is off and the throw sails wide. When the Packers were running these last year, the routes at this depth were typically off motion. From a static alignment, it was usually a deeper route. It’s possible they’re looking to lean a bit more into an Oops, All Out-Breakers offense to all levels of the field. It’d be nice to see automatic timing here, so I assume this is something they’ll be working on. Dropback 2 This was the longest Love held the ball all day. We’ve got stop routes on the outside with Christian Watson and Matthew Golden, and Jayden Reed is running a crosser from the slot. It’s originally a 2×2 formation, but Josh Whyle shifts before the snap to the right, making it a 3×1 Trips formation. A defender follows Whyle across the formation, giving Love a Man coverage tell. With Reed running a crosser to Golden’s side – and the Steelers showing Man coverage – the read essentially becomes the same you’d see in Slant/Flat. Love waits for Whyle’s defender to clear the middle, then fires to Reed in the middle. There is still one man that needs to be held in place. Patrick Queen [6] is in the middle of the field, watching Love. Love doesn’t give anything away. He’s looking right and doesn’t come back to the middle of the field until he’s ready to throw. That keeps Queen pinned to the middle, allowing Reed clear the middle. Well done by Love to hold that window open. Dropback 3 The Packers are using Hank, a quick-game staple. Golden runs the hitch from the outside while Whyle runs a flat underneath. Love hits the top of his drop and hits Whyle for a minimal gain. This is a quick-game staple, so getting the quick read/timing down on this is important. My hope is that that Packers lean more into the passing game this year and if they do that, using quick-game to replace some of the running game would be a nice way to do that. If you’re going to do that, timing on these is important. Dropback 4 Here we have MarShawn Lloyd on a WR screen. You’ll see this as part of the Packers RPO game, but, with Lloyd motioning to create an empty formation, this is basically a predetermined read. Matthew Golden is running a slant on the backside — Golden at the X! — so that’s an option if Love wants it. Unless it’s a super-clean pre-snap look, Love isn’t going to Golden on this. The only thing I’m really concerned with here is Christian Watson getting blown up on the block on the outside. Watson is a willing blocker — and can be a very good one — but he hasn’t been quite the same over the last couple years. He’s still above average in terms of a WR, but he loses or misses more than I would like lately. With the departure of Doubs and Wicks, the WR room has gotten smaller, meaning more of the WR blocking heavy lifting may ride on Watson’s shoulders. If he’s not quite the blocker he once was, that would give me some concern. I’m certainly not hitting the panic button — everybody has bad reps, after all — but it’s something to monitor early in the season. Dropback 5 Verts and Love looking to get the ball out on 3 steps. He has a choice of Love, Watson or Reed, but, with a single-high safety, Reed is the right decision. There’s good coverage on the play, with the defender playing over the top, so Love goes back shoulder to Reed. Reed doesn’t seem to pick it up right away and drifts a bit, and the ball is knocked away. It’s a fine read and throw by Love (especially with the onus on him getting the ball out quickly), but Reed is just a tick late on coming back to the ball. Can you glean a ton from 5 plays? Not really. If there are a couple things to look out for early in the season they’re in Dropback 1 (timing on short out-breakers) and Dropback 4 (Christian Watson as a blocker). Albums listened to: Phoebe Bridgers – Lost Weekend ; Lydia Withem – Yonder Rd.

title: Groupthink: Over-reactions to Texans’ preseason loss
summary: The dust has settled at Reliant Stadium after the first preseason game ended in a disappointing loss. Houston was beat by the Los Angeles Chargers 27-7. After the frustrating loss, it was easy to slip into a frustrating spiral of worry and exasperation. All the hype and excitement of football being back escaped immediately. With […]
full_text: Aug 13, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Houston Texans wide receiver Jared Wayne (89) makes a reception for a touchdown as Los Angeles Chargers cornerback Avery Smith (36) defends during the third quarter at Reliant Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The dust has settled at Reliant Stadium after the first preseason game ended in a disappointing loss. Houston was beat by the Los Angeles Chargers 27-7. After the frustrating loss, it was easy to slip into a frustrating spiral of worry and exasperation. All the hype and excitement of football being back escaped immediately. With that, I asked the writers of the Battle Red Blog for their hot takes on the Texans first preseason game of the 2026 slate. The Houston Texans were drubbed in the second half of their first preseason game against the LA Chargers. Give me your over-reactions to this game Kenneth L.: Going to go first since these are super fresh. First, I don’t care what string was out there, without Nico Collins this offense is a bottom five team in the league. After three full rebuilds of the offensive line they still can’t block anything. The ROI for this offensive line has to be the worst in the league. Second and more specifically, Blake Fisher could be the biggest bust in franchise history. At least Kenyon Green started games. Fisher looked overwhelmed by third stringers. I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s cut and the Texans sign a free agent or another team’s cut tackle. He looked faster than before, but was overpowered in pass protection and led to multipe errant throws by Mills. Third, the CB4 role is still very much up for grabs. The options were Alijah Huzzie, Tremon Smith, and Collin Wright. None of which played well today. Wright was picked on by Trey Lance. Huzzie looked slow and was at the point of inflection for two TDs. Tremon Smith is actually slow and can only play off coverage. Not an exciting night by our vaunted secondary. L4Blitzer : First preseason game, so any analysis could and should be taken with a massive amount of salt. Be that as it may, the game came across as your standard acme first preseason game. Interesting to see the 1st team oline open the game, but that is a good thing. Defense seems to have decent depth, even if it was mainly against the Chargers 2-4th string. The short yardage struggles were not cool, and it would appear that Houston might need at least another arm to get through camp/preseason. otherwise, a loss that means…nothing. At least the regular season is that much closer. VBallRetired : Hard to overreact but we do get a new third string quarterback so let’s start the Marcus Mariota to Houston rumors. It was disappointing to see so many short yardage failures but otherwise it’s a nothing burger. Joe Critz: Overall, I’m pretty happy with how the defensive rookies and how some of the young DBs looked, but I’m disappointed with how many pressures the offensive line gave up in the second half. It’s not all of their fault, but I wasn’t happy to see some of the pressures that Sam Hagen, Jarrett Patterson, and Blake Fisher appeared to give up. Also, this goes without saying, but I was really disappointed to see Graham Mertz go down. I know he’s a sixth-round QB that ideally won’t ever see the field during the regular season, but it would have been nice to get a full preseason look at him in his second year with the Texans. Davis Mills may not be here for much longer, and this season could have been the chance for us to see if Graham Mertz could be his heir apparent, and now that’s gone. As for the good, I thought the starting offensive line looked solid, and both Josh Kelly and Jared Wayne stood out more than I expected. Merlin Klein also looked like a good receiver and blocker in the few snaps he was out there, hopefully Brevin Jordan will be out there next week. I was also happy with how both Jaylen Reed and Kamari Ramsey looked. I’m still a little nervous about the CBs’ depth behind Stingley and Lassiter, which will likely be made up of players like Jaylin Smith, Tremon Smith, and/or Collin Wright, but it’s at least better than it was last year…I think. Was hoping for a big game from Solomon Byrd, and got some highlight plays from him, but was, as he often is during his preseason games, a mixed bag. In fact, I think that describes this game pretty well, overall. Mike Bullock: At the risk of sounding like jaded old guy, I’m pretty out on these preseason games nowadays. They just feel like glorified joint-practices used as cash grabs. You can say Davis Mills didn’t look great and Graham looked worse, but neither had the benefit of a starting O-Line or solid chemistry with the other 10 guys on the field. Blah. Wake me when the season starts… VBallRetired : I’m older than all you guys. I’m the only one allowed to cry old, but I can’t disagree with this. The fear of injuries is so great that it doesn’t make financial sense to play starters. Yet, I don’t see any better way to shake the rust off. It’s a real catch 22. Patrick H.: To echo the sentiments of the old guys, as a near-old, it’s hard to really get much of a feel on anything except how good you should feel about your backups. Given how much the backups struggled against the Chargers, it’s not a great sign. But it’s also the first game. A single data point does not a correlation make, and to be honest if we get to a point in the season where any of these guys are playing at all, we’ve got bigger problems than our lack of depth. I’ll feel like I know more, both about the starters and the backups, with Thursday’s game against Las Vegas. But with the data we have, the starters looked kinda good the backups looked kinda bad, not a whole lot more to glean beyond that.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: Can Colts fans wrap their arms around Daniel Jones?
summary: The only QB competition going on in Colts camp, is for the backup role. Our starting QB will be making north of 40 million dollars, this year and next, whether it is believed that is a good number or not. He doesn’t have to show anything in the preseason and anyone who has laid eyes […]
full_text: The only QB competition going on in Colts camp, is for the backup role. Our starting QB will be making north of 40 million dollars, this year and next, whether it is believed that is a good number or not. He doesn’t have to show anything in the preseason and anyone who has laid eyes on his practices, report that they can’t tell that he has had an injury. If you put him out there after his ankle/leg injury last year, you are putting him out there this year with what you have witnessed. Not much is disclosed about jersey sales, but I can say that he was not listed among the top 50 sold in the league. He may not even have been the top selling Colts #17 last year? Granted, a Rivers #17 might complete some collections or be a nice novelty, but everyone knew that it would be a five game run at best. I’m not saying that Colts fans should have been all in on DJ. Heck, they didn’t even know that he would be the starter until AR took an ill advised sack in preseason. Still, at some point, you would think that the jersey of the starting QB of a team sitting atop the standings and putting up points at a “historic” rate, would be in demand. It might well have been, had he been able to stay on the field and complete in what would have surely been a welcomed playoff appearance. I can understand the reluctance. After all, he would be a free agent at the end of the season. Again, no shaming from me for our fans, as I tend to purchase a jersey of a player I expect to be around a while. Full disclosure, the last one I bought was a Darius Leonard. Now we move into a new season and Jones returns from a serious injury. We had a touch and go off-season contract negotiation period, where we didn’t know if he would be signed or franchise tagged. Many thought that he got a better contract than he should be given, although I believe most fans wanted his return. It is true that he now is still only locked in as a Colt for two years (there is actually an out after this year), with some void years that do not guarantee his being a Colt past 2027. My question is, “Given the chasm that we have had at QB since Luck’s untimely retirement, when will you feel comfortable saying that you want him here for the next 8 – 10 years and maybe even wear #17 proudly?” I’m personally already there. I feel he is an easy guy to root for. I see him as a grounded guy that his teammates embrace as their leader. He made some throws last year that were above “league average” throws. He no doubt benefitted from a scheme that played to his strengths, but he also made his pre and post snap reads that gave the play the best chance to work. Given the normal timeline for an achilles return, he had to have taken his rehab very seriously. Cool nicknames like, Danny Dimes, Indiana Jones, or just DJ are positives. Lastly, I saw what I saw last year and I liked it. I’m pretty sure that the most common response will be, “Let me see him do it for a whole year, before I embrace him.” and I guess that’s fair, but him becoming that guy would check a lot of positive boxes moving forward. I imagine that there may be a few holding out hope for AR or even Leonard and there are some that I think would rather be right than happy, so they want the money paid to DJ to represent another Ballard failure and be the one that finally gets him fired. It may not be a big deal? We didn’t buy Brissett, Rivers, Wentz, Ryan, Minshew, or Flacco jerseys and oddly enough more Richardson jerseys may have been purchased than any of them. After all, as the 4th pick, he did represent the future. So what would it take for you to embrace Daniel Jones as the future?

(Photo by Zach Bolinger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Before their last training camp practices, which are joint practices with the Atlanta Falcons this week, the Indianapolis Colts made a handful of roster moves. The Colts signed free agent offensive tackle Roy Mbaeteka, tight end Tyler Moore, and offensive tackle Trey Wedig. Regarding Wedig, he previously had worked out with the Colts on Monday. The Colts also placed tight end Carson Towt on the injured reserve and waived both wide receiver E.J. Horton Jr. and offensive tackle Bayron Matos in corresponding roster moves. Meanwhile, Moore is a 6,5”, 255 pound tight end who was signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the New York Giants earlier this offseason. At Iowa State, Moore caught 21 receptions for 245 yards (11.7 avg.) and two touchdowns during 45 career games (12 starts). Lastly, Wedig is is a 6,7”, 313 pound offensive tackle who played his final collegiate season with the Indiana Hoosiers (2024). Signed as an undrafted rookie free agent by the Los Angeles Rams in 2025, he’s also spent time with the Arizona Cardinals organization and most recently, the UFL’s DC Defenders.

title: Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor cracks Top 20 of NFL Top 100
summary: With a new lucrative contract extension recently in place, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor now has another honor to his name, as he cracked the Top 20 of the NFL Top 100, which is voted on by his peers: It’s a major leap for Taylor, who wasn’t even considered on last year’s Top […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts following an NFL preseason football game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images With a new lucrative contract extension recently in place, Indianapolis Colts star running back Jonathan Taylor now has another honor to his name, as he cracked the Top 20 of the NFL Top 100, which is voted on by his peers: No. 17 on the NFL Top 100 Players of 2026… @Colts RB Jonathan Taylor! @NFLFilms pic.twitter.com/ZVhrL5Te4i — NFL (@NFL) August 18, 2026 It’s a major leap for Taylor, who wasn’t even considered on last year’s Top 100, despite making the list before. The Colts star workhorse had another highly productive season, rushing for 1,585 total rushing yards and 18 rushing touchdowns on 323 total carries during all 17 starts. His rushing touchdowns and carries led the league, while he finished 3rd in total rushing yards respectively. He earned Pro Bowl honors for a consecutive year. At one point, Taylor was a bona fide NFL MVP candidate before starting quarterback Daniel Jones was limited by injuries, eventually succumbing to a season-ending torn Achilles, and it derailed both Taylor and the Colts team success down the final stretch run. Taylor has been a monster rushing the football for the Colts, and his unique combination of vision, speed, and power is unmatched, with the ability to take the football to the house with any carry and just a crack of daylight. He’s one of the team’s best players collectively, and it’s great to see him receive such a national shoutout. Here’s hoping he has at least a few more Top 100 nods left in his future Hall of Fame track career with the Colts.

title: What does the Colts signing  Keenan Allen tell us about Alec Pierce?
summary: The veteran help the Indianapolis Colts desperately needed has finally arrived in the form of Keenan Allen. The long-time Charger is winding down his career and adding at least one more pit stop before calling it quits. The Colts hope he has enough gas in the tank to help in 2026. This is great news, […]
full_text: The veteran help the Indianapolis Colts desperately needed has finally arrived in the form of Keenan Allen. The long-time Charger is winding down his career and adding at least one more pit stop before calling it quits. The Colts hope he has enough gas in the tank to help in 2026. This is great news, but it brings up a big question. What, if anything, does this tell us about the health and availability of Alec Pierce? After signing a huge contract, Pierce immediately underwent ankle surgery. That has kept him on the sideline ever since. Even at Saturday night’s practice, I witnessed Pierce taking passes from Reggie Wayne, but everything was stationary. Bringing in Allen could put more weight behind what fans have been feeling this whole time. From phantom second injections to non-committal statements from Shane Steichen, the whole thing hasn’t sat right from the beginning. On the other hand, signing Allen may be a completely separate move. Fans, myself included, were begging for the Colts to beef up their receiver room. Even with a healthy Pierce, that group left something to be desired. Signing a veteran to ease the pressure on everyone was always the right call. With Pierce out and Josh Downs a bit banged up, things were looking dicey. Consider the Allen signing as insurance, whether Pierce was a full go or not. The worst part of it all is that we have no idea the real reason. Will we be told? Most likely not. Will all be revealed in time? Yes, especially if Alec Pierce isn’t ready to go Week 1. That will be a huge indicator that Keenan Allen was a necessity, not a luxury. Regardless, a lot is riding on the newly signed veteran, and much will be needed. Hopefully, he will get to work with Pierce by his side, sooner rather than later.

title: Who is the Jaguars’ new RB1: Bhayshul Tuten or Chris Rodriguez Jr.?
summary: If there’s one thing that’s stayed consistent throughout the lifetime of the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s that they’ve always had a darn good running back. Fred Taylor and Maurice Jones-Drew are the first two names that come to mind, but let’s not forget about backfield pioneer James Stewart, or modern workhorses like Leonard Fournette, James Robinson, […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - AUGUST 06: Chris Rodriguez Jr. #24 of the Jacksonville Jaguars looks on during Training Camp at The Miller Electric Center on August 06, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by James Gilbert/Getty Images) | Getty Images If there’s one thing that’s stayed consistent throughout the lifetime of the Jacksonville Jaguars, it’s that they’ve always had a darn good running back. Fred Taylor and Maurice Jones-Drew are the first two names that come to mind, but let’s not forget about backfield pioneer James Stewart, or modern workhorses like Leonard Fournette, James Robinson, and Travis Etienne. Those names have led the franchise in rushing all but six times in its 31-season existence. During this offseason’s free agency period, Etienne cashed in on a four-year, $47 million deal with his hometown New Orleans Saints, leaving the running back room perhaps the No. 1 question surrounding the 2026 Jaguars. “Last year, Travis Etienne was our bellcow. He was the back. He was the guy,” executive vice president of football operations Tony Boselli told 1010XL . “We love Travis. A lot of times, fans and people look at it and say, ‘Well they didn’t re-sign him, must not’ve liked him.’ That’s not the case at all. There’s a thing called the salary cap. We have X dollars, and when you invest in one area, it limits where you can invest in other areas.” “We knew Travis was going to get paid a lot of money, as he should. He’s a very good football player. We also knew we wanted to be more efficient in the run game. Travis is great outside, big-play, really electric in the pass game. We saw that last year. Does so many things well. And talk about just a great guy, great in the locker room. We said, ‘Hey, we need to get better.’ I think we were 31st as far as 3rd-and-to-go yards last year.” The numbers from Sports Info Solutions back that up. When handing the ball to a running back on third down last season, Jacksonville “moved those chains” at the second-lowest clip in the NFL (32.4%). On such plays, the Jags also ranked bottom-five in yards per attempt, yards after contact per attempt, Expected Points Added (EPA) per attempt, and success rate. Etienne is a dangerous ball-carrier in the open field, but when the picture got muddy — as it so often does in the NFL — the Jaguars’ run game waned. 2025’s early-season mirage of a potent rushing attack eventually revealed itself as a struggling unit. Head coach Liam Coen called it the underlying “stink” of Jacksonville’s 8-0 streak to cap the regular season. Weeks 1-6 Weeks 7-12 Weeks 13-18 Yards per game 102.0 (6th) 108.0 (12th) 64.8 (30th) Yards per attempt 4.9 (7th) 4.2 (18th) 3.3 (30th) 1st down rate 18.4% (29th) 27.7% (6th) 16.1% (31st) EPA per play 0.00 (13th) 0.05 (8th) -0.27 (32nd) Success rate 44.0% (21st) 46.9% (12th) 36.4% (32nd) There’s some blame to go around. Jaguars running backs were hit at/behind the line of scrimmage on 37.6% of carries in Weeks 1-6, then 42.3% in Weeks 7-12, then a league-high 56.8% in Weeks 13-18. Midseason injuries to the tight end group somewhat limited Coen’s playbook. Maybe there was an unreported stomach bug in the running back room. At the end of the day, though, Next Gen Stats charted the backfield with just 30 rushing yards over expected in 2025. That includes -40 rushing yards over expected from Weeks 13-18. “Rushing yards over expected and yards after contact is what I give a crap about personally,” Coen said in late March. Jacksonville’s running backs as a whole ranked bottom-10 in both last season. “It’s like, what are you doing outside of what we’re blocking? And what does that look like? Because I can’t coach that. Guys that get more than what’s there, I can’t coach that. The guys that break tackles at a high level, whether it’s via Reggie Bush, whether it’s with stiff arms, jumping over them, running through them, I don’t care how you do it, I just care that you do it, because I can’t coach it. … If the run is blocked for eight yards and we get eight yards, well, it’s kind of like, I need more, I want to see more.” Based on reports about Kenneth Walker III and J.K. Dobbins , the Jaguars wished to add a star slugger in free agency. When that market dried up, Jacksonville looked to sign a player who regularly gets on base. Enter Chris Rodriguez Jr., who rushed for 67 yards over expected last season. He ranked third among 51 running backs in percentage of runs that went for more yardage than expected (45.5%). “I love C-Rod. He’s going to get downhill and he’s going to run somebody over,” tight end Brenton Strange said at training camp . “In those short-yardage situations sometimes last year, not saying anything about anybody, but that’s just the type of back we need. You need a back like that and you need somebody that’s going to get downhill and get those dirty yards. It’s all about the hidden yards. Can you get plus-two on contact? And C-Rod does that.” “I think he’s going to be great for us because he can get those dirty yards,” quarterback Trevor Lawrence reiterated. “And he also has the capability to make people miss. So, I think he’s really well-rounded and he has been doing a good job for us.” Count offensive coordinator Grant Udinski among those excited to work with Rodriguez. “He gives you an element of the run game that might not always be 80-yard runs, but when you look at it, how often are 80-yard runs really showing up in the NFL nowadays? Pretty few and far between, but what he does give you is the opportunity to still get explosive runs and then be efficient on the runs that might not always be perfectly blocked.” There’s plenty of excitement in the Jaguars’ building for their newest running back. Jacksonville Jaguars RB Chris Rodriguez pic.twitter.com/MSQeEAluaG — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) March 12, 2026 Rodriguez is far from a household name. He was a three-star recruit, a sixth-round draft pick, and an inexpensive free agent signing. At this point in his career, he only has one 1,000-yard season on his Pro Football Reference page, and one accolade listed under his Wikipedia page: Second-team All-SEC (2021). That 1,000-yard campaign and All-SEC nod coincided in 2021 — when Coen called plays for the Kentucky Wildcats. Rodriguez captured a second-place finish in yards per game (106.1) and a top-five mark in yards per carry (6.1) among SEC running backs. Only six other players in the conference scored more touchdowns than his 12. It was a productive marriage between running back and playcaller. “He just doesn’t get tackled,” Coen gushed on the John Keim Report after Washington drafted Rodriguez in 2023. “It’s so hard to evaluate running backs when you’re not live. And so I’d watch him, and I’d watch him go throughout [practice], and I went, ‘Yeah, okay, he’s a good player. Seems it, you can tell, maybe he’s got it in him.’ But we would go to scrimmage, and go to games, and it was a totally different movie. He was a kid that, just, nobody wanted to tackle. And, also, he gets better as the game goes.” Coen has echoed those sentiments this offseason. “I think Chris will be a good added thump that we continue to need and get some of those hard yards, which is very difficult to see at this time of year [before pads come on],” he said in May. He added in July: “Until we play tackle football, it’s going to be very difficult for all of us here to gain a true appreciation for who he is and what he does … he’s one of those glass eaters. I mean, he’s going to run through a wall for his teammates, for his coaches, for this organization when the time comes.” So when Rodriguez made his presence felt with a jarring hit on the first day of pads in training camp, Coen wasn’t surprised. “He did kind of what you think he’s going to do in a way, right?” Because he has familiarity with the playbook, Jacksonville can slow-play Rodriguez’s return to action as he recovers from an offseason foot procedure . Coen said the offense is “running a lot of the concepts” that he…

title: Eric Bieniemy did more than just watch the Chiefs practice remotely
summary: Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy has been back at training camp for a week now after a leave of absence due to his wife, Mia Bieniemy, suffering a gunshot wound in a domestic incident involving one of the couple’s sons. “Thank you to the Hunt family, the entire Chiefs family,” Bieniemy began. “For […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Eric Bieniemy and Patrick Mahomes #15 on the sidelines during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on Aug 11, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Kansas City Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy has been back at training camp for a week now after a leave of absence due to his wife, Mia Bieniemy, suffering a gunshot wound in a domestic incident involving one of the couple’s sons. “Thank you to the Hunt family, the entire Chiefs family,” Bieniemy began. “For the outpouring of love and support that my family has received through this particular situation.” “She is on the road to recovery,” Bieniemy described Mia. “She is doing great. It’s one of the main reasons why I’m back here because of her recovery. She is truly a soldier; she is a saint; it has been incredible to watch.” Eric Bieniemy speaks for first time since return. Later says his wife, Mia, is on road to full recovery and gave her blessing for his return. Also said at times watching live streams remotely was yelling at screen, players, coaches and even himself. pic.twitter.com/HkRjQpf2bs — Vahe Gregorian (@vgregorian) August 18, 2026 “With that said, I know I was driving her and a bunch of family members crazy in the house,” Bieniemy smiled. “So she was like, ‘You have my blessing to leave.’ It was time to get back.” As the long-time assistant coach alluded to, Bieniemy’s football brain didn’t shut off when he was away from the dorm rooms at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe. He kept in touch with the team by watching practice remotely via live stream. “I wasn’t always watching, but when things kind of settled back home, I had an opportunity to tap in,” Bieniemy explained. “Technology is pretty impressive now… I had an opportunity to go through the script, and my language probably got a little colorful in the house. “I had a bunch of family members that were there that never really heard some of the language that was used,” Bieniemy shared lightheartedly. “It felt good just to see the guys work,” Bieniemy elaborated. “But on top of that, just to feel like I was still a part of it.” It would be a lie to say Bieniemy was simply observing practice, or watching and taking notes to share with the team in the future. No, it was hard for the former NFL running back to turn off the mentality he has when he’s on the gridiron. “Yelling at the screen, yelling at players,” Bieniemy reflected. “Yelling at coaches, ‘What the hell are we doing?‘ “I was yelling at myself, ‘Why would you put that play in?’” “It was just to keep making sure I can keep up with what’s going on,” Bieniemy continued. “I didn’t want to get away too far, but I just wanted to make sure I could remain focused and locked in when I could have the opportunity to do so.” While Bieniemy tended to his wife and his family as a whole, his “other family” was preparing for the season. He has been away from Kansas City since 2022, but the long-time ties to head coach Andy Reid have made this year’s reunion feel like old times, a benefit to Bieniemy during a difficult time for him personally. “It feels good to be back because obviously, when you’ve been in this environment, it becomes your family,” Bieniemy said. “This is your family away from your family, so it feels good to be in this environment.” With only a week under his belt since returning to the Chiefs’ coaching staff, Bieniemy knows there is plenty of work to do ahead of the season opener on September 14th.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Fourth Chiefs player on NFL’s ‘Top 100’ countdown is Patrick Mahomes, No. 18
summary: On Tuesday, quarterback Patrick Mahomes became the fourth Kansas City Chiefs player to be revealed on this year’s “NFL Top 100 list.” The league revealed Mahomes as the No. 18 player on its official X account. title: Jared Wiley prides himself on making catches like the one from Saturday
summary: There wasn’t an abundance of highlights from the Kansas City Chiefs’ first preseason game, and one of the top plays was initially called an incompletion before head coach Andy Reid decided to throw the red challenge flag. You can even see one of the two officials on the play nearly confirm this nine-yard catch by […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Jared Wiley #12 and Chris Jones #95 walk to the field during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on Aug 11, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There wasn’t an abundance of highlights from the Kansas City Chiefs ’ first preseason game, and one of the top plays was initially called an incompletion before head coach Andy Reid decided to throw the red challenge flag. Jared Wiley on this toe-tap catch (that was initially called incomplete) "Those types of catches are what I’ve prided myself on since I was in college. Making those hard grabs. I’m a big guy, and the quarterback trusts me to put it up there where nobody else can reach it." pic.twitter.com/vx15pEPxZR — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 18, 2026 You can even see one of the two officials on the play nearly confirm this nine-yard catch by tight end Jared Wiley on the field, but regardless, the toe tap worked. It was the only reception Wiley had over the 16 snaps he was on the field with the Chiefs’ offense, but it was the kind of play he has always taken pride in. He talked about that at the podium following Monday’s training camp practice at Missouri Western State University in St. Joe. “Those types of catches are what I’ve prided myself on since I was in college,” Wiley said to local media. “Making those hard grabs. I’m a big guy, and the quarterback trusts me to put it up there where nobody else can reach it… Being able to be kind of a safety net or safety blanket for my quarterback whenever he is in trouble, however that needs to look.” After Wiley tore his ACL during his rookie season, the 6-foot-6 tight end hasn’t had the chance to showcase the skill he takes so much pride in. During his final season at TCU, Wiley led all FBS tight ends in red-zone touchdowns (5). He shared some of the obstacles he has overcome since tearing up his knee in November 2024. “Stiffness. I had a lot of stiffness last year,” Wiley shared. “Still was dealing with some swelling and stuff like that. “I would say the main thing though is mentally – just mentally trust yourself,” Wiley continued. “Being able to do OTAs this offseason was a huge help. Just working through a bunch of that stuff and then by the time the season gets here you repeat these things so many times that you don’t even think about it anymore. Where last year, I felt like I was thinking about a lot before I was going in and out of breaks, before I was doing stuff.” Wiley was asked when he felt like he got over the hump of the injury. “Honestly, just a lot of stuff in the offseason that I did this year,” he answered. “I was able to actually work out instead of rehab this offseason, so that was big. You know, getting with some of my guys, route running, weightlifting, stuff like that. I was even doing Pilates. Literally whatever I could do to just try to work through some of those growing pains again.” In a better spot physically and mentally, the former fourth-round pick has been firmly in the mix with the starting offense, working into multi-tight end sets alongside Travis Kelce and Noah Gray more so than young teammates like Jake Briningstool and Tre Watson. Head coach Andy Reid is a fan of what he is seeing out of the position overall. “They’re all getting better, which leads to great competition there, so I like what we see. Jake and Tre are doing a nice job. Jared’s doing a good job, so happy with that spot. We’ve just got to keep growing. They’ve got a few things they can correct from this game, which will be good for them, but the energy’s right; the willingness to block is right. We’ve just got to keep growing there.”

title: Chiefs News: Chiefs fans rank second in Nielsen ‘fandom index’
summary: The latest Kansas City Chiefs fans have been loud and proud for a long time. It’s no surprise that a recent Nielsen study found them in the top 2 among all NFL fan bases. The only team that ranked higher isn’t too big of a surprise: the Buffalo Bills have a habit of topping Kansas […]

(Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest Kansas City Chiefs fans have been loud and proud for a long time. It’s no surprise that a recent Nielsen study found them in the top 2 among all NFL fan bases. The only team that ranked higher isn’t too big of a surprise: the Buffalo Bills have a habit of topping Kansas City in empty, meaningless matchups. Nielsen ranks Chiefs fans second in ‘ NFL Fandom Index’ | FOX 2 Nielsen used this study to measure the best fanbases in the NFL beyond their typical ratings scale. These were following the criteria’s to determine the best fans: Apparel purchases General interest levels Live event attendance Betting intent Social media engagement Radio listenership Streaming habits Linear TV viewership Kansas City was ranked second in the fandom index with a score of 194, just behind Buffalo, which had a score of 208, and ahead of Green Bay’s 171, reflecting a trend of mid-sized towns showing ardent love for their teams. Five Observations from Monday’s Practice | Chiefs Training Camp 8/17 | The Mothership 2. Safety Alohi Gilman hauled in an interception during 11-on-11 drills. Gilman tallied an interception at the goal line during an 11-on-11 period early in Monday’s practice. The veteran safety was playing over the middle of the field when the pass – which may have been tipped at the line – fell short of its target and feel into Gilman’s waiting grasp. Elsewhere on defense, cornerback Nohl Williams logged a pass breakup on a contested throw in the flat earlier in the aforementioned 11-on-11 period. Defensive tackle Peter Woods also made a play during the segment with a batted pass at the line of scrimmage. Did the Chiefs just give away plans of their offensive scheme changes? | The Kansas City Star Among the 23 designed rushes, the quarterback began under center on 16 of them, a rate of 69.6%. The Chiefs ran just seven times from the shotgun (30.4%). The statistical production doesn’t all that mean much, but I will share them anyway. On Saturday, the 16 under-center carries produced 63 yards (3.9 yards per carry). They ran seven times for 17 yards in the shotgun (2.4 yards per carry). Chiefs 53-Man Roster Projection 2.0: Who Earned a Spot After Preseason Opener? | Sports Illustrated My best guess for the Chiefs’ starting slot corner/nickel defender is “safety” Chris Roland-Wallace. Rookie Jadon Canady is a long-term investment as a slot defender, leaving Kader Kohou in an odd spot. Kohou could feasibly be the Chiefs’ best slot corner, or he could be a surprise cutdown casualty. That decision could also be impacted by L’Jarius Sneed’s health and KC’s need for another core special teamer, which would favor Kevin Knowles or Melvin Smith. Ultimately, I think this group truly comes down to the wire. One of these NFL-quality depth corners will probably miss the cut in favor of the Chiefs’ preferred special teams ace; it’s just a matter of who trades places. — Brisco The Chiefs gave undrafted tackle Khalil Benson a shot. Now he’s helping to protect Patrick Mahomes | Associated Press Benson was similarly overlooked coming out of Southaven High School, which sits just across the Mississippi line from Memphis, Tennessee. He wound up going to Indiana but tore his ACL during preseason practices, forcing him to redshirt that season. He did not play at all the following year, which was the season played amid the coronavirus pandemic. Benson finally played in 2022, including five starts for the Hoosiers at right guard, and he started all 12 games the next year, when it seemed as if his star was ascending. But then coach Tom Allen was fired after a 3-9 finish and Benson transferred to Colorado, where he played nine games for coach Deion Sanders and protected his son and quarterback, Shedeur Sanders. Jaydn Ott and 4 more Kansas City Chiefs players I want to see more of in preseason Week 2 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers | A to Z Sports RB Jaydn Ott The undrafted free agent out of Oklahoma followed his running backs coach, DeMarco Murray, to Kansas City. Frankly, Ott didn’t disappoint in his first performance with the team. While he didn’t get any carries on Saturday, he had the longest reception of the day at 27 yards. He went 2-of-3 receiving for 40 yards total, which topped all Chiefs receivers on the day. Most of his work came late in the game, which is precisely why we need to see more of him. His performance as a receiver was equal to, if not better than, running back Brashard Smith, who saw snaps with the second-team offense and was getting snaps ahead of rookie running back Emmett Johnson. Around the NFL O.J. Brigance, Ravens’ ‘beloved legend,’ dies at 56 after ALS fight | ESPN O.J. Brigance, a former Baltimore Ravens linebacker and the team’s longtime adviser in player engagement, has died 19 years after being diagnosed with ALS. He was 56. The Ravens announced Brigance’s death Monday. Brigance, who won a Super Bowl with Baltimore in 2000, served as an inspiration to the organization for nearly two decades with his determination to fight the disease and surpass the initial prognosis. How fast can Daniel Jones go? It’s the last question in his return from Achilles tear | The Athletic Now, watching Jones at practice, there’s no hint of the injury to the casual observer. Wide receiver Josh Downs said Jones looked so good at the start of camp that he forgot about the injury. Two team sources, not authorized to discuss Jones’s health, echoed that, saying Jones has looked like he never suffered an injury, let alone the sort that can be devastating for professional athletes. NFL Network: Saints rookie WR Jordyn Tyson (Hamstring) expected to miss 2 months | NFL.com Receiver Jordyn Tyson will miss approximately two months due to a hamstring injury, NFL Network Insiders Mike Garafolo and Ian Rapoport reported on Monday. Tyson, the No. 8 overall pick in April’s draft, initially suffered the injury in practice last week and sought multiple medical opinions prior to Monday’s prognosis, per Garafolo. The injury is not related to the hamstring ailments previously affected Tyson in the spring, head coach Kellen Moore said last week. However, only 19 of those reps occurred with the former Kansas State Wildcat aligned on the edge. The other eight snaps were spent lined up further inside, in the B gap, according to PFF . That’s notable because no other defensive end aligned anywhere but over or outside the tackle. title: Do Rams have a rookie blind spot?
summary: For another year, the Los Angeles Rams are unlikely to get much value out of their rookie class. Given the success that recent Super Bowl winners have had thanks to contributions from rookies, is the draft Les Snead’s biggest blindspot and could it hold the Rams back from winning the Super Bowl in 2026? 2026 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 15: Los Angeles Rams tight end Max Klare (86) reaches for a pass around Kansas City Chiefs safety Jaden Hicks (21) during the first halfon August 15th at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by William Purnell/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For another year, the Los Angeles Rams are unlikely to get much value out of their rookie class. Given the success that recent Super Bowl winners have had thanks to contributions from rookies, is the draft Les Snead’s biggest blindspot and could it hold the Rams back from winning the Super Bowl in 2026? 2026 class probably won’t contribute Ty Simpson was drafted to not play this year. That’s the first sign that once again L.A. still doesn’t intend to let rookies to help the team win games. Max Klare played so many snaps in the first preseason game that fans can’t expect him to play a lot in the regular season, or that the tight end depth chart has changed in his favor at all since the start of training camp. Klare is not only behind Terrance Ferguson, but at least two other tight ends, if not three. Max Klare having 7 receptions in his preseason debut (given typical rookie TE usages) I feel at the very least is encouraging for 2027 and beyond I don’t expect him to have much of an impact in 2026, but love the fit with him in LA — Football Analysis (@FBallAnalysisYT) August 17, 2026 And now Keagen Trost, the Rams’ third-round pick, is set to miss a few weeks with injury . Trost was already trending to ride the bench this season with an eye on 2027, but rookies missing August is a bad sign for their immediate development. It comes across as a “red shirt year”, which we already knew. Furthermore, and to be expected, sixth and seventh-round picks C.J. Daniels and Tim Keenan III are just battling for a spot on the 53-man roster. Daniels looks firmly entrenched behind four receivers, at least, and someone like Xavier Smith makes the most solid argument to be the fifth. That puts Daniels in a position where he may need someone to get injured before he moves up the depth chart. This is rather normal for the Rams. And the Rams usually make the playoffs. So what’s the problem? Nobody’s saying there’s a problem . However, the Rams haven’t won or reached the Super Bowl since 2021, which must make Sean McVay—a Super Bowl winner—feel rather uncomfortable. In the most competitive division in the NFL, and the harder conference of the two, every small advantage you can get matters. Yet — aside from trading a first-round pick for Trent McDuffie — the Rams didn’t use their potential advantage with the draft at all. McDuffie is one player and a major use of the draft pick they got from the Atlanta Falcons. It doesn’t change the fact that their five other picks may offer zero value to the team in 2026, and that’s something past Super Bowl winners haven’t done. Every team that has won the Super Bowl since the Rams has gotten major contributions from their rookie class, even including one with McDuffie. 2022 Chiefs: McDuffie, Karlaftis, Pacheco, Watson In 2022, the Kansas City Chiefs drafted Trent McDuffie and George Karlaftis in the first round, Jaylen Watson (another Ram) and Isiah Pacheco in the seventh. These were all MAJOR contributors to the team in 2022, en route to a 38-35 win over the Eagles in the Super Bowl. Other draft picks that year like Leo Chenal, Bryan Cook, Skyy Moore, and Joshua Williams also had contributions as rookies. The Rams may get less from their entire rookie class than Kansas City got just from Joshua Williams that season. The other team, the Eagles, didn’t get as much from their rookie class as the Chiefs, but still added Jordan Davis, Cam Jurgens, and Nakobe Dean. 2023 Chiefs: Rashee Rice Kansas City had fewer openings in 2023 because their 2022 class was so good, but second-round pick Rashee Rice had 79 catches for 938 yards and seven touchdowns as a rookie. He was the second-most important skill player in the playoffs behind Travis Kelce. The Chiefs also got contributions from fourth round corner Chamarri Conner, especially in the playoffs. 2024 Eagles: Quinyon Mitchell, Cooper DeJean, Jalyx Hunt Two years ago, Philadelphia overhauled their secondary with draft picks and it immediately paid off: Quinyon Mitchell finished second in DROY voting and Cooper DeJean was fourth. They were both major players in the playoffs too, including a pick-six for DeJean and two picks for Mitchell—and they were both first-team All-Pros in 2025. The Rams didn’t want to risk going this route despite having two first-round draft picks. Instead, they went with Simpson and McDuffie for picks, while signing Watson to fill the other corner role. The 2024 Eagles, who went 14-3 and beat the Chiefs in the Super Bowl by a lot, also had rookie contributions from Will Shipley and Jeremiah Trotter, Jr. 2025 Seahawks: Grey Zabel, Nick Emmanwori The Rams got three up-close looks at Seattle’s rookie class last year, including the NFC Championship game. Zabel fixed Seattle’s greatest weakness on offense and even got some votes for OROY despite playing guard. Emmanwori finished second in DROY voting and had three pass breakups in the NFC Championship. The Seahawks specifically targeted finding immediate contributors in the 2025 draft, including trading up for Emmanwori at the top of the second round when they knew he could be the exact type of “Kyle Hamilton-ish” player that head coach Mike Macdonald didn’t have yet and could use as early as Week 1 of his rookie season. Seattle also got contributions from Tory Horton, Robbie Ouzts, Elijah Arroyo, and Rylie Mills. Horton was only a fifth-round pick, but had five touchdowns in eight games. Mills missed virtually all of the season, but had a sack in the Super Bowl. Speaking of which, the Patriots also had a ton of contributions from their 2025 draft class. The Patriots drafted 11 players in 2025, including starting tackle Will Campbell, starting center Jared Wilson, running back TreVeyon Henderson, kicker Andres Borregales, and starting safety Craig Woodson, adding up to well over 100 combined games by their rookies. The Rams have taken a complete opposite approach There is no one way to win a Super Bowl and L.A.’s plan could end up being the best one. The Rams were criticized for how they built the 2021 roster and look how that turned out. But if the Rams don’t win the Super Bowl, if they don’t even get that far, the little extra they left on the table by not trying to get even one 2026 contributor directly from the draft, that could be the decision people question the most. Not one expected contributor. A keen eye? Or a blind spot?

title: 5Qs, 5As with Canal Street Chronicles: Is a division title ‘in sight’ for Saints?
summary: The Los Angeles Rams head to SoFi Stadium for the second week of preseason action against the New Orleans Saints. This will be LA’s only preseason game in front of the Ramily, and won’t play in front of the home crowd until Week 2 in a Monday Night Football date with the New York Giants. […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - JANUARY 04: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints and head coach Kellen Moore react after Shough's touchdown during the second quarter of the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Los Angeles Rams head to SoFi Stadium for the second week of preseason action against the New Orleans Saints. This will be LA’s only preseason game in front of the Ramily, and won’t play in front of the home crowd until Week 2 in a Monday Night Football date with the New York Giants. New Orleans is coming off a 6-11 season and a finish in the NFC South basement. Both teams faced off last November, with Los Angeles securing a 34-10 win. Then-rookie quarterback Tyler Shough made his first NFL start and watched a masterclass as Matthew Stafford threw four touchdown passes in the rout. Things are projected to be much different in NOLA this season. Ahead of the Rams’ second preseason bout, I spoke with Nic Jennings from Canal Street Chronicles to learn more about the Saints’ worst-to-first odds, Kellen Moore’s growth ahead of his second season in charge and more in this week’s Q&A. Q – What did you learn about the Saints following their preseason opening loss to the Jaguars? A – One of the most important things I learned from the opener and training camp as a whole is that the Saints and Mickey Loomis appear to have done it again. New Orleans may have another talented rookie class on its hands, with several players already showing the potential to make an immediate impact. Whether it’s Barion Brown, Jeremiah Wright, Oscar Delp, Christen Miller, Michael Heldman and Lorenzo Styles putting together strong training camps and preseason debuts, or Jordyn Tyson, Bryce Lance and T.J. Hall making their presence felt throughout camp, the Saints have seen encouraging signs from their rookie class. It looks like New Orleans may have another impactful group of young players on its hands as the Saints look to take the next step. Q – Who have been some training camp/preseason standouts on offense that Rams fans should know? What about on defense? A – On offense, it has to be Barion Brown. For a sixth-round pick, Brown has established himself as one of the stars of training camp and put together a solid debut Saturday against Jacksonville. His teammates and coaches continue to rave about him, with All-Pro receiver Chris Olave even comparing him to former Saints standout Rashid Shaheed. “They’re basically the same player. He reminds me a lot of him,” Olave said. New Orleans triple-dipped at wide receiver in this year’s draft, and it looks like each of them has the potential to become a major contributor in this league. Jordyn Tyson, Barion Brown and Bryce Lance have all shown encouraging signs early on, giving the Saints plenty of reason to be excited about their young receiver room. On defense, it has to be defensive back Jayden Price. The 26-year-old defensive back posted one tackle, one quarterback hurry, a pass breakup and an interception while not allowing a single reception on three targets. Price only played 21 total snaps, all of which came in the slot. He earned a team-high 95.3 overall defensive grade from Pro Football Focus for his performance, along with a 94.6 coverage grade. Price has already put together a strong training camp to this point, and back-to-back strong performances could help earn him a roster spot when it’s all said and done. Q – Kellen Moore did a respectable job in the Bayou during his first season as head coach. Where would you like to see Moore grow entering Year 2 on the job? A – It will be interesting to see how Moore is able to get off to a hotter start this season now that his roster more closely fits his scheme rather than the one he inherited last offseason. The Saints finished strong once the quarterback Moore and his staff selected in the draft took over, which gives me no reason to believe they can’t start strong this season after adding playmakers across the board and giving Moore a full season and offseason as an NFL head coach under his belt. Q – After starting 2-10 last season, New Orleans won four of their final five games to finish 6-11. They even had slight playoff hopes near the end, thanks to playing in the painfully weak NFC South. The team has been projected as a dark horse worst-to-first candidate, so how do you anticipate their season playing out in 2025? A – Considering the vibes around the facility and the talent on paper, the sky’s the limit for this Saints team. If Tyler Shough can build off his strong finish to his rookie season, I think this team will go as far as he can take them. For me personally, I see a division title in sight. Time will tell if they can achieve that and turn it into a deep playoff run, but so far, Kellen Moore appears to be doing all the right things and has his team ready to compete in 2026. Q – What is something you’re hoping to see out of the Saints in LA this week? A – I’ve said similar things in recent weeks and nothing has changed after the preseason opener. Someone has to win this kicking competition, and so far, neither Charlie Smyth nor Tanner Brown has really established himself. Smyth has the leg power, but he’s dealt with consistency issues throughout camp and missed a kick against the Jaguars on Saturday. The Irishman was expected to enter the season with a firm lead in the battle as he heads into his third season with the team, but Brown has kept the competition alive. If both kickers struggle again against Los Angeles, it could force New Orleans to explore the veteran market at the position. That’s probably the biggest thing I’ll be watching throughout the game.
author: Evan Craig

title: Ty Simpson’s first impression matters in a big way
summary: First impressions are extremely important in the NFL, especially for first-round picks and even more so for quarterbacks. While Ty Simpson was far from setting the world ablaze on Saturday against the Kansas City Chiefs, he still had a strong debut with the Los Angeles Rams. The rookie first-round pick left a positive impression that […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Quarterback Ty Simpson #15 of the Los Angeles Rams looks for an open receiver during the second quarter of an NFL preseason game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images First impressions are extremely important in the NFL, especially for first-round picks and even more so for quarterbacks. While Ty Simpson was far from setting the world ablaze on Saturday against the Kansas City Chiefs, he still had a strong debut with the Los Angeles Rams. The rookie first-round pick left a positive impression that should earn him some goodwill no matter how the rest of the preseason turns out. If all goes according to plan, we won’t see much of Simpson after the next two weeks. A plus performance on a small stage would potentially allow him to enter the 2027 season as the presumed starter. Don’t believe me? Well, ask Jared Goff how much first impressions matter. The Rams were on HBO’s Hard Knocks during Goff’s rookie year in 2016. Infamously, Goff was unable to name which direction the sun set despite living in a coastal state for most of his life. This was his introduction to NFL fans, and he never really bucked this reputation during the remainder of his time in Los Angeles. It also didn’t help matters much that Jeff Fisher was running a high school offensive scheme during his final season as head coach. Fisher was reluctant to start Goff in favor of Case Keenum, and then turned the keys over to the rookie after the veteran exhausted his shorter leash. The Rams’ offense was untalented and not well prepared. Goff was destined for failure, even if he was able to show some glimpses of why he was the first overall pick in the draft. And then enter Sean McVay in 2017—the young brainiac and cutting-edge play caller that salvaged Goff’s career. Even as Goff took steps forward as a quarterback, he never seemed to get the respect he deserved from the NFL media. He was often called a “system quarterback”. Anytime the offense played well, the media was quick to credit McVay. Goff was only ever the reason why the team fell short of lofty expectations. This was a dynamic that didn’t make sense from 2016 through 2020 and still does not make sense. Perception and labels in this context can matter more than real results. Reputations are not easily shed. Fortunately for Simpson, his career is already off to a more positive start than Goff managed. In the grand scheme of things, the rookie’s preseason debut means very little. Perhaps the most important outcome is the fact his introduction was overwhelmingly positive. His first game easily could have went off the rails. Simpson mismanaged a wild snap only to not panic, secure the ball and then get rid of it. He had another late-down scramble that looked like he was on the verge of disaster, only to avoid a sack, keep the ball in play, and convert a pass. At every moment of adversity, Simpson remain poised and made the best of his situation. He looked like a gamer. He competed. That is what most will remember about his first NFL game. Whatever happens from this point forward, Simpson has at least demonstrated that the player the Rams thought they were getting at thirteenth overall is somewhere within him. How long will a strong first impression last? Well, it may be a while before we find out the answer to that question.

Still, B/R observed that the Chiefs had removed their top pass rushers before Simpson’s first series, so he worked through his reads against a preseason defense made up largely of reserves.“ Sean McVay talks standout players from Chiefs matchup, Saints joint practice, injury updates & more (therams.com) “Los Angeles Rams head coach Sean McVay spoke with the media on Monday about expectations for the Rams’ second preseason game, upcoming joint practice with the New Orleans Saints, injury updates & more.” ESPN Ranks Rams 5th in Future Power Rankings (sports.yahoo) “The Rams received an 85.3 overall score, in the “very good” range; a 73.75 score for quarterback, 24th in the NFL; a 95 score for coaching, best in the league; and an 83.25 score for front office. Reason for hope moving forward The Rams are tricky to rank because we don’t know for certain whether coach Sean McVay, who has contemplated retirement, will stay in Los Angeles after quarterback Matthew Stafford hangs up the pads,” ESPN’s Ben Solak wrote, calling it the Rams’ reason for hope moving forward.” Sean McVay: Myles Garrett, Puka Nacua likely to return to practice next week (nbcsports) “As McVay has said before when it comes to injuries and key players, he’s stressing that both Garrett and Nacua need to come back and perform at a high level. “It gets to a point where, hey, we need our guys out there to be able to practice to get ready to simulate what’s going to be a great, long, challenging season,” McVay said. “No matter how great you are when you’re in those guys’ roles, we need to be able to get them out there. But we want to make sure that it’s a return to performance, not just return to play.” Additionally, McVay noted offensive lineman Keagan Trost and receiver Mario Williams are likely to miss a few weeks as both are dealing with hamstring injuries.“ BEST PHOTOS: Ty Simpson’s standout debut, Dean Connors’ pair of touchdowns & more | Best of Rams’ preseason win over the Chiefs (therams.com) “Los Angeles Rams opened the 2026 preseason with a win over the Kansas City Chiefs at Arrowhead Stadium.
