title: Nakobe Dean embracing leadership role during Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp
summary: When the Las Vegas Raiders signed linebacker Nakobe Dean during free agency this offseason, the team wasn’t just getting a defender who can patrol the second level of the defense. It added a much-needed leader to a young position group and defense. While Maxx Crosby has done a good job in that role over the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 14: Nakobe Dean #17 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Las Vegas Raiders at Lincoln Financial Field on December 14, 2025 in Philadelphia, United States. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Las Vegas Raiders signed linebacker Nakobe Dean during free agency this offseason, the team wasn’t just getting a defender who can patrol the second level of the defense. It added a much-needed leader to a young position group and defense. While Maxx Crosby has done a good job in that role over the last several years, serving as the alpha on the Raiders’ defense, the defensive end’s position limits how much he can do as a leader. NFL defensive coordinators typically lean on a linebacker to wear the green dot; relaying the play call, getting everyone aligned pre-snap and taking overall command of the defense. From his time at the University of Georgia to the last four years with the Philadelphia Eagles, Dean’s football IQ and leadership skills have allowed him to successfully take on that role on several occasions. And during the early stages of training camp, it sounds like the Raiders have gotten what they were looking for in that department. “Command. Confidence. ‘Robbie, get out of my huddle. I got it,’” defensive coordinator Rob Leonard replied when asked about what’s stood out about Dean. “I want to get up in there and start up, but that’s not reality of how the game’s played. Just leadership. It feels good to have that at the MIKE linebacker.” One might expect there to be a hand-holding period—so to speak—during the beginning of camp, where the defensive coordinator is more involved with the defense than he would be during a game. Especially since Las Vegas has so many new defenders and a new system, with Leonard getting a promotion and replacing Patrick Graham in the offseason. But that isn’t how Dean operates. “When you’re the MIKE, you want to hear your coordinator talk,” the linebacker explained on why he kicked the play-caller out of the huddle. “You want to hear him talk to you. You want to hear how he’s going to call the calls. You want to hear if he is going to just say the call and get off the mic, or is he going to give you checks and everything. “So, you don’t want him just in the huddle making the call. You want the team to hear you too. I mean, I’m from Mississippi–I don’t have trouble anymore–but I’ve had trouble before with guys not understanding some of the things that I say. So, I want the guys to hear me and hear how I make the play calls and everything too.” Dean went on to say that he doesn’t want “training wheels” since Leonard won’t be on the field with the defense on gamedays. Beyond making the calls and ensuring everyone can understand him, the free-agent addition is doing his part to set the standard and build relationships with his teammates. “You just got to hold everybody accountable,” Dean said. “As far as carrying into gameplay, first you got to know your personnel, what I like to say, know your guys. That’s going to be built through connection with the guys and everything like that. So, know your personnel and hold everybody accountable because at the end of the day, we all just want to win games. I know I came here to win. So whatever we got to do to win, we’re going to make sure we do that.” When asked about getting the young players—of which there are many on the Raiders’ defense this season—up to speed, Dean continued to convey that message. “Holding everybody accountable, holding everybody accountable,” he replied. “So, getting them up to speed is not only holding them accountable, but also holding the guys who have played some football accountable so they can see that nobody, including myself, is exempt from being corrected or needing to know what to do down in and down out.” While the former Bulldog was one of Georgia’s captains on the 2021 National Championship team, he surprisingly never had the ‘C’ patch on his chest with the Eagles. Granted, part of that is likely due to injuries since he struggled to stay healthy and on the field in Philadelphia. However, it sounds like that will change in Las Vegas this fall, meaning the silver and black No. 17 jersey will likely have a new accessory by Sept. 13.
author: Matt Holder

title: Mike Washington Jr. embracing ‘physical mindset’ in Klint Kubiak’s offense during Las Vegas Raiders training camp
summary: Part of the reason the Las Vegas Raiders hired Klint Kubiak as head coach this offseason is because of his impressive rushing attack. The Seattle Seahawks ranked 10th in the NFL in rushing yards, totaling nearly 2,100 yards during the 2025 regular season en route to hoisting the Lombardi Trophy last February. Kubiak accomplished that […]
full_text: May 2, 2026; Henderson, NV, USA; Las Vegas Raiders running back Mike Washington Jr. (30) runs through a drill during a Rookie Minicamp at Intermountain Health Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Candice Ward-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Part of the reason the Las Vegas Raiders hired Klint Kubiak as head coach this offseason is because of his impressive rushing attack. The Seattle Seahawks ranked 10th in the NFL in rushing yards , totaling nearly 2,100 yards during the 2025 regular season en route to hoisting the Lombardi Trophy last February. Kubiak accomplished that with a two-running back system, as Kenneth Walker III accounted for 221 rushes for 1,027 yards (4.6 ypc) and five touchdowns while Zach Charbonnet had 184 carries, 730 yards (4.0) and 12 touchdowns. For the Raiders, that made finding a complement to 2025 first-round pick Ashton Jeanty a priority during the offseason, drafting former Arkansas running back Mike Washington Jr. in the fourth round last April. Las Vegas’ need for a second running back can be crossed off the list on paper, but training camp brings the hard part: learning and mastering Kubiak’s complex playbook. This offense—which has been in the NFL for decades and was passed down to Klint by his father, Gary Kubiak —includes a lot of checks and adjustments based on the defense and requires a collection of detail-oriented coaches and players to execute at a high level. That can make it difficult for a rookie to pick up, and Washington admitted as much, telling local reporters on Aug. 11 that it’s a “hard playbook” and that he “started off slow” in camp. The fourth-round pick also said he’s starting to get more comfortable in the Raiders’ system, though, and it sounds like the coach is doing a good job of setting the standard. “It makes our room a better room,” Washington said of Kubiak being focused on the details. “Like you said, he’s very detail-oriented, so he doesn’t want us running a route how we run it, but how he wants it because everything is scheme-based and concept-based. So, it makes our room a detailed room.” Getting into the nitty-gritty of the Arkansas product’s role in the Raiders’ offense, he described himself as a “downhill runner” and “punishing back” who is “hard to catch”. Running for over 1,000 yards and 6.4 ypc as a Razorback last year, while clocking a 4.33-second 40-yard dash at 223 pounds during the NFL combine serves as evidence and is part of what the coaching staff is looking for him to bring to Vegas’ backfield. “Really just being physical and coming in and running with that mindset,” Washington replied when asked what he’s looking to bring to the rushing attack. “When you run with a physical mindset, nobody really wants to tackle you. Especially being a bigger back, nobody really wants to deal with that physicality.” On top of that, Kubiak likes to get his running backs involved in the passing game. Walker and Charbonnet combined for 51 catches and 426 receiving yards a year ago, with the former finishing as the Seahawks’ fourth-leading receiver and the latter recording the fifth-most receptions on the team. According to local reporters, that’s also been noticeable about the Raiders’ offense in training camp, and will be on Washington’s plate. “Definitely something that I’m still getting better at,” the running back said of being comfortable in the passing game. “Being in [Bobby] Petrino’s offense back in Arkansas, he kind of put me everywhere. And then coming here, it’s kind of the same thing where coach [Kubiak] is very detail-oriented, so he wants the best for us, and he wants to put all the running backs in different positions. So, whether it’s in the slot or having us out wide, he puts us everywhere.” For running backs, involvement in the passing game also comes with involvement in pass protection. That can often be the steepest learning curve for young backs, especially with the evolution of simulated pressures and how overall complex NFL defenses have become. To help flatten the curve, the rookie has been putting in work off the field and leaning on the rest of the room. “Really just been watching film, honestly,” Washington replied when asked about improving in this phase of the game. “Meeting with my running back coach, talking to [Ashton] Jeanty and Dylan Laube. They’ve been great mentors with me in pass protection and understanding the game, because it is different compared to how it was coming out of college.” And the results of Washington’s work ethic have been noticeable to the coaching staff. “Mike’s been great, man,” running backs coach Omar Young said on Aug. 3. “He really worked his butt off during the offseason, and you could really tell and see that. And it’s a great deal for him to just be able to come out here every single day and put forth and show the work that he put on in the offseason and let it come to fruition. So, I’m really proud of him and excited to see what he continues to do.”

title: Fernando Mendoza gets some work against Texans’ 1st team
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders held a joint practice with the host Houston Texans on Tuesday and, as head coach Klint Kubiak suggested might happen last week, rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza did, indeed, get some work with the first-team offense. Mendoza got extensive work with the first- team offense for the first time in training camp […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders leaves the field after the team's 27-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals in a preseason game at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders held a joint practice with the host Houston Texans on Tuesday and, as head coach Klint Kubiak suggested might happen last week , rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza did, indeed, get some work with the first-team offense. Mendoza got extensive work with the first- team offense for the first time in training camp and it came against the Texans’ stout defense. He had some nice moments, but also struggled along with the rest of the Raiders’ offense. He and expected starter Kirk Cousins threw Pick 6s. Kubiak wouldn’t say if the first team would play Thursday night against the Texans, but he did say Mendoza will get a lot of reps. He played from late in the first quarter until early in the fourth quarter against Arizona last week. In other notes from the joint practice: While it seemed like the Texans’ defense won the day, the Raiders’ had some highlights. Tight end Brock Bowers had some nice plays. Running back Ashton Jeanty made some plays in their receiving game and rookie running back Mike Washington had some big runs against the Texans’ second-team defense. The Raiders’ defense, especially the run defense, struggled in the practice. Maxx Crosby, who got in a brief scuffle, had good pressure and linebacker Quay Walker had an interception. Right tackle D.J Glaze struggled against Houston’s star pass-rusher Will Anderson. Guard Jackson Powers-Johnson didn’t practice after getting hurt in practice Monday. Kubiak said he doesn’t expect Powers-Johnson to play Thursday against the Texans. ESPN reported the injury isn’t considered serious. Receiver Dont’e Thornton didn’t practice and he has been out for more than a week. Rookie cornerback Jermod McCoy got some work with the first-team defense. Kubiak’s father, Gary, who once was the Texans’ head coach and who is a Houston native, as at the practice. Raiders’ part owner Tom Brady was at the practice as he was at the preseason opener last week.

title: Breaking down Fernando Mendoza’s preseason debut for Las Vegas Raiders against Arizona Cardinals
summary: Thursday night provided the moment we’ve all been waiting for: Fernando Mendoza’s Las Vegas Raiders debut! Kind of… Of course, it’s just the preseason, and we don’t know when Mendoza will be on the field for the regular season. Regardless, he was sharp against the Arizona Cardinals, completing 10 of 16 pass attempts (62.5%) for […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders waits to run a play in the first quarter of a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thursday night provided the moment we’ve all been waiting for: Fernando Mendoza’s Las Vegas Raiders debut ! Kind of… Of course, it’s just the preseason , and we don’t know when Mendoza will be on the field for the regular season. Regardless, he was sharp against the Arizona Cardinals, completing 10 of 16 pass attempts (62.5%) for 97 yards and a touchdown with no interceptions. To add some more context, Pro Football Focus attributed two of the rookie’s incompletions to throwaways, bumping his adjusted completion percentage up to 71.4 percent. So, let’s flip on the tape and break down Mendoza’s first throws in the silver and black! There were a couple of examples of him still learning the playbook, which is expected at this stage Looks like he wanted to hit Deven Thompkins in the slot but hesitated and had to scramble instead pic.twitter.com/9hQx0BmiF5 — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17, 2026 We’ll start with a couple of plays where there’s room for improvement to get those out of the way and end on a high note. It’s to be expected at this stage in the process, but he did show a few signs of someone who is still learning and mastering Klint Kubiak’s playbook. The Raiders come out in a three-by-one formation and motion Jack Bech to the other side to get into a two-by-two formation. Meanwhile, the Cardinals don’t have a defender follow Bech and instead have the nickel widen, indicating they’re in zone coverage pre-snap. However, Arizona ends up playing Cover 1 or is in man coverage post-snap. That could be part of what throws Mendoza off because he has an opportunity to hit Deven Thompkins on an in route against a corner with outside leverage. Also, the middle linebacker, who is the low-hole defender, widens toward Bech/the wide side of the field to open that window up even more. Mendoza sees the backer take Bech away and does a good job of getting his head around to find Thompkins, and it looks like he wants to let it rip. But he hesitates instead of pulling the trigger, and the window closes as Bech also comes into that area. As a side note, I wouldn’t be surprised if Bech is supposed to either sit after breaking on the slant route or cross the linebacker’s face against this coverage because this is bad spacing on the route concepts. Instead, the quarterback ends up scrambling and does pick up seven yards, but leaves some meat on the bone and takes an unnecessary hit. Scramble drill, would like to see him keep his eyes up and find Thomas, whose defender slips, for a 3rd down conversion pic.twitter.com/iwrdUNkIam — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17, 2026 It’s third and four this time, and there’s another potential opportunity to hit Thompkins to move the chains. The receiver runs an angle route from the slot, pushing outside to keep the nickel corner wide before breaking inside and creating some separation. A throw with good anticipation and some heat on it could lead to a first down. But it’s understandable why Mendoza turns it down because the nickel does a pretty good job of breaking on the route to potentially make a play at the catchpoint for a PBU. Personally, I can live with that decision. The bigger problem comes on the scramble drill. Mendoza doesn’t have his eyes all the way up while running, so he doesn’t see that the defender covering Ian Thomas slips, missing an opportunity to move the sticks and for an explosive play. A simple check down, but nice job throwing Laube away from the LB to set up the YAC for a 1st pic.twitter.com/ALd6Uf1yVF — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17, 2026 Now that that’s out of the way, let’s move on to the positives because the No. 1 pick had plenty of encouraging throws last Thursday night. Especially with the RPO merchant claims this offseason, something that stood out about his preseason debut was how well he did going through the progressions and finding his checkdowns when nothing was open. That also makes the first two clips less discouraging because he did show signs of picking up the playbook and understanding the structure of the play call. The Raiders run a mirrored concept—meaning the route combinations are the same on both sides of the formation—with double outs from a two-by-two set. But the Cardinals are in a great defense for that, running Cover 4, where the outside corners can drive on the (slightly) deeper out routes and the curl-to-flat defenders are in good spots to take away the slots. So, Mendoza starts his read to the left and immediately comes off it since the defense has the out routes coverage. Since it’s a mirrored concept, he doesn’t even have to check the other side of the field and gets right to his checkdown, running back Dylan Laube on a short curl out of the backfield. With the middle linebacker or middle hook defender getting depth initially, that’s wide open. This throw is pretty simple since it’s just a checkdown, but look at the ball placement from the end zone view above. Mendoza does a good job of throwing Laube away from the defender by putting the ball on the ‘2’ of ‘23’, leading the running back to turn away from the linebacker and force a missed tackle to pick up the first down with some yards after the catch. Again, this isn’t a difficult throw by any means, but it is a good read and accuracy to help move the chains. 2nd and goal from the 12, works thru his reads but nothing's open, pressures coming, finds the checkdown and gets the ball out before taking a hit to set up 3rd and 6 pic.twitter.com/dflUcT2Kzz — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17, 2026 I promise, this is the last checkdown we’ll dive into! It’s second and goal from the 12-yard line, and Las Vegas is trying to set up a pick or rub route to running back Mike Washington Jr. in the flat. However, Arizona’s linebacker does a good job of avoiding the contact to be in a position to cover the flat by the time Washington gets his head around. So, the quarterback comes off the back and works the other side of the read. Unfortunately, nothing is open there either. Now the pass-rush starts to come, and the pocket is collapsing on Mendoza. Luckily, he finds Thomas—who creates some separation on a whip route against the nickelback—and hits the tight end before taking a hit. Despite being under pressure, the pass is on the money for a completion that turns what could have been third and long into a third and manageable situation. Works through his reads and hits the backside dig before the pressure can get there, well done 👏 pic.twitter.com/UCUMgTpJeb — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17, 2026 We’re moving on from the checkdowns, but the theme of the rookie working through his reads continues. It’s second and 12 again, and the Raiders dial up another double-outs or bench concept at the top of the screen. But the Cardinals are in Cover 1 and have the two playside routes well-covered. As a result, Mendoza comes off that read and works to the backside of the progression, where he has a dig route against a corner with outside leverage. On top of that, the middle linebacker widens toward the hash marks since the quarterback started the read to the wide side of the field, creating a bigger window in the middle of the field. So, Mendoza hits the backside dig before the pressure gets to him and manages to move the chains. That’s great processing and a great decision, all from…under center! He also has nice footwork in the pocket with his feet tied to his eyes while working through the reads. 🧵Fernando Mendoza's 1st preseason game: -Play action, takes advantage of the LBs freezing and rips the curl to Malik Benson and threads the needle for a tight-window throw and 1 down #RaiderNation pic.twitter.com/XFMXQA6tmC — Matt Holder (@MHolder95) August 17,…

title: Raiders-Texans joint practice keys
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are having a joint training camp practice with at the Houston Texans on Tuesday morning before they play a preseason game there Thursday night. This will be some of the most important work of training camp and the preseason because the starters should get a lot of work. Here are some […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - DECEMBER 21: Ashton Jeanty #2 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs for a fourth quarter touchdown against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on December 21, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Alex Slitz/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are having a joint training camp practice with at the Houston Texans on Tuesday morning before they play a preseason game there Thursday night. This will be some of the most important work of training camp and the preseason because the starters should get a lot of work. Here are some things to watch at the joint practice: Fundamentals: The Raiders are entering their fourth straight season with a new head coach. New coach Klint Kubiak, a first-time head coach, has preached urgency. We will see in this practice how the Raiders are coming along in terms of fundamentals. Kubiak wants the team to get the details right and that will be important to establish in this practice. Tough challenge for offense: Houston has one of the best defenses in the NFL. It will be interesting to see how much the Raiders’ first-team offense goes against the Texans’ first-unit defense. The Texans’ defense is fast and they pressure offenses. Keys for Las Vegas will be protection from the offensive line and ball security. Limit fighting: Yes, there will likely be, at least, one skirmish in this workout. It happens al the time around the league during joint practices and it’s been happening for years. It will be hot and players will have a short fuse and they will want to make a statement. The Raiders have had their share of joint-practice brawls. While it’s expected, Kubiak will likely warn his players about fighting, especially after Saturday’s dust up between Maxx Crosby and Kirk Cousins. Football must be the focus. Health: Just like the actual preseason games, staying healthy has to be major focus in joint workouts. As much as the getting quality work accomplished, getting out of the day healthy must be the main priority.

title: Raiders News: Players gear up for joint practice against Houston Texans
summary: Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp will be a little different today, Tuesday, Aug. 18, with a joint practice against the Houston Texans ahead of their preseason game on Thursday evening. On Sunday, head coach Klint Kubiak was asked about the session in Houston and said “the intensity is going to ramp up,” but the standards […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - DECEMBER 21: Houston Texans wide receiver Nico Collins (12) holds on to the ball as he gets tackled in the fourth quarter during the NFL game between the Las Vegas Raiders and Houston Texans on December 21, 2025 at NRG Stadium in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Leslie Plaza Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp will be a little different today, Tuesday, Aug. 18, with a joint practice against the Houston Texans ahead of their preseason game on Thursday evening. On Sunday, head coach Klint Kubiak was asked about the session in Houston and said “the intensity is going to ramp up,” but the standards the Raiders have set for practice shouldn’t change. Meanwhile, defensive tackle Adam Butler and safety Isaiah Pola-Mao are gearing up for “mayhem”. “There’s no need for balance. It’s supposed to be mayhem,” Butler said about the intensity of joint practices. “It’s a joint practice. Everybody’s fighting for a spot. A lot of money on the line, people’s dreams are on the line, so it’s supposed to be mayhem.” “Yeah, definitely,” Pola-Mao replied when asked about the defensive tackle’s comments. “It’s a little bit chaotic. You’ve got guys out there definitely ready for a fight, but that’s our mindset as a defense. Every play, we’ve got to go out there ready to punch somebody in the mouth.” Both players also shared what they feel the team gets out of these sessions. “You get a lot more out of it because going against our team, our team does one thing, but somebody else does another,” Butler explained. “Especially in the beginning weeks of training camp, you normally get just one look. Every team has their own different style and their own different schemes and stuff like that, and you have to adjust your game. You have to adjust your techniques to accommodate whatever schemes that they run. And it’s very beneficial to get those different looks. I’m excited.” “It’s another day for everybody to get better together,” Pola-Mao said. “Going against another team, it’s just a good time for us…Preseason, coaches don’t want to show everything, but joint practices, definitely. We’ll see some things that we have been working on, so it’ll be good for us.” This will be the Raiders’ first true measuring stick to see where they are as a team since the Texans are widely expected to be a playoff contender this season. In Other Raiders’ Links: Candidates to lead Raiders in takeaways: “Surprised to see Pola-Mao atop the list? Despite facing competition from second-round pick Treydan Stukes, the 27-year-old veteran took the majority of snaps at free safety in 2025 and appears primed to man the spot again this coming season,” via S&BP’s Ray Aspuria . Training camp stars face tough test in joint practices: “Whether it’s in one-on-ones, seven-on-seven or the full team periods, [Malik] Benson will get a chance to prove himself against an elite secondary,” via S&BP . “And if he’s breaking free from the likes of [Derek] Stingley, [Kamari] Lassiter and [Jalen] Pitre, that’s a strong sign that the Raiders found a diamond in the rough with the sixth-round pick.” Kirk Cousins touchdown to Brock Bowers: Ryan McFadden of ESPN posted video with one of five touchdowns Cousins threw on Monday’s practice, connecting with Bowers this time. Early mock draft sends Texas wide receiver to Vegas: “‘Cam Coleman is a physically gifted pass-catcher with dominant traits and abilities,’” Bleacher Report’s Dame Parson said. “‘The 6’3″, 203-pound junior prospect is an explosive leaper with the catch-radius to win on 50/50 balls and back-shoulder fades. He can create a dynamic duo with star tight end Brock Bowers, allowing Mendoza to develop into the highly precise passer the Raiders need.’” Join the conversation! title: The Las Vegas Raiders joint practice in Houston are critical
summary: Monday afternoon, the Las Vegas Raiders boarded a plane headed for Houston, Texas. Setting the stage for a joint practice Tuesday with the Texans before the Week 2 preseason contest on Thursday. Texans are premium grade-A beef Fresh off a 27- 14 Week 1 loss to the Arizona Cardinals, the Raiders have had an opportunity […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - AUGUST 13: Head coach Klint Kubiak of the Las Vegas Raiders looks on as players warm up before a preseason game against the Arizona Cardinals at Allegiant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. The Cardinals defeated the Raiders 27-14. (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images Monday afternoon, the Las Vegas Raiders boarded a plane headed for Houston, Texas. Setting the stage for a joint practice Tuesday with the Texans before the Week 2 preseason contest on Thursday. Texans are premium grade-A beef Fresh off a 27- 14 Week 1 loss to the Arizona Cardinals, the Raiders have had an opportunity to watch film and make corrections. The Houston Texans are in another class in terms of capabilities and roster. If iron sharpens iron, then practicing with the AFC South runner-ups should be an absolute blessing. The Texans finished 12-5 and were a playoff team in 2025, relying on the second-best defense in the league. A stingy, hard-hitting unit that finished second in points allowed, third in takeaways, fourth in interceptions, fourth in run defense, tied for sixth in rushing touchdowns, seventh in sacks, and ninth-least in passing touchdowns. On offense, the Texans are better than in 2025. Quarterback CJ Stroud has a healthy Tank Dell to throw the ball to, along with pairing David Montgomery with Jo’Quavious Marks to anchor the ground game. The Texans, much like the Cardinals, have big, fast, and physical wide receivers to battle. Upgrading their offensive line is what they hope will be the final piece to help them get over the hump. If iron sharpens iron, then these joint practices will serve a multifold benefit. Helping to better the Raiders as a whole then providing a clearer understanding of their potential standing. Improvement vs exposure As a whole, the Raiders offensive line had a fairly solid showing in its first preseason action. It has yet to face a challenging pass rush quite like Houston’s, as its own defensive line isn’t as heavily decorated, if at all. While practicing against Maxx Crosby may be a war of attrition, facing Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter will place the tackles in the crucible with every rep. Shaking free of coverage was incredibly difficult for a majority of the Raiders’ receivers against the Cardinals. The Texans’ secondary is superior in nearly every way and offers an even stiffer challenge to Raiders pass catchers. Will players be able to recognize and correct their mistakes in real time? Will the Raiders’ defense be able to muster up not only pressure but critical stops on third down? Nobody wants to see the entire Texans quarterback depth chart complete every pass in the first half again. Fans certainly don’t want any more cornerbacks getting “welcomed to the NFL rookie” into giving up touchdowns. In this league, the fight for the ball is savage. Joint practice more important than the game Practice makes perfect; it also aids the evaluation process for the coaching staff. Both Kirk Cousins and Fernando Mendoza will get a chance to battle for the starting quarterback position against a dominant defense. Both had good showings against the Cardinals and will face stiff competition not only against the Texans but also against each other. Making each rep critical and consistency king. The offensive line will have multiple opportunities to face premier defenders in every setting imaginable, one-on-ones, double teams, zone blocks and goal-line situations. Allowing us to see just how much improvement the line has or hasn’t made. Multiple bites at the apple will give us a better glimpse of what the Raiders are all about, In the Week 2 game, it should be the starters playing, typically between a quarter to a half. Will it be enough for players in competition to rotate action on a drive-to-drive basis? Or will the coaching staff be content with the results of joint practice and just play the two’s, three’s, and four’s? Whichever way the staff answers this last question will point towards the potential depth chart heading into Week 1 of the regular season.

title: Giants sign Najee Harris ahead of Dolphins preseason game
summary: The Miami Dolphins are set to host the New York Giants this week, having the visitors join them for a joint practice on Thursday before meeting in Preseason Week 2 on Saturday. The Giants made a major roster move on Tuesday, adding former Pro Bowl running back Najee Harris to their roster on a one-year […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - SEPTEMBER 15: Najee Harris #22 of the Los Angeles Chargers carries the ball during an NFL football game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Allegiant Stadium on September 15, 2025 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins are set to host the New York Giants this week, having the visitors join them for a joint practice on Thursday before meeting in Preseason Week 2 on Saturday. The Giants made a major roster move on Tuesday, adding former Pro Bowl running back Najee Harris to their roster on a one-year deal. The signing had been rumored over the last few days, but became official on Tuesday. ESPN and NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported the move . Harris spent 2025 with the Los Angeles Chargers, rushing 15 times in three games for 61 yards before an Achilles tear ended his year. He spent the first four years of his career with the Pittsburgh Steelers after being selected 24th overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft, coming out of Alabama. Harris will presumably have minimal impact on the Giants plans for the joint practice or in the preseason game this weekend. Head coach John Harbaugh explained of Harris’ recovery timeline, “He’s not back 100 percent. He’s not in football shape yet. It’ll be a process.” The Giants’ running back group includes Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary along with Harris. Harris likely slides in as a rotational option, at least early in the season, with Skattebo and Tracy. For more on the signing of Harris and all things Giants, check out Big Blue View .

title: Jeff Hafley ‘hopeful’ Chris Bell will be ready for regular season
summary: Yesterday, Miami Dolphins rookie receiver Chris Bell was activated off of the team’s non-football injury list nine months removed from an ACL tear that ended his final season at Louisville prematurely. He practiced with the team in a red, non-contact jersey on Monday. Today, ahead of Miami’s practice, head coach Jeff Hafley met with the […]
full_text: Yesterday, Miami Dolphins rookie receiver Chris Bell was activated off of the team’s non-football injury list nine months removed from an ACL tear that ended his final season at Louisville prematurely. He practiced with the team in a red, non-contact jersey on Monday. Today, ahead of Miami’s practice, head coach Jeff Hafley met with the South Florida media and was asked about the possibility of having his young pass catcher available at the beginning of the regular season. “He’s back at practice, so there’s always hope. We have to be careful, right? Yesterday he was in individual [drills] and today he’ll do a little bit more in individual, but he’ll be in a red jersey, so it’s non-contact. And then, [it’s up to] how he progresses… There’s still a lot of steps to go, so let’s just see how he progresses, you know? I mean, with any injury, could there be setbacks? Sure. Could it go smoothly? I hope… Step two will be getting involved in some team activities with a red jersey on. I don’t see him practicing against the Giants or playing against the Giants [this weekend], but we’ll go day-to-day and see how he progresses.” Hafley went on to express how excited the organization is that Bell is back practicing with the team, but cautioned that the youngster still needs to get back into “football shape.” “He’s got to get some timing and rhythm with the quarterbacks, but it’s good to have him out there… He’s big, he’s strong, he’s fast. He can run through the football — his catch and run — I just love his play style. He plays with a violence to him, at least looking back at his college tape. He’s an explosive player with size.” Before wrapping up his thoughts on Bell, Hafley once again intimated that the team would like to take things slowly with the rookie. “Like I said, it’s really early, guys. So I don’t want to sit here and tell you that Chris is back, but it’s a lot better than it was a couple of weeks ago, because he’s out there.”

Miami’s first round pick from the 2025 NFL Draft — defensive tackle Kenneth Grant — […]

Miami’s first round pick from the 2025 NFL Draft — defensive tackle Kenneth Grant — is out with injury, and head coach Jeff Hafley said the youngster will be “week-to-week” for the foreseeable future. Jeff Hafley updates Grant’s status Speaking with the South Florida media ahead of practice on Tuesday, Hafley had this to say about Grant’s ailment. “We will not see [Kenneth Grant] today and we will not see him the remainder of this week.” Miami’s new regime isn’t the most forthcoming when it comes to injury details, so it is unclear what type of injury Grant is dealing with at the moment, but for the time being, the Dolphins defensive tackle will be focusing more on rehabbing than getting after opposing ball carriers. Good news for Zach Sieler However, when speaking about fellow defensive tackle Zach Sieler, Hafley offered a bit of good news. The 30-year old is expected back for Miami’s first regular season contest against the Las Vegas Raiders. We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team progresses towards meaningful football games in less than one month’s time.

title: Dolphins preseason update: What is Miami’s biggest area of concern?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Dolphins fans and fans across the country. The Miami Dolphins’ first preseason game did not go as well as hoped, with the Washington Commanders dominating the team throughout most of the contest. The […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - AUGUST 14: Detail view of a Miami Dolphins helmet prior to the NFL preseason football game between the Miami Dolphins and the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Dolphins fans and fans across the country. The Miami Dolphins’ first preseason game did not go as well as hoped, with the Washington Commanders dominating the team throughout most of the contest. The Dolphins lost 20-7, and while the result does not matter in the long run, the concerns it raised do. Miami’s starting offense was able to move down the field on the opening drive for a touchdown, but the team was unable to do anything after that as the depth of the team raised major concerns. Today’s SB Nation Reacts survey asks us where Miami’s biggest area of concern is for you. Is it backup quarterback, where Quinn Ewers and Cam Miller struggled to even complete passes? Is it the defensive secondary, which Washington picked apart in the joint practice earlier in the week and on Friday night? Is it punting, which was shaky at best during the game? Is it the fact that injuries are already starting to pick up for Miami? title: Vikings Stock Market Report After First Preseason Game
summary: After the Minnesota Vikings beat the New York Giants in their first preseason game, we have some more tangible play on which to base early evaluations of players on the Vikings’ roster. So which players helped their cause on Saturday- and which ones hurt it? Here is a stock market report for the Vikings as […]
full_text: Aug 15, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo (44) carries the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the first half at MetLife Stadium. Mandatory Credit: John Jones-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After the Minnesota Vikings beat the New York Giants in their first preseason game, we have some more tangible play on which to base early evaluations of players on the Vikings’ roster. So which players helped their cause on Saturday- and which ones hurt it? Here is a stock market report for the Vikings as they head into joint practices with the Baltimore Ravens later this week. I focused on the quarterbacks, rookies, and those further down the depth chart. Stock Up Kyler Murray . Nothing spectacular here, but he was able to run the offense without any big hiccups and at least managed a scoring drive on the one drive he played. A good first trial run. Carson Wentz . Also showed he can run the offense well after he was given a half-game of snaps. Looking more like QB2 at this point. Jacob Thomas . Not to be confused with third-round pick Jakobe Thomas. Jacob Thomas is a safety and a UDFA rookie out of James Madison. He had the most reps of any player on both defense and special teams and had the highest PFF grade of any special teamer (82.3) and was tied for the most special teams tackles (2) and was also the second-highest PFF graded defender (92.5) with one tackle for a stop, 2 assists, and an interception. He has impressed in training camp as well and all that is how an unheralded UDFA makes the roster. He was taking some first-team reps in Monday’s practice. Max Bredeson . He only had seven snaps on offense, but he showed he can be an effective role player at fullback in the Vikings’ evolving offensive scheme. He also did well as a core special teamer. He looks like he’ll be an upgrade over C.J. Ham. Myles Price . He had 4 catches on 4 targets for 51 yards and three of them were contested catches. He is showing he can play as a wide receiver in addition to a return man. Walter Rouse . Rouse had a total of 33 reps split roughly equally between both guard spots and looked good. He’s a better guard than tackle and he helped his chances of gaining a roster spot with his performance. He was the second-highest graded offensive lineman in pass protection (0 pressures allowed) and also solid in run blocking and the second-highest overall PFF graded offensive lineman. Demond Claiborne . He had a few run stuffs up the middle due to poor blocking up front, but he also showed his burst and speed around the corner outside while also having a good pass blocking rep. Zavier Scott having a tougher go of it pass blocking on Saturday doesn’t help his chances at a roster spot either. I wouldn’t be surprised to see Claiborne get a couple hundred reps this season and perhaps more if Aaron Jones misses some time. Ryan Van Demark . He was the top PFF-graded offensive lineman for the Vikings on Saturday, with good grades in both pass (83.2) and run (78.2) blocking. That was somewhat reassuring as he’s had some struggles in training camp. Henry Byrd . Byrd was solid through 36 reps at both left guard and right tackle on Sunday, no pressures allowed and solid in run blocking- I didn’t see any blown blocks. His versatility helps his chances too. Brett Thorson . Thorson basically dueled to a draw with Johnny Hekker in both punting and holding, which I expect favors Thorson as the younger player under a cheap UDFA contract. So far in practice and in preseason, Thorson has been able to hold for Will Reichard without any problems and that may be his ticket to making the roster and beating out the 36-year-old Hekker. Stock Down Jamal Adams . After showing that he could potentially step up in Brian Flores’ scheme, and being a positive locker room presence, Adams was lost for the season with a right knee injury. That is especially tough for Adams that has spent several years recovering from a torn quadricep tendon injury and could potentially be a career-ending injury at his age after struggling to gain much of a foothold with any team the past few seasons. J.J. McCarthy . A botched first play of preseason (a jet sweep that he mis-timed) and an uncatchable throw on a routine out route from a clean pocket on 3rd and 3 may be anecdotal, but they speak to an ongoing unreadiness that may move him to QB3 and perhaps even a trade. Perhaps even more relevant, if you compare this preseason game to his only preseason game in 2024 , there appears to be no progress and possibly even regression. He also continues to stare down his first read and is often a tick late with the throw. Caleb Tiernan . It was a rough first outing for Tiernan, who couldn’t hold a run block all afternoon. Pass protection was only a bit better. He gave up one QB hit on 20 pass blocking reps, which isn’t a good rate, and also looked shaky doing so. He also had back-to-back holding and offsides penalties. He doesn’t appear ready to be an effective swing tackle at this point if called upon. Caleb Banks . Banks is learning that size alone doesn’t cut it in the league. Better technique beats size every time. Without consistently better pad level, his size is rendered useless as he loses the leverage battle. He needs to improve his technique across the board from hand usage to pass rush moves. He has the physical tools to be good, but his timeline is likely to be more like Dallas Turner’s. The more immediate goal is for him to improve pad level and technique so he isn’t a liability in rotation. Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins . TID was largely ineffectual on Saturday. He seemed intent on hand fighting and using his length to push into blockers, which can be effective in setting an edge, but the problem he had almost every time is he’d get tied up and not be able to disengage effectively. He was credited with two hurries, one tackle for a stop, and two missed tackles- both because he couldn’t disengage quickly enough. He’ll need to work on that if he’s to be effective off the edge. Other Mentions Jake Golday had a solid afternoon and graded well too overall. He had some of the blame for the long run-after-catch by Devin Singletary to start the second quarter as it was his coverage, but it was a cleverly designed screen pass as the center came over to block him and effectively took him out of the play, while Ivan Pace Jr. took a bad angle and overran Singletary, allowing the big gain. Having watched the play back several times, it’s not clear what Golday could have done differently under the circumstances to prevent the big gain- he took an outside line against the center forcing Singletary to cut back inside- but there was nobody inside to make the tackle. Other players further down the depth chart that graded well, but on fewer reps and so may not move the needle much include LB Jacob Roberts, LB Bangally Kamara, CB Zemaiah Vaughn, DI Isaiahh Loudermilk, TE Marshall Lang, and OL Vershon Lee (reps split between guard and center). All of these players face uphill battles to make the roster, and maybe their performance on Saturday earned them more reps in some cases, but not sure they moved the needle much overall. Joint practices with the Ravens begin on Wednesday at noon and go through Thursday. I’ll be there. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Vikings Preseason Week 1 Film Breakdown: Murray Comfortable, Backups Catastrophic
summary: The Minnesota Vikings won their first preseason game, but the real story is in the film. Tyler Forness broke down every snap for The Real Forno Show, revealing a clean Kyler Murray operation, an alarming backup quarterback crisis, a breakout from Myles Price, and a linebacker group that might be the best unit on the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 15: Kyler Murray #1 of the Minnesota Vikings looks down the field after a pass during a preseason game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on August 15, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Mike Coppola/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings won their first preseason game, but the real story is in the film. Tyler Forness broke down every snap for The Real Forno Show , revealing a clean Kyler Murray operation, an alarming backup quarterback crisis, a breakout from Myles Price, and a linebacker group that might be the best unit on the roster. Vikings preseason film breakdown, McCarthy struggles, Myles Price, Bangally Kamara, Caleb Banks, Brian Flores defense — there’s a lot to unpack, and not all of it is pretty. If you think preseason doesn’t matter, the backup quarterback tape will change your mind. Tyler Forness opened the show with measured optimism about the first-team offense under Kyler Murray. “Kyler Murray operating under center looked good. He looked comfortable, and that was the number one thing I was looking for,” Forness said. He noted that six of Murray’s nine snaps under center looked natural and clean — a critical data point for a quarterback transitioning to a new system. However, the backup quarterback situation drew scathing criticism. “I thought they were atrocious. I thought they were both terrible,” Forness said of J.J. McCarthy and Carson Wentz. “If you go by the performances on Saturday, J.J. McCarthy and Carson Wentz are unplayable in a regular season game. It’s at a point where it’s borderline catastrophic.” On McCarthy’s mechanics, Forness was blunt: “They’re never consistent. He’s either way too wide, way too narrow, or just right. It’s like the porridge in the three bears story.” Dave Stefano offered a slight correction — “rarely in sync” — but the concern was unanimous. Forness even admitted he misses Nick Mullens, saying the Vikings may need to find a backup quarterback from “the scrap heap.” Key Points from the Episode: Kyler Murray’s comfort under center — Clean operation, good quarterback-center exchange, felt natural on six of nine snaps. “I feel a lot more comfortable with him under center now than I would have if you had asked me a week ago.” J.J. McCarthy and Carson Wentz “unplayable” — Both slow to the line, mechanically inconsistent, and unable to reliably operate the offense. “You cannot trust either of these guys to operate the offense.” Myles Price earning a roster role — The converted return man bailed out Wentz on multiple plays. “Price has taken every advantage afforded to him and really shown that he deserves to play wide receiver in the NFL.” Demond Claiborne flashed but needs more — Showed real burst and a vicious blitz pickup, but dropped four passes in practice and got the ball at the goal line, which Forness called “objectively stupid” for a 5’9″, 188-pound back. Caleb Tiernan’s struggles are structural — The rookie tackle’s 6’8″ frame with short arms and limited bend is a potentially unfixable problem. “This is limitations because of the way he’s built, and you can’t fix that.” Caleb Banks and Domonique Orange show promise — Banks will get stood up due to his size but showed encouraging penetration. Orange exceeded expectations. Linebacker group might be the best on the roster — Blake Cashman is “one of the best blitzers in the NFL,” Ivan Pace Jr. looks “improved” after a rough offseason narrative, and Bangally Kamara was “all over the field.” Forness admitted: “I gotta eat a little crow here. He looks improved” regarding Pace. Edge rusher depth is a major concern — Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins can’t be trusted as edge three. “Edge three is in dire straits.” Jacob Thomas and Charles Demmings bolstering the secondary — Thomas had an easy interception and is a “real possibility” for a roster spot. “Charles Demmings has locked down a spot on this roster.” Dallas Turner sack prediction — Both hosts predict double-digit sacks. “If he stays healthy, I’d smash the over” on nine-plus sacks. Harrison Smith likely done — Forness doesn’t expect a return and would prefer the cap allocation go elsewhere. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: The film doesn’t lie, and Tyler Forness watches every frame so you don’t have to. From the encouraging signs with Kyler Murray to the alarming backup quarterback crisis, this episode of The Real Forno Show delivers the kind of unfiltered, tape-based analysis that Vikings fans need before the regular season kicks off. Whether you’re optimistic about the first-team offense or terrified by what’s behind Murray, this is the conversation that connects the dots. title: Patriots welcoming increased competition during Eagles joint practices
summary: Competition continues to fuel the New England Patriots heading into 2026. Upcoming joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles in Foxboro on Wednesday and Thursday offer another opportunity for the team to contend against new faces.  Different opponents create different matchups, making those sessions more competitive and productive. “It’s competitiveness. Not going against the same guys […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 15: New England Patriots wide receivers Kayshon Boutte, Mack Hollins, and A.J. Brown at practice on August 15, 2026. (Photo by Barry Chin/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images Competition continues to fuel the New England Patriots heading into 2026. Upcoming joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles in Foxboro on Wednesday and Thursday offer another opportunity for the team to contend against new faces. Different opponents create different matchups, making those sessions more competitive and productive. “It’s competitiveness. Not going against the same guys every day,” wide receiver Kayshon Boutte said after Monday’s training camp practice about what makes joint practices valuable learning experiences. “At receiver, we get good matchups this upcoming week. We got [Quinyon Mitchell], [Cooper DeJean] and we got [Tariq Woolen]. So, I mean, that’s good for all us guys, seeing different guys.” Over the last several years, the Eagles have been known for their dominance on both sides of the trenches. Their offense, in particular, is composed of a hard-nosed unit that blocks in front of their star running back, Saquon Barkley. Head coach Mike Vrabel sees the upcoming practices as a chance to emphasize physicality. “I think the message this week is really just physicality,” Boutte said of Vrabel’s message entering this week. “[Philadelphia’s] coming here this week. A great team, but it all starts up front. So, we have to handle our thing up front [and] win our battles outside. They’re known for winning. They’re a good team. They came here three years ago. We joint-practiced [with] them. So, I think that was pretty cool. So, another opportunity, two days, to get better.” Boutte’s focus on the Eagles’ secondary is only one aspect of the competition New England will contend with across the two sessions. For right tackle Morgan Moses, it begins at the line of scrimmage, where physicality is the focal point of his role on offense. “Obviously, establish ourselves as what we need to do up front,” Moses said about what he’d like to accomplish against the Eagles. “They have a great [defensive] line and a great offensive line, and football’s never changed over the course of years that it’s been played. It’s won at the line of scrimmage. So, we have a great task at hand to see where we’re at, and we’re going to step on this football field and go at it.” On the other side of the trenches, second-year outside linebacker Elijah Ponder kept his goal for the joint practices simple: “to get better.” Last week, New England hosted the Indianapolis Colts for a joint practice ahead of their preseason matchup on Aug. 13 . In preparation for Philadelphia, Vrabel wants to see continued consistency with his team. “We have to just continue to be more consistent; we have to continue to understand the opponent changes, that what we see in the beginning of practice is usually going to be some of the same things that we see in the end,” Vrabel said Monday morning. “If you don’t fix problems or get things addressed or recognize new plays, that’s going to be what it’s like in the game. So, I don’t know if I learned anything other than we have to continue to keep improving, and that’s the goal.” With the Eagles staying in town for two days, the Patriots can focus on several areas rather than condensing everything into a single practice, as they did with the Colts. “I think that we’ll be able to do a lot more field work on the first day and then probably focus on the red zone the next day,” Vrabel added. “But other than that, we tried to put everything into one day versus [Indianapolis], and now we’ll have much more concentrated work the second day in the red zone.” Following the practices, New England will host the Eagles in Gillette Stadium on Saturday for the team’s second preseason game at 7 p.m.

title: Jared Wilson’s collaboration with Doug Marrone already proving valuable
summary: While New England Patriots second-year center Jared Wilson has focused on developing his communication and chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye this offseason, constructive dialogue is also at the root of his learning with offensive line coach Doug Marrone. Before Sunday’s training camp practice, Marrone noted how intentional Wilson has been about communicating with him throughout […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 4: New England Patriots center Jared Wilson meets with the media at training camp on August 4, 2026. (Photo by David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images While New England Patriots second-year center Jared Wilson has focused on developing his communication and chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye this offseason, constructive dialogue is also at the root of his learning with offensive line coach Doug Marrone. Before Sunday’s training camp practice, Marrone noted how intentional Wilson has been about communicating with him throughout the offseason. “Our communication is outstanding. So, [Wilson is] someone that’s very easy to communicate with,” Marrone said. “He’ll tell you how he feels, and that’s what you like as a coach. You have that communication. You have the player today: ‘This feels good; this doesn’t feel good.’ Because there are a lot of different ways to do things. “And then we’re just trying to find a way of what he’s thinking, what’s comfortable for him and what’s going to give us the most chance of success in whatever we’re doing, whether it’s the pass or run.” The Patriots selected Wilson in the third round of the 2025 NFL Draft as a center prospect from Georgia. But as he struggled delivering snaps to Maye that offseason and veteran Garrett Bradbury proved reliable manning the middle of the offensive line, he moved to left guard, where he became a starter. Now, with the signing of Alijah Vera-Tucker in free agency, Wilson is transitioning back to center. “I think it was easy for him because he’s done it, and that’s where he felt comfortable prior to it,” Marrone said about how Wilson is handling the return to his college position. “I think it was a tougher transition last year, going from being a center in college and going to guard. So, I think that’s been easier.” Marrone adds that playing center in college is very different from the NFL, incorporating varied looks and techniques that young players are exposed to. Wilson, at 23 years old amidst the switch, will need to adjust. Still, according to his coach, he’s “competing his butt off.” “There are things that may come up that he might not have had experience before in college. You know, we talk about it, we go over it, and he’s very steady,” Marrone added. “That’s the one thing about Jared I would say as far as you never see him really too high. He’s never really too low. “He kind of approaches the job very well [from] an understanding, and he’s a very good communicator. ‘Hey, this doesn’t feel right. This doesn’t feel good. What can we do to make it better?’” The willingness to communicate proactively with Marrone has fostered a strong relationship between them. Wilson uses his coach’s league knowledge as a resource. “Man, I love Doug. I can just come to him — he’s been around this game for so long, I kind of don’t know how to say what I just saw, but he says it, and I’m like, ‘Yeah, that’s exactly what I just saw,’” Wilson said after Tuesday’s practice of Marrone. “So, our connection is great. I love talking to Doug. I’m very grateful to have him as the offensive line coach.” As a pair, Vera-Tucker joined Wilson to speak with the media on Tuesday. Entering 2026, the left guard is sandwiched between two second-year linemen in Wilson and left tackle Will Campbell. However, Vera-Tucker said he doesn’t feel like he’s working alongside year-two players as he approaches his first season in New England. And for Wilson, he says his connection with Maye has always been strong for a “really long time” with their shared North Carolina backgrounds.

full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Mitch Van Vooren #46 of the New England Patriots looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images As soon as veteran offensive lineman Greg Van Roten signing with the New England Patriots as a free agent was reported, one logical question was raised: what would the follow-up move be to keep the team under the offseason roster limit? We now know that it was waiving tight end Mitch Van Vooren . Let’s analyze what the move means (for the same breakdown about Van Roten, please click here ). Unsurprising move The Patriots used 29 players on the offensive side of the ball in their preseason opener against the Colts last Thursday, and not one of them was on the field for fewer snaps than Van Vooren. The second-year tight end played just three snaps on the night without registering any statistics; he also played a pair of snaps on special teams as well. His lack of quality opportunities in that game and pretty much ever since he arrived in New England ahead of training camp made it pretty clear that the 25-year-old was facing a major uphill battle not just for the 53-man roster but the practice squad as well. Him being let go now in response to the Van Roten signing is therefore no real surprise. Depth changes With Van Vooren out of the picture, the Patriots’ active tight end group now stands at just five players deep. Tight end (5): Hunter Henry (85), Eli Raridon (82), Tanner Arkin (84), Jack Westover (37), C.J. Dippre (81) IR (1): Julian Hill Out of the five tight ends on the roster, Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon are locks to make the team. This leaves the other three to compete for what might not be more than one spot on the 53-man squad. Undrafted rookie Tanner Arkin still looks like the frontrunner even though he has been quiet lately after a relatively eventful start to his rookie training camp. The question whether the Patriots will go two or three deep at tight end will depend on how he or the other backups perform relative to, for example, a seventh wide receiver or other depth piece elsewhere on the roster. What we do know is that Van Vooren is no longer able to leave his mark on the competition. No cap impact When the Patriots signed Van Vooren they did so via a one-year contract that consisted entirely of a non-guaranteed $885,000 base salary. With that number not high enough to qualify for the Top 51 list, he had no actual impact on New England’s salary cap — something that does not change now that he has been released. (That does no mean Van Vooren spent the last four weeks in Foxborough working for free; every player receives per-diem compensation during training camp. As a first-year player with no credited seasons under his belt, he earned $2,000 per week.) While Van Vooren being waived does not change the Patriots’ books, the aforementioned Greg Van Roten signing does. Instead of signing a veteran minimum deal with a $1.3 million base salary, as we speculated after the two sides reached an agreement, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported that Van Roten’s contract with the Patriots is for one year with a $3 million base value and play-time incentives that could push it to $4.5 million. This makes it a solid deal for a veteran player who had been unsigned since March.

title: Patriots waive tight end after signing veteran lineman Greg Van Roten
summary: After agreeing to terms with veteran offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, the New England Patriots had a corresponding move to make. The organization officially opened a spot on Tuesday by waiving tight end Mitch Van Vooren. The follow-up transaction keeps the 91-man roster at capacity ahead of joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles. Van Vooren, […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Mitch Van Vooren #46 of the New England Patriots runs with the ball prior to an NFL preseason football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images After agreeing to terms with veteran offensive lineman Greg Van Roten, the New England Patriots had a corresponding move to make. The organization officially opened a spot on Tuesday by waiving tight end Mitch Van Vooren. The follow-up transaction keeps the 91-man roster at capacity ahead of joint practices with the Philadelphia Eagles. Van Vooren, 25, signed in Foxborough leading up to training camp in July after visiting for a workout. The 6-foot-5, 255-pound tight end caught one pass for four yards from rookie quarterback Behren Morton in last week’s preseason opener versus the Indianapolis Colts. He saw five snaps between offense and special teams during what became a 13-13 tie. Originally entering the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2025, Van Vooren spent his rookie summer with the Seattle Seahawks and Cleveland Browns. The product of St. Norbert College did so after catching 33 passes for 510 yards and 10 touchdowns on the way to first-team All-NACC honors as a graduate student in 2024. Van Vooren began his collegiate career at Marquette University, where he earned four varsity letters as a track athlete and broke the school record with a time of 51.38 seconds in the 400-meter hurdles. New England’s tight end depth chart moves further into August with five, including team captain Hunter Henry, rookies Eli Raridon and Tanner Arkin, as well as the returning Jack Westover and C.J. Dippre. Also on Tuesday, the club hosted defensive tackle DaQuan Jones and linebacker Shaq Thompson on free agency visits, according to the NFL transaction wire. Joint practices with Philadelphia are set for 10:15 a.m. ET on Wednesday and Thursday. A 7 p.m. ET preseason kickoff at Gillette Stadium will follow on Saturday.

title: 3 performances of note from the Patriots’ 18th training camp practice
summary: With the Philadelphia Eagles set to join them on the practice fields the next two days, the New England Patriots decided to take things slow on Tuesday. The club held its second walkthrough in three days in order to get ready of what projects to be two intense joint sessions. To recap the 18th practice […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JUNE 02: Efton Chism III #86 of the New England Patriots during warmups in New England Patriots OTA on June 2, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images With the Philadelphia Eagles set to join them on the practice fields the next two days, the New England Patriots decided to take things slow on Tuesday. The club held its second walkthrough in three days in order to get ready of what projects to be two intense joint sessions. To recap the 18th practice of the summer, please head over to our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eyes. Standout of the day N/A: As usual, we are not naming a player of the day for a walkthrough. The focus of the session, after all, is not on competition but rather the mental element of getting ready for the upcoming season. As a consequence, our observations are based on usage rather than performance. Other performances of note WR Efton Chism III: The second-year wide receivers continues to be prominently featured on offense and in the kicking game. On Tuesday, he was part of the first-team offense around starting quarterback Drake Maye again while also serving as a personal protector on the punt team. It very much is starting to feel like the Patriots are trying to find as many roles as possible for him in order to justify having him on the roster. ED Quintayvious Hutchins: The seventh-round draft choice has had his moments this summer, and the team is making sure to get a proper look at him. This means that he keeps seeing reps with the top-level defense. On Tuesday, that was the case yet again: together with fellow rookie Gabe Jacas, he was part of the second edge grouping alongside starters Dre’Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder. S Mike Brown: Time will tell whether or not Brown can make a late push for the third safety spot, but he very much has held onto a valuable job throughout training camp: personal punt protector, a position he again played on Tuesday. While the aforementioned Efton Chism has started seeing reps in that role as of late, Brown’s experience — he has 141 in-game snaps as a PP on his career résumé — might give him an edge and could ultimately secure him a spot on the 53-man team. The Patriots will be back on the practice fields on Wednesday for their first of two joint practices with the Eagles. The session will be open to the general public and is set to begin at 10:15 p.m. ET, with doors opening an hour earlier.

summary: Ahead of a pair of joint practices, the New England Patriots dialed things down on Tuesday holding a walkthrough practice. Here’s what went down on the fields behind Gillette Stadium. Setting Attire: Jerseys, shorts, sneakers and bucket hats Duration: ca. 80 minutes (10:10 a.m.-11:30 a.m. ET) Conditions: Sunny, temperatures in the high 70s In typical walkthrough fashion, players […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - JULY 27: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots during New England Patriots Training Camp on July 27, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Ahead of a pair of joint practices, the New England Patriots dialed things down on Tuesday holding a walkthrough practice. Here’s what went down on the fields behind Gillette Stadium. Setting Attire: Jerseys, shorts, sneakers and bucket hats Duration: ca. 80 minutes (10:10 a.m.-11:30 a.m. ET) Conditions: Sunny, temperatures in the high 70s In typical walkthrough fashion, players wore sneakers and just their jerseys throughout practice. Attendance Absent: CB Christian Gonzalez, OLB Xavier Holmes, LB Chad Muma, OL Ben Brown, WR Kyle Dixon Returnee: WR Kobe Prentice PUP/NFI: ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler New England’s usual group remain sidelined on Tuesday, again headlined by cornerback Christian Gonzalez. “He’s just in the return to play,” Mike Vrabel said on Monday. “We’ll continue to work through that, and he’ll continue to try to improve and try to get back out on the field.” The Patriots did see wide receiver Kobe Prentice return to the field while outside linebacker Jesse Luketa was also present after leaving Monday’s session early. Takeaways Walkthrough notes: As they have done under Mike Vrabel, work was done at a walkthrough pace in order to manage players’ workloads while keeping the focus on the mental side of the game. In a slower setting, just a few things stood out: Efton Chism III continues to be used with the first team offense and also has worked as a personal protector the past two practices for the first time. Veteran running backs Hassan Haskins and JaMycal Hasty appear to be the top options behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. Rookie pass rushers Gabe Jacas and Quintayvious Hutchins continue to rep with the first-team defense behind Dre’Mont Jones and Elijah Ponder. Julian Edelman was in attendance. Guard depth: After top interior backups Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich suffered injuries in the preseason opener, the Patriots reportedly signed veteran guard Greg Van Roten this week. Van Roten was not in attendance for Tuesday’s walkthrough, but should hit the ground running upon his arrival as he has plenty of connections with the team — such as playing under Josh McDaniels in Las Vegas and top personnel figures Eliot Wolf and Ryan Cowden in Green Bay and New York, in addition to Morgan Moses and Alijah Vera-Tucker with the Jets. “Very smart player,” Vera-Tucker said of Van Roten. Preview The Patriots will be back on the practice fields Wednesday and welcome the Philadelphia Eagles to town for a pair of joint practices. The first is slated to start at 10:15 a.m. ET with Mike Vrabel set to speak beforehand.
