title: All-around improvement has Elijah Ponder positioned for second-year jump
summary: Mike Vrabel’s first ever 53-man roster as head coach of the New England Patriots featured a pair of undrafted rookies. But while Efton Chism had a relatively quiet first year as a reserve wide receiver, Elijah Ponder was much more involved in the operation along the defensive edge and in the kicking game. Sure, a […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Elijah Ponder #91 of the New England Patriots looks on following an NFL preseason football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Mike Vrabel’s first ever 53-man roster as head coach of the New England Patriots featured a pair of undrafted rookies. But while Efton Chism had a relatively quiet first year as a reserve wide receiver, Elijah Ponder was much more involved in the operation along the defensive edge and in the kicking game. Sure, a nagging injury suffered by starter Harold Landry helped his cause on defense, but Ponder did manage to make the most of his opportunities en route to playing one fourth of snaps on the year. And with Landry currently on the physically unable to perform list and second-round rookie Gabe Jacas still growing into his own, a bigger role very well might be on the table for the 23-year-old. Of course, circumstance is not the only reason why. Ponder himself has also shown signs of making the famous second-year jump this summer. “It definitely feels different coming into Year 2, with the same system and the same coaches,” he said. “Just building all those relationships and building with the team. It feels good compared to coming in and not knowing anybody, not knowing the system, not knowing really just the NFL and how it works. … “Definitely much more comfortable. Not just making new relationships with the new guys coming in, but building on the old relationships from last year with all the people that were here already. So, definitely making strides and definitely feeling more comfortable.” His comfort is not all that has changed for Ponder in his second summer as a pro. He also has taken strides on the field, and as a consequence has been given regular starter-level reps opposite free agency pickup Dre’Mont Jones. For Ponder himself, those strides are not easily quantifiable. Instead, he claimed that his development was “all around” both in terms of his abilities and his understanding of the New England defense. “Whether that’s stopping the run, getting to the quarterback, and just focusing on the little details to do those things, I’ll just say all around,” he said. “I think the main thing for me was probably the playbook. Just being able to know what you’re doing and be able to play freely because you have the knowledge to do so. Coming into Year 2, having the playbook — I had a little play here and there, but just being able to hone in on little details of those plays.” Ponder appeared in 19 of a possible 21 regular season and playoff games during his rookie season, and served as a rotational option on the edge as well as a core four special teamer. In those roles, he registered a combined 28 tackles, four sacks, and also recovered three fumbles — including a pivotal one in the AFC Championship Game to set up the game’s only touchdown. Heading into his sophomore campaign off such a solid foundation, he is not the only one feeling good about his development. “I think he continues to just be more comfortable and understand what the game is,” said head coach Mike Vrabel ahead of the Patriots’ 17th practice of training camp on Monday. “What it is from a special teams standpoint, what it is from a first and second down standpoint, what some of the formations are, what he may be looking at, some of his keys. He doesn’t seem to be overly stressed or panic.” For Ponder, this is the result of increased experience and an overall higher level of confidence. “Confidence does a lot for any player,” he said. “When you come in day in and day out and put the work in, you start seeing yourself grow and your confidence grows as well. I think that plays a big part for me.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Undrafted rookie Jacob Rizy taking increased Patriots role in stride
summary: When Ben Brown went down in the first quarter of the preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, the New England Patriots were forced to adapt. That meant inserting third-string center Jacob Rizy into the lineup much sooner than initially anticipated. Rizy ended up playing 55 straight snaps to close out the 13-13 game, taking the […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - AUGUST 13: Jacob Rizy #64 of the New England Patriots runs following an NFL preseason football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Gillette Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images When Ben Brown went down in the first quarter of the preseason opener against the Indianapolis Colts, the New England Patriots were forced to adapt. That meant inserting third-string center Jacob Rizy into the lineup much sooner than initially anticipated. Rizy ended up playing 55 straight snaps to close out the 13-13 game, taking the field alongside both of the team’s backup quarterbacks, Tommy DeVito and Behren Morton. And with Brown expected to miss multiple weeks, more of the same might be on the menu for the undrafted rookie over the next two preseason contests against the Eagles and Browns. But, there is no time to think about expectations, depth charts or projections. For Rizy, the focus is on the here and now. “I don’t really know what to expect. It’s the NFL. I’ve only ever played high school and then college, and I knew this would be a step up,” he said following Monday’s training camp practice at Gillette Stadium. “Just trying to find my way around, get better every day. Trying to get 1% better ever day.” Rizy spent his six-year college career at Harvard and Florida State, where he started 27 total games and saw action all over the offensive line. After joining the Patriots as an undrafted free agent earlier this year, he focused extensively on playing center and eventually entered the Colts game as the No. 3 on the position depth chart behind Jared Wilson and Ben Brown. With Brown now sidelined for the foreseeable future, Rizy finds himself moving up a spot and into “one snap away” territory. He is not intimidated by that prospect, though. “The first thing that crossed my mind was I know how much Ben has been working, and it was really unfortunate to see that happen. You never wish that for your teammates, and that was super unfortunate,” he said. “But I knew I had to go play, so I just kind of went play football, pretty much. … It’s been pretty fun. Speed’s been pretty fast. But I’m just trying to enjoy it and get better.” Rizy’s NFL debut had its expected ups and downs, but head coach Mike Vrabel was pleased with the young center’s performance overall. “He’s battled, he’s competed, he’s studied. For a young center to go in there, it was good,” Vrabel said. “I didn’t think that the game, the way that he got thrown into the game by injury, was too big for him. He was prepared, and I think he’ll continue to work and understand that this is a little different game than probably what he was used to in college. But he is figuring it out, figuring out angles, and those things are so critical for interior linemen where they have to go to get ‘backers at the second level. ‘These guys maybe react a little quicker at this level, so I have to take a little better angle.’” It will be seen whether or not Rizy will continue to stay on an upwards trajectory as the Patriots’ backup center for the remainder of training camp and preseason, or whether he will even keep the job in light of veteran interior lineman Greg Van Roten getting signed as a free agent. Regardless, the first step was a positive one and the 24-year-old ready to take more.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

(Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints brought in wide receivers Chase Claypool and Josh Reynolds for workouts following the recent injury news about first-round selection Jordyn Tyson. With Jordyn Tyson dealing with a hamstring injury, the #Saints worked out veteran WRs Chase Claypool and Josh Reynolds today. — Mike Garafolo (@MikeGarafolo) August 18, 2026 Claypool is a former second-round pick out of Notre Dame. The wideout began his career with the Pittsburgh Steelers, where he played for three seasons before heading to the Chicago Bears, and then the Miami Dolphins. Claypool has 175 career receptions for 2,261 yards and 13 touchdowns in 58 games played. He most recently signed with the Buffalo Bills, but departed shortly after agreeing to an injury settlement with the team and has not played in a game since 2023. Reynolds played with the New York Jets in 2025, but has taken a sort of journeyman approach to his NFL career. The Texas A&M product was chosen in the fourth round of the 2017 draft by the Los Angeles Rams. After spending four years in LA, he played for the Tennessee Titans, Detroit Lions, Denver Broncos, and the Jacksonville Jaguars before playing in five games with NYJ last year. Reynolds has 244 receptions, 3,228 yards, and 20 TDs in his pro career. After it was announced that eighth-overall pick WR Jordyn Tyson’s hamstring injury would keep him out “around two months,” New Orleans wasted no time in bringing in players they believe could be viable options for added depth to the pass-catching group. While Tyson’s injury is not considered to be serious or severe, the extended amount of missed time is certainly a blow to the Saints’ offensive potential for 2026.

title: When should we expect Jordyn Tyson to return from his injury?
summary: The New Orleans Saints may have hoped that Jordyn Tyson would stay healthy, but unfortunately, that hope has already proved false. He was having a a really good training camp and looked like one of the best offensive players. The only issue was the fear of an injury occurring. His hamstring issue from college could […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - AUGUST 13: Jordyn Tyson #0 of the New Orleans Saints participates in drills during a joint practice at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on August 13, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints may have hoped that Jordyn Tyson would stay healthy, but unfortunately, that hope has already proved false. He was having a a really good training camp and looked like one of the best offensive players. The only issue was the fear of an injury occurring. His hamstring issue from college could pop right back up in the future. Oddly enough, that is not the one we are talking about today, as Tyson suffered a different hamstring injury in practice. With hamstring issues, it can get tricky. They can linger throughout a career, not just a season, so being patient is extremely important. Although the Saints want to start winning and should have a better season than last year, they are unlikely to win a Super Bowl now. There is absolutely no need to rush their rookie star WR back if they do not have to as there are players on the roster, such as Devaughn Vele, Barion Brown, Bryce Lance and Bub Means who should be able to step up in Tyson’s absence. So, his timetable to return may be a bit longer than what’s currently expected. As of now, Tyson is expected to be out around 2 months, which would be close to the Saints’ matchup with the New York Giants… in New York. Having an injury-prone rookie WR come back from his injury at MetLife seems like a bad decision ever. If the Saints can avoid that (they should), their next game is against the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris. Traveling abroad could also cause some issues with any player or the team’s process, so waiting another week might be best. This, in turn, makes the November 9th matchup against the Cleveland Browns an ideal return date. It gives Tyson more time to recover and brings lower risk than the two previous matchups. Hopefully, there are no complications in the rehab, and he is back on the field making standout plays like he was during training camp.
author: Caleb Yaccarino

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints loss to the Jaguars
summary: The Good: Zach Wilson The New Orleans Saints 3rd string QB provided a spark to the offense late in the second half when he came in to relieve starter Spencer Rattler. The Saints scored 13 points in the second quarter to take a 20-6 lead, the last of which came on an 84 yard drive […]
full_text: The Good: Zach Wilson The New Orleans Saints 3rd string QB provided a spark to the offense late in the second half when he came in to relieve starter Spencer Rattler. The Saints scored 13 points in the second quarter to take a 20-6 lead, the last of which came on an 84 yard drive in 1:02 led by Wilson and two completions of 28+ yards. Wilson finished with 145 yards on 8/11 passing and 1 touchdown on 4 total drives between the second and third quarters. If Wilson keeps this up he may wind up being named the Saints backup QB. The next two preseason games will show us more in what is becoming an intriguing battle for the backup QB position. The Bad: Second half defense The Saints played great defense in the first half, holding the Jaguars to just 6 points and intercepting two passes. In the second half however, they allowed 18 points and didn’t have any takeaways. The Saints gave up scoring drives of 10 plays for 79 yards, 17 plays for 41 yards, and 5 plays of 57 yards. The third string defense looked worse than the second string despite also playing against Jacksonville’s third string offense. This is to be expected of course, as there is a reason they are the third team, but depth issues hopefully won’t come up on the Saints defense this year as this was not the best debut. The Ugly: Sustaining drives The Saints went three and out four times on Saturday, and punted a total of five times. The were 4/13 on third down, and their only touchdown drives were of 9 yards and 28 yards following a long kick return and a turnover. The Saints only put together three drives of 50+ yards, mainly due to the fact that they were not able to establish the run. The only ran 16 times for 56 yards as opposed to the Jags running 36 times for 118 yards. This can be expected from constantly changing the personnel as you do in the preseason, but the offense should appear more effective going forward.
author: Hayden Reel

title: Saints vs. Jaguars: Game MVP
summary: The New Orleans Saints vs. Jacksonville Jaguars game was a very interesting one to watch. The first half was exciting, and even with some of the struggles that were present, the Saints gave fans plenty of what they wanted to see. It was unfortunate that as the team got deeper into its reserves, the Saints […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints vs. Jacksonville Jaguars game was a very interesting one to watch. The first half was exciting, and even with some of the struggles that were present, the Saints gave fans plenty of what they wanted to see. It was unfortunate that as the team got deeper into its reserves, the Saints were unable to hold the lead and finish the game. Even though the Saints lost, there were still several players who showed up and showed out. Zach Wilson was not thought to be in a battle for the backup quarterback job, but after this game, he certainly made his case. Wilson entered midway through the second quarter and finished 11-of-16 for 145 yards, one touchdown, a quarterback rating of 118.0, and a PFF grade of 81.2. Wilson looked really good and efficient. He seemed in control and comfortable with the entire offense while he was in the game. But in my opinion, he was not the MVP of this game. Let’s talk about the primary target for the quarterbacks in the first half: Bub Means. Means finished the game with four receptions for 77 yards and averaged 4.8 yards after the catch. He also finished with the highest PFF grade among Saints receivers, earning an 81.0 overall offensive grade. Means was just a big toe away from having a touchdown on a deep throw from Zach Wilson. It was good to see Means play meaningful minutes while healthy. On the defensive side of the ball, Jaylan Ford was a player who stood out throughout his time on the field Saturday. Ford made an interception in the red zone on Jacksonville’s first offensive possession of the game, ruining an opportunity for the Jaguars to put points on the board after the Saints scored on their opening drive. This was a vital play that gave early momentum to a very excited Superdome crowd. But my overall game MVP is Jayden Price. Price finished the game with the highest defensive grade on PFF at 95.3, while his coverage grade was nearly as impressive at 94.6. Price finished with one tackle, one assist, and a quarterback hurry. He was also targeted three times in coverage and did not allow a single reception. He recorded a pass breakup and an interception as well. Price was locked in defensively and made the most of his opportunity this past Saturday. It will be interesting to see how not only Price, but also the other players mentioned, follow up their strong performances. Who is your game MVP, and do you think Price will be able to follow this great performance with another one?

title: Saints roster 2026: Jonas Sanker, Kaden Elliss and Oscar Delp are underrated
summary: Hey, remember when the New Orleans Saints selected Louisville quarterback Tyler Shough with the 40th overall pick in the 2025 draft, and a lot of alleged draft experts thought that they were nuts? Yeah, I’m one of the geniuses who’s now taking a second look between bites of crow. Not that Shough was the second […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - NOVEMBER 27: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers runs for yards in the first half as Kaden Elliss #55 of the New Orleans Saints looks to make a stop at Levi's Stadium on November 27, 2022 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hey, remember when the New Orleans Saints selected Louisville quarterback Tyler Shough with the 40th overall pick in the 2025 draft, and a lot of alleged draft experts thought that they were nuts ? Yeah, I’m one of the geniuses who’s now taking a second look between bites of crow. Not that Shough was the second coming of Drew Brees or anything — at least, not yet — but the Saints were 2-10 at one point in the season, and Shough getting the hang of head coach Kellen Moore’s passing game was a major part of the turnaround that led to a 6-11 final record, and a lot of encouragement about the future at a position that has been (to put it kindly) undefined since Brees’ retirement after the 2020 season. Tyler Shough's first NFL start came against the Rams. That's quite the baptism by fire, but the guy had some throws upon which you can build. Pocket movement was the thing you wanted to see here. pic.twitter.com/YR024gEAAO — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) December 16, 2025 Of course, the challenge is different for Shough now — he’s not anyone’s underdog anymore. He’s the starter, and every upcoming Saints opponent has had all offseason to pick his tape apart. “I think what we’re really excited about, and what Tyler’s certainly really excited about, is just the opportunity to really take control of this thing through the philosophy and the leadership,” Moore told Rich Eisen in April regarding Shough’s further development. ”Rallying the group together, all the different throwing sessions that they’re a part of, and all the different opportunities they have to spend together. Then, we get to double down on our system. Last year, [we] introduced the system. [Now], we build it, we make adjustments from a roster standpoint, we get to make adjustments from a scheme standpoint, and we really tailor this thing what ultimately we want to do collectively. “Tyler finished the season off really well last year; we’re really excited about that, and just a great offseason start so far.” Of course, it will take more than an interesting young quarterback for the Saints to make the playoffs for the first time since Brees’ final season of 2020. Everybody on the roster — both old and new — will have to bring their level best, and that’s as true for the underrated guys on the roster as it is for the recognized stars. To that end, I’ve identified three Hidden Gems for the 2026 Saints — one underrated veteran, one underrated free-agent signing, and one underrated draft pick. Underrated veteran: Safety Jonas Sanker When the Saints selected Virginia’s Jonas Sanker with the 93rd overall pick in the third round of the 2025 draft, they didn’t expect him to start right away — the plan was for Justin Reid and Julian Blackmon to patrol the defensive backfield as the main safeties. But when Blackmon suffered a season-ending torn labrum in Week 1, the rookie was thrown into the proverbial fire, and he handled it like a champ. “His story follows my story,” Reid said of Sanker . “My rookie year, I started the second game of the season for the same reason — that there was an injury that came up in the first game and I started the second game — so I already talked to Jonas a little bit about that. (For the 2018 Houston Texans, Reid became a starting safety when Kareem Jackson was moved back to cornerback following an injury to cornerback Aaron Colvin). “And [Sanker will be] ready for the moment. He shined in preseason, he was flying around all over the ball, and we just need that same player to play on Sunday. And his best will be good enough for us.” Sanker’s best was indeed good enough. In 976 overall snaps and 575 coverage snaps, the 6’0⅜, 206-pound Sanker allowed 14 catches on 24 targets for 179 yards, 47 yards after the catch, one touchdown, two interceptions, four pass breakups, and an opponent passer rating of 60.9. He also had 57 solo tackles, 14 stops, three tackles for loss, and one quarterback hurry on two pass-rushing snaps. The @saints really needed rookie safety Jonas Sanker to step in and step up after Julian Blackmon's injury last season, and the rookie did so with authority as a deep-third guy with box and slot abilities. pic.twitter.com/XKUbQzLHxb — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) August 14, 2026 The Saints hope that Blackmon’s injury history doesn’t rear its ugly head once again, because a trio of Reid, Blackmon, and Sanker would allow defensive coordinator Brandon Staley to do all kinds of funky stuff with his coverages. But at the very least, we now know what Sanker’s capable of if he needs to become That Guy once again. Underrated free agent: LB Kaden Elliss Kaden Elliss’ NFL career did not get off to the strongest possible start. A 2019 seventh-round pick of the Saints in 2019 out of Idaho, Elliss missed most of his first season with a knee injury, and totaled just 11 defensive snaps in 2020. It wasn’t until 2022 when the breakout happened, and Elliss began to show his true value as a two-level defender (linebacker and edge) with eight sacks and 20 pressures, all the while blowing up run fits and being at least credible in coverage. That prompted the Atlanta Falcons to give Elliss a three-year, $21.5 million contract with $10.16 million guaranteed. With at least 700 snaps at linebacker and at least 200 snaps on the defensive line over each of the next three seasons, Elliss defined the Falcons’ defense as much as anybody else. . @AtlantaFalcons linebacker Kaden Elliss has sacks in each of his last four games, so it makes sense that the @Commanders would be focusing on him as a blitzer. pic.twitter.com/NsLJed87f0 — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) December 30, 2024 This offseason, the Saints made sure Elliss wasn’t getting away again, signing him to a three-year, $33 million contract with $23 million guaranteed. It’s expected that he’ll be a major part of Brandon Staley’s defense, and Elliss is excited for the possibilities. “We’re going,” Elliss said in June . “It’s really awesome to spend time with [linebackers coach] Peter Sirmon and Brandon Staley and all these guys, to hear how they skin the cat. “There’s a lot of ways to do it, and the way they do it is a lot of the same things I’ve done, and it’s a lot of different things that I haven’t done before. It’s really cool to learn from them. They’re special minds and Brandon’s got a really special defense here. Everybody is bought in, everybody is dialed, and I’m excited to play my part in it. “There’s some truly different things that I haven’t done before and different aspects of the game, different coverages and whatnot. It’s really cool to learn how they do it, and we’ll be good to go.” Elliss will need to be up to speed quickly — he was the green-dot guy with the Falcons, and it’s likely that he’ll serve the same role for Staley. What he allows Staley to do with all Staley’s light fronts and multiple coverages is to have that reliable man in the middle who can disrupt and demolish in multiple roles, so when it all comes together, Elliss will once again help to define the defense he’s playing in. Underrated draft pick: TE Oscar Delp In 2017. the San Francisco 49ers selected an under-the-radar tight end from Iowa in the fifth round, and it was a stretch to say that anybody in the NFL expected a ton of production from him, as the guy had just 43 catches for 624 yards and 10 touchdowns over three collegiate seasons. But when George Kittle got in Kyle Shanahan’s offense, he became one of the NFL’s true force multipliers at his position. What happened in college didn’t automatically align with Kittle’s NFL future. We’re bringing up George Kittle here because of the tape Oscar Delp put up in the 2025 season. Yes, the…

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to scrimmage the Miami Dolphins this week. Reasons for optimism for all 32 NFL teams | PFF New York Giants: The 2025 draft class. There was plenty to like about the Giants’ 2025 draft class, with several […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to scrimmage the Miami Dolphins this week. Reasons for optimism for all 32 NFL teams | PFF New York Giants: The 2025 draft class. There was plenty to like about the Giants’ 2025 draft class, with several rookies making an immediate impact. Jaxson Dart earned a 68.1 PFF grade, the second-best mark among rookie quarterbacks, while his 5.2% big-time throw rate led all rookies with at least 100 dropbacks and ranked ninth among all quarterbacks. Running back Cam Skattebo also impressed. His 80.5 PFF grade led all rookie running backs, and he proved incredibly difficult to bring down, averaging 4.1 yards per carry with 3.04 of those yards coming after contact. On defense, edge defender Abdul Carter wasted no time making his presence felt. His 84.5 PFF pass-rush grade ranked 10th among all edge defenders, while his 66 pressures ranked 11th at the position during the regular season. Abdul Carter, numerologist "It was the best number available after I had 51. It is some crazy numerology. I was born on October 3, 2003, and I was the third pick" Abdul Carter talks about switching to No. 3 this season: pic.twitter.com/bv50aBwq1v — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) August 18, 2026 2026 NFL Top-10 Pass Rushers | FOX Sports 7. Brian Burns, New York Giants. In the midst of a miserable season for the Giants, the seven-year veteran re-established himself as a star with a career-high 16.5 sacks and a pass rush win-rate of 16% that ranked him just outside the top 10. Considering it was a down year for Burns’ defensive line mates — defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence had just a half sack and edge rusher Kayvon Thibodeaux played in only 10 games — his explosion was even more surprising. This year, Burns might have to share the wealth, with Thibodeaux plus young stars Abdul Carter and Arvell Reese (whom the Giants took in the last two first rounds) all figuring to be a part of New York’s pass rush. But that’s the only thing standing in his way. He showed he’s still got the speed and explosiveness that made him so dangerous during his years in Carolina. He hasn’t slowed down at all at age 28 and should be a centerpiece of new defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson’s scheme. 2026 New York Giants training camp: Latest intel, updates | ESPN.com The referee at practice threw a flag on Colton Hood after he cut off wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. in the end zone. The rookie cornerback didn’t like the call and made it known. Coach John Harbaugh saw it unfold. He didn’t agree with Hood’s assessment and sent him to the sideline. But not until they had a quick chat. “I wasn’t angry. I just wanted to make the point that, you know, what are you arguing about?” Harbaugh said. “The ball was in the air and you pushed the receiver and redirected him. It was a restriction. That’s going to be pass interference. But he’s competitive. He’s competitive. He wants to win every snap. And I think [that’s] part of the journey for the young corners.” Malik Nabers’ return to team reps provides hope for Giants offense| New York Daily News Malik Nabers’ first day back in live team reps at Monday’s practice didn’t go perfectly. He stumbled on his first release when planting on his surgically repaired right knee. He limped while running his first 11-on-11 route. He only ran about 10 total routes in the practice. And he showed some restless emotion after an awkward half-jump to make one of his three catches in 7-on-7. NFL hot seat for all 32 teams | CBSSports.com Giants: Kayvon Thibodeaux has seen the Giants both draft (Edge Abdul Carter) and trade (Edge Brian Burns) over him, and both players have been more productive than he has. The 2022 No. 5 overall pick registered just 2.5 sacks in 10 games (shoulder), a far cry from his 11.5-sack 2023 season that seemed to hold so much promise. Thibodeaux is heading into the fifth-year option of his rookie contract, so it’s a big year for his wallet, too. D-line break down each other’s strengths If these Giants pass rushers could steal one thing from each other's game, what would it be? 🤔 Brian Burns, Kayvon Thibodeaux, Adbul Carter and Arvell Reese share their answers… 🎙️ @AKinkhabwala pic.twitter.com/mxPDCQXzNL — NFL on CBS 🏈 (@NFLonCBS) August 17, 2026 Trending after Preseason Week 1, with Giants rookies impressing | The Athletic Giants rookies. First-round linebacker Arvell Reese looks like an instant star in New York. The Ohio State product was a standout in training camp, and while his debut wasn’t perfect, it had everything you want to see from a top-five pick. Third-round receiver Malachi Fields is also among the Giants’ biggest risers after catching all three of his targets for 34 yards and this touchdown. The 6-foot-4, 220-pound Fields offers a Tee Higgins-like threat opposite Malik Nabers, and he should be the Giants’ WR2 before long. Fantasy managers take note. The Giants’ Jaxson Dart challenge goes way beyond sliding | New York Post The lasting image of Saturday’s Giants game, even more than the 13-10 final score — because, of course, it’s the preseason — and more than the positional battles that will shape the final roster spots, unfolded on the final play of the first quarter. There was Vikings safety Jay Ward, unblocked, closing in on Jaxson Dart. NFL: Giants QB Jaxson Dart’s blue tent trip was ‘standard medical timeout’ | USAToday.com The NFL has clarified that New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart’s evaluation in the blue medical tent during the team’s preseason opener was a “standard medical timeout.” League protocol involves multiple independent neurologists and medical trainers reviewing replay for signs of impact or injury behavior that can trigger a check. Dart was forced into the tent late in the first quarter Saturday against the Minnesota Vikings after safety Jay Ward delivered a crushing hit to the torso. title: NY Giants practice takeaways: Malik Nabers, Arvell Reese, Andrew Thomas, more
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants held their last padded practice before traveling to hold a joint practice with the Miami Dolphins on Thursday. Here are some of the takeaways. Malik Nabers’ update The Giants star wide receiver practiced for a second straight day. This was a lighter day for Nabers after he […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants held their last padded practice before traveling to hold a joint practice with the Miami Dolphins on Thursday. Here are some of the takeaways. Malik Nabers’ update The Giants star wide receiver practiced for a second straight day. This was a lighter day for Nabers after he took seven team reps on Monday, his first of the summer as he works to return from a torn ACL. Nabers, again in a red jersey, was in shells while the rest of his teammates practiced in full pads. He did take a couple of team reps. He caught a long pass from Jaxson Dart in 7-on-7, a play where it was clear defensive backs Tyler Nubin and Jevon Holland understood that they were not to hit Nabers. In real game action, the two defensive backs could have laid a big hit on the wide receiver. Head coach John Harbaugh said Nabers will need to “get bumped around and hit and fronted up” in practice before the Giants consider playing him in a game. The Giants aren’t ready for that to happen yet. Injury updates Cornerback Colton Hood (unknown), wide receiver Jalin Hyatt (ankle/leg), and defensive tackle Josh Tupou and Bobby Jamison-Travis (both unknown) did not practice. Arvell’s impact Rookie linebacker Arvell Reese made back-to-back big plays during 11-on-11 red zone work. First, he used his size and athleticism to swat away a pass Dart tried to float over him to tight end Isaiah Likely at the goal line. On the next play, Reese and Chauncey Golston barreled into the backfield to stop Cam Skattebo for a loss. Andrew’s revenge In West Virginia, there were a couple of days where edge defender Abdul Carter got the better of Andrew Thomas. During 1-on-1 blocking/rushing drills on Tuesday, Thomas got a measure of revenge. The two squared off in back-to-back reps. First, Thomas used his left arm to simply force the speed-rushing Carter around the pocket. On the next rep, Carter tried to bull rush Thomas and wound up going nowhere. A few other highlights from the blocking/rushing 1-on-1 drills: Sisi Mauigoa won reps against Chauncey Golston and Darius Alexander. Rookie Anquin Barnes smoked Evan Neal, getting to his left shoulder and ripping past him. Daniel Faalele had two reps against Kayvon Thibodeaux. He lost the first one, when Thibodeaux went inside of him. On the second, he pushed Thibodeaux past the pocket. Jake Kubas, bidding to rise up the depth chart, had teammates whooping when he stoned Thibodeaux on a power rush. The Giants also did wide receiver vs. cornerback 1-on-1 drills. Here are a couple of highlights: Dru Phillips, who is back after missing time with a knee sprain, batted away a short out intended for Darnell Mooney. Ryan Miller smoked Paulson Adebo on an out-and-up, and was clearly frustrated when quarterback Brandon Allen let the play go without throwing the ball. Malachi Fields also beat Adebo on a deep ball. Adebo was in position, but didn’t locate the ball in the air. Nabers lined up to take a rep in this session, but as soon as he did the whistle was blown to end the drill. Notes Josh Ezeudu was working exclusively at guard on Tuesday. Marcus Mbow was the second-team right tackle, and J.C. Davis was at left tackle. Adebo got a few first-team reps, but did a lot of his work with the second unit. The Giants continued to mix and match at both cornerback and safety. Korie Black even got a rep or two at cornerback with the first team. The Giants did a lot of work on fourth-down situations of 5 yards or less. Both Ben Sauls and Dominic Zvada kicked field goals. I couldn’t see all of the kicks, but Sauls missed back-to-back kicks from what looked like 45-50 yards. He made what appeared to be a 55-yarder. I did not see Zvada miss any kicks. Practice, scheduled to go from 1:40-4:00 p.m., wrapped at 3:30. Harbaugh must be getting soft! The Giants will practice in shells on Wednesday and then head to Miami for Thursday’s joint practice with the Miami Dolphins. There is no media availability on Wednesday.
author: Ed Valentine

title: NY Giants’ RB Najee Harris thinks he has ‘good opportunity’ in New York
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Najee Harris and John Harbaugh were on opposite sides of the Pittsburgh Steelers-Baltimore Ravens rivalry for four seasons, with Harris running the ball for Pittsburgh and Harbaugh coaching Baltimore. Now, they find themselves on the same team after the Giants signed the 6-foot-1, 242-pound 28-year-old running back on Tuesday. After Harris, […]
full_text: Najee Harris leaning on the podium while answering questions from media on Tuesday. | Photo by Ed Valentine EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — Najee Harris and John Harbaugh were on opposite sides of the Pittsburgh Steelers-Baltimore Ravens rivalry for four seasons, with Harris running the ball for Pittsburgh and Harbaugh coaching Baltimore. Now, they find themselves on the same team after the Giants signed the 6-foot-1, 242-pound 28-year-old running back on Tuesday. After Harris, coming back from a 2025 torn Achilles tendon, worked out for the Giants on Monday, Harbaugh had said “I felt like the hair on the back of my neck stood up when I saw him.” On Tuesday, after Harris had gone through his first practice with the Giants, Harbaugh said he was “excited for the possibilities” now that the four-time 1,000-yard rusher was a Giant. “He’s an experienced back,” Harbaugh said. “Anybody that’s watched him play knows what type of a back he is. He’s a downhill runner, physical runner. I’ve played against him a lot, have a good feel for who he is as a player. “Everybody that’s been around him, my brother [Jim Harbaugh], G-Ro [Giants senior offensive assstant Greg Roman], Mike, Tomlin, love him as a teammate. So, excited for the possibilities.” Harris had 1,000-yard rushing seasons in all four of his seasons after being a first-round pick by the Steelers. He played just three games for Jim Harbaugh’s Los Angeles Chargers last season before being injured. Why did he choose the Giants? “I want opportunity. I think this is a good opportunity here,” Harris said. “I think the style of play that they’re heading towards is the style of play that aligns with me. Harbaugh coming from the AFC North, me playing against him a lot of times. I know the type of style of football he wants. “And, I think that we align each other with each other with what type of football we want to play. So I think that just coming here is a good opportunity. And I’m just willing to just put my foot in there and help out any time, any way I can.” Harbaugh had said on Monday that Harris was “not back 100%. He’s not in football shape yet.” Harris said Tuesday it was “not going to take a long time” for him to get there. “Am I fully in like in football shape? No, I just got on pads today,” Harris said. “It’s the difference between getting in shape and in football shape because it’s hard to replicate pads in an offseason other than just putting it on and going out there and work. “So, I mean, can I go out there and run some plays? Of course I can. am I where I want to be like Najee want to be? No, probably not … But, I’ll be good. It’s not going to take a long time.” Harbaugh said he figured it would “take a couple weeks” for Harris to ramp up, and that he could be ready “just in time probably” for the season to start. Harris joins a backfield that currently includes Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary. Harris has the best resume of anyone in the room, but knows he has to prove himself with the Giants. “I have a lot to prove,” Harris said. “Somebody who’s coming back from a torn Achilles. Really, everything that I did in the past is in the past. “And really everything I do now is really what matters. I know it’s going to be a lot of questions of how I’ll come back looking. And I’m ready to answer all those.” Harbaugh and the Giants can’t want to see what that looks like.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Roster move: Veteran WR JuJu Smith-Schuster released
summary: The New York Giants announced Tuesday afternoon that they’ve released veteran wide receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster. The Giants initially signed Smith-Schuster along with Odell Beckham Jr. and Braxton Berrios earlier this summer following a veteran workout. The Giants sought to add both depth and competition to a receiver position that’s being rebuilt on the fly. Smith-Schuster […]
full_text: ﻿Wide receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster at Giants practice | Getty Images The New York Giants announced Tuesday afternoon that they’ve released veteran wide receiver JuJu Smith-Schuster. The Giants initially signed Smith-Schuster along with Odell Beckham Jr. and Braxton Berrios earlier this summer following a veteran workout. The Giants sought to add both depth and competition to a receiver position that’s being rebuilt on the fly. Smith-Schuster spent the last week dealing with an “old knee” (in the words of Giants head coach John Harbaugh). Smith-Schuster wasn’t mentioned often in practice reports, even before his knee flared up. Conversely, Beckham has been carving out a larger role for himself with the starters while Berrios has been a fixture on special teams. At the same time, rookie receiver Malachi Fields has been ascending, giving the Giants sorely-needed size, strength, and perimeter blocking on their offense. This is the corresponding move to create a roster spot after the team signed running back Najee Harris earlier Tuesday. The team has signaled that they intend to emphasize the power run game, making the 240-pound Harris more valuable to their plans.

title: Fantasy Football 2026: NY Giants fantasy preview
summary: Happy August, readers! We’re two weeks into training camp, and the Giants’ first preseason game is history. This feels like the right time for me to take a break from my league-wide fantasy coverage to focus on one team and one team only. Boo-yah — It’s time for my annual New York Football Giants fantasy […]
full_text: The future ion NY is now | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Happy August, readers! We’re two weeks into training camp, and the Giants’ first preseason game is history. This feels like the right time for me to take a break from my league-wide fantasy coverage to focus on one team and one team only. Boo-yah — It’s time for my annual New York Football Giants fantasy football preview! If you haven’t started prepping for your drafts in season-long redraft fantasy leagues, it’s time to get going. The season kicks off in less than a month! You can check out my preliminary preseason rankings and tiers, sleepers, division previews, and other draft prep pieces at this link: Fantasy Football Hub . I’ll have more content as the month rolls along. Here’s a sad reality, Giant fans: For much of the 2020s, the Giants have been a team to avoid for fantasy. Before last season, the team ranked 30 th or lower in either points scored, total offense, or both in four of the five seasons this decade. I won’t sugarcoat it — it’s been ugly. But that was then, and this is now. And right now, the Giants have a player at each of the four primary positions who could be a significant factor in fantasy this season. The first glimmer came two seasons ago with the fantastic rookie season of the electric Malik Nabers , who burst onto the scene as a clear alpha and finished that season as the WR7 with a 109-1,204-7 stat line on 170 targets. He also led the NFL with 11.3 targets per game. And he did that despite a revolving door of, at best, sub-par QBs (sorry, Tommy Cutlets). The team built on that success in 2025 as two more exciting rookies emerged in dual-threat QB Jaxson Dart (QB13 for the year) and human battering ram RB Cam Skattebo (RB11 in eight games before a season-ending leg injury). With Dart leading the way, and despite season-ending injuries to Nabers in Week 4 and Skattebo, the team jumped all the way to 13 th in total offense, at 333 yards per game, up from 295 yards per game (30 th in the NFL) the year before. With a new coaching staff in place, and everyone hopefully healthy to start the season, there are reasons to be excited about the Giants this season, and while their offensive players won’t be confused with the playmakers on the Cowboys, Lions, or Bengals, they aren’t the Jets or Titans either, and should no longer be viewed as a fantasy wasteland. I won’t dwell on the offseason changes. You can find lots of great content all over this website – which covers the Giants like no other source — about the hiring of new HC John Harbaugh and OC Matt Nagy, the choice of Miami offensive lineman Francis Mauigoa with the tenth overall pick in the 2026 draft, and the additions of former Ravens Patrick Ricard and Isaiah Likely . Throw in the departure of slot merchant Wan’Dale Robinson , and the offense is going to look different this season. I wasn’t thrilled with the Nagy hire, but overall, the arrow is pointing up. Let’s examine the Giants for fantasy football, 2026. I’ll go position by position for today’s exercise. All prior season rankings shown are for Half-point PPR, on a Fantasy Points Per Game (FPPG) basis and exclude the final week of the season. Fantasy draft rankings represent Expert Consensus Rankings (ECR) as of August 15. Quarterback Dart wowed fans last year with exciting scrambles, runs, and passing. His nine rushing TDs tied for second among QBs with Trevor Lawrence, and significantly bolstered his excellent rookie performance for fantasy. He was quite the pleasant surprise – from both a real and fantasy football perspective — given that he was a back-half of the first round draft pick. It looks like Big Blue found its guy for the next decade. That said, all of Dart’s designed and not-so-designed runs might be part of what got Brian Daboll fired, and his propensity to take off as a ball carrier creates a big risk. He isn’t afraid of contact (some would say he invites it), and the new staff is reportedly trying hard to coach him on when and how to avoid unnecessary hits. We’ll never know how many times Dart actually was concussed in 2025, but self-preservation is something he needs to work on. The arm and rushing talent are there, in spades. Did you see his scramble, and across-the-body TD pass to rookie WR Malachi Fields in the first preseason game, right after a bone-crushing hit resulted in yet another frequent-flier trip to the blue tent? Yeah, so did I. And that sequence is the Jaxson Dart experience in a nutshell. Dart is currently ranked as the QB12 for redraft, with an ECR of 95. QB is insanely deep this year and he’s one of multiple QBs who could be Top-10 options this season but are fairly cheap in one-QB leagues. He’ll miss the easy-button throws to Robinson, but getting Nabers back at anything close to full strength, for anything close to the full season, would be huge for his fantasy prospects. There’s enough weaponry here for Dart to thrive, if he can stay upright. That’s the big “if” with him for fantasy this season. And if Dart misses time, Jameis Winston is always a super fun waiver wire ride for fantasy. Just close your eyes and wait for the box score. Running Back Skattebo appears to be fully recovered from the gruesome injuries that ended his rookie campaign and that’s good news for the Giants. He quickly became a fan favorite with his ability to make plays, toughness, and nose for the end zone. He hit paydirt seven times in the eight games he played, and his skillset is ideal for a three-down role. He can handle early down rushing work, is a good pass catcher, is strong in short-yardage, and can pass block. Like Dart, his aggressive play style raises durability concerns, so there’s some risk here. His current ECR of 50 (RB19) has him going off boards as a mid-range RB2, around the 4/5 turn. I think that’s fair value for one of the better RB2 options out there, given the upside and potential three-down role. If you’re in a league with Giant fans, good luck getting any kind of bargain on him though. Behind Skattebo, there’s decent depth, but some uncertainty. Tyrone Tracy, Jr. has proven himself more than capable when given the chance, although his missed block is what got Dart blown up. He’s the top candidate to be the #2 who shares work with Skattebo, for now. And if anything happens to Skattebo, he could be a big asset for fantasy. He’s one of a multitude of backup runners that I tend to go after in the double digit rounds. Devin Singletary is competent but is simply depth at this point and shouldn’t be drafted in typical leagues. Newly signed Najee Harris is a wild card who missed almost all of last season with a torn achilles, after four straight 1,000 yard seasons in Pittsburgh. I’m curious to see how the depth chart shakes out in the next month. The Harris signing followed the loss of running back Dante Miller for the season. Wide Receiver Let’s make one thing clear: A fully healthy Nabers is a Top-5 wideout in fantasy, and an obvious difference-maker for the Giants in terms of actual football. He’s that good. That’s why so much hand-wringing has accompanied his recovery from a serious knee injury suffered in Week 4 last season, including a setback this spring. Sad but true: Dart’s first NFL start was Week 4, so he and Nabers have played less than one half of football together. Will Nabers be ready for Week 1, and what strength will he play at? That’s been one of the top question sets in fantasy this spring and summer. His current ECR of 28 (WR13) is still at a decent discount from his ceiling, and reflects the risks associated with his early-season availability and play strength this season. But that ECR has been rising steadily, and the fact that Nabers didn’t start camp on PUP is a good sign. But this is the year after the ACL tear, and some players take two seasons to get back to full explosiveness. At his current third round price, I’m intrigued. If he rises close to the 1-2 turn, where he belongs on talent, that’s a very…

title: NY Giants signing Najee Harris to bolster running back position
summary: The New York Giants are signing four-time 1,000-yard rusher Najee Harris to bolster their running back room. The news was first reported by Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo, and has been confirmed by a source within the Giants. Harris, a 2021 first-round draft pick by the Pittsburgh Steelers, rushed for more than 1,000 yards in […]
full_text: Najee Harris | Getty Images The New York Giants are signing four-time 1,000-yard rusher Najee Harris to bolster their running back room. The news was first reported by Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo , and has been confirmed by a source within the Giants. Harris, a 2021 first-round draft pick by the Pittsburgh Steelers, rushed for more than 1,000 yards in each of his four seasons with the Steelers. He signed with the Los Angeles Chargers as a free agent in 2025, but played just three games before tearing an Achilles tendon. Harris, 28, worked out for the Giants on Monday. Giants coach John Harbaugh had plenty of experience against Harris from his time with the Baltimore Ravens. The Giants’ interest in Harris had been rumored since early in the offseason. “He looks good in the workout. He’s not back 100%. He’s not in football shape yet,” Harbaugh said on Monday. “It’ll be a process. But that would be a guy that has got a lot of experience. He’s a decorated vet. And with those guys, generally, you just have to kind of see where they’re at when you get them. And sometimes it works out great. Sometimes it’s just okay, and other times it doesn’t work out. But based on the workout, I would say we feel like he’s got a shot.” The Giants waived/injured running back Dante Miller on Monday, so they needed another back. Harris, though, is more than a player to fill a roster spot and help the Giants get through the remainder of the preseason. He seems like a player destined for a big role if he is fully recovered from the Achilles injury. Harris joins a backfield that includes Cam Skattebo, Tyrone Tracy, and Devin Singletary. Harris is not a breakaway back. He averages just 3.9 yards per carry for his career. Rather, Harris is a big back, a 6-foot-1, 242-pound between-the-tackles runner who fits the power running game Harbaugh likes to employ and is installing in New York. Could Harris supplant Tracy as the primary second back in a time share with Skattebo? We will see.

title: The Giants’ offensive line is the NFL’s…19th best?
summary: At this point, after one preseason game, there are still many questions about how good the 2026 New York Giants are going to be. Most of those questions have been about how the change in defensive coordinators will help what was an atrocious defense last year; how Jaxson Dart will acclimate to a new offensive […]
full_text: Francis Mauigoa | Getty Images At this point, after one preseason game, there are still many questions about how good the 2026 New York Giants are going to be. Most of those questions have been about how the change in defensive coordinators will help what was an atrocious defense last year; how Jaxson Dart will acclimate to a new offensive coordinator and assistant coaches, especially given John Harbaugh’s desire to have him line up behind center a lot more; where quality play in the secondary is going to come from; and who the heck is going to be catching Dart’s passes. In the first pre-season game, it looked like the Dennard Wilson defense could be good, especially with rookies Arvell Reese and Jack Kelly flying to the ball; that Dart looks a lot like last year’s version, right down to the visit to the blue tent but also the great TD pass off his back foot to Malachi Fields; that quality secondary play is yet to be found on this roster; and that Fields at least looks like a keeper, maybe OBJ too if any of his quarterbacks notice him beating his defender and throw to him. One thing we don’t hear much about is the offensive line. That’s for two reasons. First, after years of being among the worst OLs in the league overall, the Giants actually had a fairly good OL last season. Pro Football Focus ranked them 10th in pass blocking and 19th in run blocking, which seems reasonable to me. They were strong at tackle, and both tackles return this season. They were mediocre in the interior, but they used the No. 10 draft pick on Sisi Mauigoa, who is expected to start at right guard. You never know what to expect from a rookie OL (see: Andrew Thomas, 2020), but according to Ed’s reporting from the Greenbriar: Mauigoa has taken every snap of training camp as the starting right guard. It has certainly looked to the naked eye as though Mauigoa has been meeting or exceeding the bar Harbaugh has set. Mauigia looked fine in his first preseason game. So the arrow should be pointing up for that particular unit, right? Not according to everyone, apparently. Football Insights has compiled pre-season rankings of all NFL offensive lines from a variety of sources. Here are the team individual and consensus rankings (compiled before the first pre-season game): Offensive Line consensus rankings pic.twitter.com/SpidnX2Md5 — Football Insights 📊 (@fball_insights) August 12, 2026 The Giants sit at a mediocre, slightly-below-average No. 19 in the consensus rankings, between the Patriots and the Ravens. As is the case though for teams in the mid-range of any ranking, that usually implies a wide divergence of opinion among individual analysts. The Giants OL’s high ranking, No. 10, is from the FTN (For the Numbers) fantasy site. Their analyst Dan Fornek says about the Giants’ OL: The effectiveness of the New York Giants’ offensive line hinges on the availability of left tackle Andrew Thomas Thomas played 13 games in 2025, allowing just one sack on a 2.9% pressure rate on 448 dropbacks. In total, the Giants return four starters from a solid group. They also upgraded the right guard position by drafting Miami’s Francis Mauigoa with the 10th overall pick in the NFL Draft. Mauigoa, a center in college, will start his career on the interior. New York also has three experienced interior offensive linemen (Aaron Stinnie, Daniel Faalele and Lucas Patrick) with developmental tackle prospects (Marcus Mbow and J.C. Davis) waiting in the wings at tackle. The Giants were a very good unit when Andrew Thomas was healthy in 2025. They enter 2026 as a top 10 group now that they addressed arguably their biggest hole with one of the best offensive line prospects in the 2026 draft class. At the opposite end of the spectrum, Fantasy Points has the Giants’ OL ranked No. 29. Their rankings are behind a paywall, but it’s hard to see that OL being that bad, unless Mauigoa is the second coming of Evan Neal and Andrew Thomas gets injured again. It could be worse, though. Take the Carolina Panthers. One analyst ranks their OL No. 3, another No. 29. How do two people look at the same group and one thinks it’s among the NFL elite while another thinks it’s awful? Fortunately at the top and bottom of the consensus rankings we get to see the teams that everyone agrees have the best and the the worst offensive lines. So considering that this 2026 Giants defense is going to have to make its name on the effectiveness of its pass rush, let’s ask: Which 2026 opponents will have the Giants’ pass rushers licking their chops and which may frustrate them the most? The good news is that the Giants won’t be facing to-o-o many of the NFL’s top offensive lines, but they will see several of the worst. The Eagles (No. 2) always give opposing pass rushers fits, but’s that’s a given for an NFC East team. The worst news is that they face the Rams (No. 6) in Week 2, although the various analysts diverge somewhat in their view of LA’s OL, with PFF and Brandon Thorn not being as impressed as the others. Matthew Stafford is as good as they get when kept clean (95.8 PFF passing grade in 2025) but very ordinary when pressured (68.4). There’s your story line for Week 2. At the other end of the spectrum, the Giants will face the consensus three worst offensive lines in the NFL this season. Houston’s ferocious defense will be a tough ask for the Giants’ offense, but C.J. Stroud is absolutely neutralized by pressure (81.4 PFF passing grade when kept clean vs. 49.0 under pressure). Likewise, vs. Tennessee in Week 3, Cam Ward graded 70.0 when kept clean but a horrendous 34.7 when pressured. As for Cleveland, we don’t know whether Deshaun Watson or Shedeur Sanders will be the starter, but both graded significantly worse under pressure the most recent season in which each played. Of considerable interest will be the Giants’ two games against the Commanders. Mike Clay of ESPN has their OL ranked No. 17, the highest of any analyst. However a lot depends on when each analyst did his rankings. PFF has the Commanders dead last in the NFL in their rankings , olely because of the serious injury to Laremy Tunsil: Before the injury to left tackle Laremy Tunsil, this was a group set to rank just inside the top 20, but the loss of Tunsil for a significant amount of time is a huge blow to the group. There will be an expectation of some improvement from Josh Conerly Jr., and his 59.9 PFF grade in 2025 was fine for a rookie, but this is a unit that could really struggle if Tunsil misses the full season. Giants fans are all too familiar with that predicament.

title: NY Giants tales from the timeline: Young players impress vs. Vikings
summary: The New York Giants hosted the Minnesota Vikings in preseason Week 1, falling 13-10 in John Harbaugh’s first game with the team. I review the All-22 film after every Giants game and post plays on my X, providing a snippet of analysis on why each play is noteworthy. Here are posts from Week 1, with […]
full_text: Malachi Fields celebrates a touchdown catch on Saturday. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants hosted the Minnesota Vikings in preseason Week 1, falling 13-10 in John Harbaugh’s first game with the team. I review the All-22 film after every Giants game and post plays on my X, providing a snippet of analysis on why each play is noteworthy. Here are posts from Week 1, with some commentary. The offense Such a Jaxson Dart play. Dart leaves the medical tent, play breaks down, he extends, and finds rookie Malachi Fields for a tuddy. Elite job by Fields to work upfield after the drag and find space in the back of the EZ. pic.twitter.com/p971QwKVl6 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 15, 2026 Dart to Fields. pic.twitter.com/ubpYguAy6d — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 The top post is spot-on — this is such a Jaxson Dart play. Everything about it stands out, from the off-script playmaking and unorthodox throwing motion to the fact that Dart had a sip of tea in the medical tent on the previous play. Dart does an excellent job diagnosing the robbing boundary safety sitting on the hash and baiting the in-breaker to Darius Slayton (18). Rather than forcing the throw, Dart shows restraint, pulls the ball down, and finds space behind quality blocks from Marcus Mbow (71) and Jon Runyan Jr. (76). From there, he delivers a beautiful touch pass, while Malachi Fields (0) makes an excellent route adjustment and shows strong awareness of the situation. The matchup between Fields and Ivan Pace Jr. (0) was one the Giants could exploit, and they did exactly that. Dart extended the play, recognized the mismatch, and trusted Fields to make the adjustment. The result was an impressive off-script play that showcased Dart’s creativity and play-making ability — and ultimately produced the Giants’ only touchdown of the game. Sisi Mauigoa, No. 65! pic.twitter.com/DjnjiGP3DF — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Francis Mauigoa didn’t have a perfect game, but his power does flash, and I am certainly excited about his presence on this offense. New York aligned in a Strong-I and ran iso-power out of 21 personnel with a draw element. Runyan Jr. pulled as the backside guard to the strong side, which prompted Pace Jr. to read his run key and attack the strong side of the offensive formation. Patrick Ricard (45) was the kick-out block, but the play-side was crowded — this is where Mauigoa and Devin Singletary (26) come into play. Singletary’s vision and patience gave Mauigoa the opportunity to turn first-round rookie Caleb Banks (95) toward the pile-up, which opened up the back-side cut lane for Singletary. Bryan Hudson (60) — who played well in the run game — helped open the initial hole against the 2i-shade. The raw power of Mauigoa was eye-popping, to say the least. The routes of Odell Beckham Jr. against the Vikings. pic.twitter.com/fsT4kRvfOF — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Odell Beckham Jr. saw preseason action and played 16 snaps, catching two passes on three targets for just 6 yards. Beckham Jr. looked to have juice in his brief time on the field. A busted coverage could have led to a massive play, but Jameis Winston checked it down; it was his final rep, where Beckham Jr. won on an outside release. Still, a player of his caliber is playing against backups. He is no lock to make the roster, but still appears to have play left in his tank. It's great to see Cam Skattebo back healthy. He picks up five yards behind the blocks of Patrick Ricard, Chris Manhertz, Jermaine Eluemunor, and the pulling BS OG (Runyan) btw, Chris Manhertz throws two Vikings defenders to the ground on this play. pic.twitter.com/Au9IDpVZkS — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 It wouldn’t be a Nick Falato article about the Giants without a Chris Manhertz appreciation post. The veteran tight end gives the Giants a run advantage, and he appears poised to have an important role in a Greg Roman-constructed running offense. Manhertz played nine snaps with the first team; he had this quality rep and also pinned a 295-pound defensive end on a T/C pin-pull sweep out of even 12 personnel. That play is located below, and it didn’t work, but the Giants trust the veteran to execute the block, which gives their rushing attack creative options: The #Giants run pin-pull sweep with the play side tackle and center pulling into space out of UC 12 personnel. Tight ends like Chris Manhertz (beast) allow offenses to pin 290-pound ends. Blake Cashman and Eric Wilson fit it well, but I like the concept from Greg Roman. pic.twitter.com/l3rOP8Vx2s — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Arvell Reese Elite run defense by the #Giants on 2nd & 8… Fotu and Carter do an excellent job constricting the rushing lane, and Arvell Reese quickly diagnoses and attacks. Tae Banks was in position as secondary contain and McFadden overlapped for support. Great rep. pic.twitter.com/ia9dLiexa5 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Arvell Reese has some serious pop on contact. pic.twitter.com/ir1268qw0f — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Arvell Reese is a DUDE!👀 Reese quickly fit and blew up the Vikings' FB behind the line of scrimmage. pic.twitter.com/cdhRqU9lUT — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Defense Arvell Reese introduced himself well in his 12 preseason snaps. What stood out the most was his physicality and pop on contact. Reese can take on blocks and surprised both the fullback and tight end ( TJ Hockenson ). He did an excellent job on the top play, fitting the run quickly for a STOP. Reese was the third-highest-graded Giants’ defender behind Tyler Nubin and Josh Tupou. Dennard Wilson ran a simulated pressure on 3rd & 3 with Cover-1 Press on the back end. Reese is stacked as Carter goes up the arc and Golston slants inward; it gets picked up as McFadden mans up the RB. Excellent reps by both Tae Banks and Colton Hood on the outside. pic.twitter.com/EZrEVdhb0t — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Cornerbacks Tae Banks and Colton Hood both had up-and-down performances, with grabbing becoming an issue at times, but each also produced quality reps — particularly when asked to play press-man in Dennard Wilson’s scheme. Wilson was creative on third down, showing multiple ways to generate four- and five-man pressures. The Giants brought pressure from different levels of the defense, including linebackers, cornerbacks, and safeties, giving opposing quarterbacks plenty to process. It was refreshing to see a more aggressive approach from the Giants’ defense, especially after the relatively conservative approach we’ve seen over the last two seasons. Of course, it was only preseason, so the true extent of Wilson’s aggressiveness remains to be seen. Still, the early signs suggest this defense could be far more willing to attack than what Giants fans have grown accustomed to. 4-3 front from Dennard Wilson on first down w/ Leki Fotu as the EMOLOS to the boundary. Caleb Murphy as the WILL w/ Washington dropped into the box. Abdul Carter does a phenomenal job working through multiple blocks to track down JJ McCarthy to the field. pic.twitter.com/5KY2mrBjY3 — Nick Falato (@nickfalato) August 16, 2026 Abdul Carter does a GREAT job as the field end, working through two blocks to track down J.J. McCarthy (9) and make a tackle at the line of scrimmage. Carter was praised by Giants’ legend Carl Banks on this play: Not many can do what Carter does here and kids dont try ot and Coaches dont try to teach.. He literally goes underneath 2 blocks and still make a tackle for loss.. This is the sh*t LT would do. Defied the laws of leverage https://t.co/yJuEE0vVDC — Carl Banks (@CarlBanksGIII) August 17, 2026 Another quality run defense rep by the #Giants defense on 1st & 10. Kayvon Thibodeaux ripped through the tackle's inside shoulder as the LBs quickly got to the LOS. Both Darius Alexander and Josh Tupou eat double teams, and Carter does enough to restrict the C-Gap.…

title: NY Giants news: Malik Nabers, Arvell Reese, and goodbye to Turbo
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to scrimmage the Miami Dolphins this week. Power jumps off Arvell Reese’s Giants debut film: ‘He’s a Ferrari’ | New York Daily News Arvell Reese may be a rookie, but he doesn’t hit like one. Minnesota […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to scrimmage the Miami Dolphins this week. Power jumps off Arvell Reese’s Giants debut film: ‘He’s a Ferrari’ | New York Daily News Arvell Reese may be a rookie, but he doesn’t hit like one. Minnesota Vikings fullback Max Bredeson, left guard Donovan Jackson and tight end T.J. Hockenson found that out in the No. 5 overall pick’s Giants preseason debut on Saturday at MetLife Stadium. Reese blew up one Jordan Mason run by diagnosing the play, shedding Jackson on the move and making the tackle. He knocked Bredeson down to the ground on his knees with a crushing 1-on-1 collision with the Vikes’ fullback on an Aaron Jones carry that the running back had to turn inside. And Reese moved Hockenson back a couple yards on another Jones run. Baldy breaks down Arvell Reese . @Giants @Vikings @arvxll "step up and blow it up!!" All 👀👀 on #52. You will miss good stuff if you do #BaldysBreakdowns pic.twitter.com/jTqvlbF7N8 — Brian Baldinger (@BaldyNFL) August 16, 2026 Former Players Association president: ‘Insane’ Dart bothered by blue tent | NJ.com Domonique Foxworth, a former president of the NFL Players Association, says it’s “insane” and “stupid” that Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart was frustrated with having to go to the blue medical tent on Saturday for a concussion evaluation during a preseason game with the Minnesota Vikings. “All quarterbacks have to change something about the way that they play,” Foxworth said Monday on ESPN’s “Get Up.” “I think Jaxson Dart’s personality is a thing that I find a little bit more unique and interesting, that he puts this kind of linebacker mentality to the game. And I think it’s insane that he’s bothered by going to the blue tent in a preseason game when he got blasted and stayed on the ground for extra seconds. If that’s what he’s pushing back on, that’s just stupid.” How Giants QB Jaxson Dart is acclimating to a new offense in New York | The Athletic But as Dart acclimates to a new offense — particularly after playing in one last year that was largely built to make his transition to the NFL as smooth as possible — growing pains were expected. And amid the process of adjusting to a new scheme, Dart actually sees all the new voices as a positive thing — he’s soaking up a lot of knowledge from coaches who have been at this for a long time. “You get to hear their perspectives. You get to hear, obviously, their coaching each and every day,” Dart said. “That alone gives this staff a really good edge for us as a team. … As players, we have all the confidence in the world in them being able to put us in the best spots to succeed.” How Malachi Fields’ value to Giants goes beyond catching the football | The Record Malachi Fields just smirked at the mere mention of the play. Sure, the New York Giants rookie wide receiver was more than happy to talk about how he and quarterback Jaxson Dart connected for the most impressive touchdown of the preseason to this point. But that wasn’t the one play Fields enjoyed making most Saturday afternoon in the Giants’ exhibition loss to the Minnesota Vikings. NFL Preseason Week 1: Rookie Team of the Week | PFF Wide Receivers: Malachi Fields, Giants (90.4). The 74th overall pick, Malachi Fields, ran only 11 routes but moved the chains three times. That included an impressive contested touchdown catch on a scramble drill, a play he executed with the awareness of an established veteran. title: Jets Defensive Optimism?
summary: The 2025 Jets stunk. That isn’t lost on anyone right now. But the stat that emphasized their ineptitude more than any other was the fact that their defense failed to record a single interception. The Jets defense was truly one of the worst units in the league last year. No one who watched them can […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - AUGUST 14: Head Coach Aaron Glenn of the New York Jets looks on during the game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at MetLife Stadium on August 14, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2025 Jets stunk. That isn’t lost on anyone right now. But the stat that emphasized their ineptitude more than any other was the fact that their defense failed to record a single interception. The Jets defense was truly one of the worst units in the league last year. No one who watched them can possibly deny it, and just about every statistical measure backs that up. That being said, what if I said there’s a ton of evidence that the Jets defense should improve this year by simply blind luck regardless if they hadn’t completely overhauled the defensive roster. Looking historically, we can examine the five worst teams in terms of season interception totals: the 2018 49ers, 2020 Texans, 2008 Lions, 2024 Browns and 2024 Giants. On average, all five defenses meaningfully increased their interception totals the following season. They averaged an increase of eight interceptions, while the two teams with the fewest interceptions averaged a 12-interception increase. Now, listen, I don’t want to suggest that the Jets’ interception drought last year was entirely bad luck. Even when you account for turnovers and omit garbage time, the Jets were consistently a bottom-5 to bottom-10 statistical unit by most measures. One stat I found surprising when looking through the Jets defense in 2025 was that they actually weren’t all that bad in pass breakups. According to FTN Fantasy, the Jets actually got their hands on the ball in pass coverage at roughly an average rate for an NFL defense in 2025. Normally, teams that generate that many opportunities don’t underachieve to the extent that the Jets did when it came to actually creating turnovers. Now that’s not to say that the Jets defense was potentially incapable of turning pass breakups into turnovers. Turnovers are certainly influenced by luck, but they also require an element of skill and playmaking ability. The Jets simply weren’t making those plays, but even then it was at a level that is unprecedented historically. Even from a fumble-recovery perspective, the Jets recovered just 35.5% of available fumbles, which ranked 31st in the league. Put all of that together, and it’s difficult to imagine a scenario in which the Jets experience the same level of turnover misfortune again. They don’t need to suddenly become a good defense for their turnover numbers to improve. They just need to stop being historically bad at turning defensive opportunities into actual takeaways. With eight potential new starters and legitimately 10-11 new bodies who should see significant snaps, there’s a lot of opportunity for that to happen. If the Jets defense doesn’t show meaningful improvement in the turnover department this year, that would be a massive disappointment. At that point, given the amount of roster turnover and investment on that side of the ball … let’s just say Aaron Glenn likely won’t have a job come January.
