title: Commanders 2026 Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Power Rankings – Week 2
summary: The annual Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Award competition is now well underway following the Commanders’ 20-7 beatdown of the Miami Dolphins.  Each week of the preseason, I will be publishing my own Bris Vegas Preseason Hype! Power Rankings ©, tracking the progress of the team’s late-round draft picks and undrafted roster hopefuls in generating hype through […]
full_text: The annual Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Award competition is now well underway following the Commanders’ 20-7 beatdown of the Miami Dolphins. Each week of the preseason, I will be publishing my own Bris Vegas Preseason Hype! Power Rankings ©, tracking the progress of the team’s late-round draft picks and undrafted roster hopefuls in generating hype through their efforts to claw their way onto the roster or practice squad. Players’ rankings reflect not only the hype they have generated to date, but also their potential to generate more hype as the preseason unfolds and position battles intensify ahead of roster cuts. For the benefit of new readers to the site, Hogs Haven’s annual Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Awards were named after Redskins sixth-round pick Colt Brennan and UDFA running back Marcus Mason to celebrate the struggles and occasional triumphs of players on the roster fringe battling against the odds to roster spots and playing time. Most of these players will end up on practice squads or washing out of the league. But, every season, a few of them will manage to keep their NFL dreams alive. And, as I recently showed, every Super Bowl team features at least a few major contributors who began their NFL journeys in a similar way to the players in this article. While the focus of the Mason/Brennan award is on hype, sometimes the hype turns into reality. And those of are some of the most exciting storylines of the NFL preseason and tend to produce fan favorites like Alfred Morris and Jeremy Reaves. Following the draft and UDFA signings, I previewed this year’s Mason/Brennan contestants, ranked by hype potential: Front Runners Chasing Pack Dark Horses and Longshots The first installment of the power rankings will track how they have fared compared to their initial offseason rankings. Before we get to that, let’s review the eligibility rules. The Rules Player must have been drafted late or signed by the Redskins as an undrafted free agent. Players that have only been on other teams’ practice squads that are signed by the team are also eligible. A player that has been on the team for several years is still eligible if most of that time has been spent on the practice squad, inactive, or with very limited productivity/time The Keenan “the Barbarian” Robinson Amendment: only sixth-round draft picks or later for their first two years in the league. Now that we’ve got that out of the way, here is how the race for the Mason/Brennan Preseason Hype! Award is shaping up, with the first preseason game in the books. Preseason Hype! – Week 2 Power Rankings 1. K Drew Stevens (1), no change As I mentioned in the intro, sometimes the hype turns into reality. Drew Stevens became the first Mason/Brennan contestant to graduate and become a roster lock when the Commanders released his competitor , Jake Moody, shortly after the first preseason game. I haven’t quite figured out whether that eliminates him from the competition or not. For now, he sits atop the power rankings as a shining beacon of hope for all of the other roster hopefuls fighting their own position battles. 2. RB Robert Henry Jr (11), +9 Robert Henry has shot up the board, thanks to a sizzling 75 yd/12 att (6.3 Y/A), 1 TD breakout performance in his first preseason outing. Henry’s quick burst out of his breaks was on full display as he broke off runs of 22, 15 and 24 yards through the right side of the line and around the right end. He made even more of a splash on kick returns with one allowed return for 30 yards and a second solid effort negated by a penalty. Henry had been flying under the radar, beneath a deep and underrated running back rotation in camp, before bursting onto the scene with a standout performance against the Dolphins. The Commanders’ decision on which running backs to keep just became a lot more complicated. Sam in BrisVegas: I was on to Henry before it was cool. He’s going to be good. 3. WR Jaden “Moss” Bradley (5), +2 In hindsight, it is hard to believe that Jaden Bradley was ranked as low as fifth before the pads came on. Bradley evaded notice of the draft media, despite posting a 58 rec, 931 yd, 4 TD stat line in his fifth college season at UNLV. As foreshadowed in the Mason/Brennan Preview , Bradley has lived up to his hype potential, with a standout performance in camp raising questions about how many receivers the Commanders will keep on the 53-man roster. Bradley’s hopes of earning a roster spot seemed to take a hit, with the Stefon Diggs signing , along with all of the other roster hopefuls at receiver. But he might force a rethink if he can maintain the momentum he established in training camp. He didn’t hurt his chances with a solid outing in the first preseason game, catching 2-of-3 targets from quarterbacks Sam Hartman and Athan Kaliakmanis for 21 total yards and 11 YAC with one drop, and nearly blocking two punts. 4. QB Athan Kaliakmanis (17), +13 Athan Kaliakmanis seemed to be facing a ceiling on his preseason hype potential when I wrote the preview, because he was battling for the third string QB position. That was before an injury to primary backup Marcus Mariota in the preseason opener created an opening. Kaliakmanis seized the opportunity, with a strong debut performance, to leapfrog Sam Hartman into the next position on the depth chart. If Mariota misses significant time — the Commanders are optmistic Mariota will be ready for Week 1 — Kaliakmanis has positioned himself to be Jayden Daniels’ game day backup. 5. RB Kaytron Allen (2), -3 Kaytron Allen hasn’t done anything to hurt his hype potential. He was simply overtaken by the hype trains building behind Robert Henry and Athan Kaliakmanis. Allen has had a solid camp and delivered a strong performance in the preseason opener, leading the Commanders in rushing yards (23 att, 85 yds, 3.7 Y/A) and scoring his first NFL TD. 6. DT Ricky Barber (6), no change Ricky Barber was almost scratched from consideration, because of his off-the charts productivity (3 comb tackles, 1 TFL, 1 sack, 1 QB hit, 25% pressure rate) in 15 defensive snaps last season. But I bent the rules to keep him in it by leaning on the fact that he has had “very limited… time .” Barber flashed hype potential with a strong performance against the Dolphins. Lining up predominantly at right defensive tackle, he was a force in the A-gaps. Barber co-led the team with three defensive stops, along with fellow interior defensive lineman Shy Tuttle, and was second in pressures with one quarterback hit and one hurry. If he keeps up that pace, he might force his way onto the roster or at least reclaim his position on the practice squad. 7. C Matt Gulbin (4), -3 The Commanders’ pivot to Julian Good-Jones when starting center Nick Allegretti was injured was a setback to Gulbin’s preseason hype campaign, without a doubt. Gulbin fought back the best way he could, with a strong outing in pass protection (0 pressures allowed). He opened running lanes for Robert Henry Jr. and Kaytron Allen and did a good job climbing to the next level to seal off defenders in the preseason opener. Those fans hoping to see Gulbin battling for the starting center job might get something to cheer for if he can keep building on that performance. 8. S Malik Spencer (7), -1 Malik Spencer announced his presence by making the first interception of training camp, then followed that up with strong practice performances and another interception in the first preseason game. Spencer is a versatile defensive back who can play everything from nickel to box and free safety and even a bit of dime ‘backer. He has the advantage of competing in the thinnest position group on the roster. If he can keep drawing the coaches’ attention with big takeaways, he has a shot of beating out Percy Butler for the last safety spot. 9. G Tanoa Togiai (10), +1 Tanoa Togiai is a super athletic but raw interior offensive lineman. The reshuffling of the offensive line, in the wake of injuries to Laremy Tunsil and…

title: How ‘conviction’ helped Drew Stevens win Commanders kicking competition
summary: Commanders special teams coordinator Larry Izzo called Drew Stevens with some important news.   The undrafted rookie had won Washington’s kicking competition. Incumbent Jake Moody was being released. The team was formally naming Stevens the starter.   The Iowa product was stunned, but not by the honor. He had been kicking well all spring and […]
full_text: Commanders special teams coordinator Larry Izzo called Drew Stevens with some important news. The undrafted rookie had won Washington’s kicking competition . Incumbent Jake Moody was being released. The team was formally naming Stevens the starter. The Iowa product was stunned, but not by the honor. He had been kicking well all spring and summer. It was the timing that set him back. “It was (Monday) when I found out, and it was crazy because I was not expecting it at all,” Stevens told on-site reporters in a Tuesday press conference . “I thought we were going to play all three preseason games and then do it. This is my first rodeo. I have no idea. I’m just trying to play (well) on the field.” Head coach Dan Quinn didn’t see a need to continue the competition any further, explaining his logic for ending it now and setting Stevens up for success. “I thought it was a good competition going all the way back to the spring,” Quinn said in his Tuesday presser. “We kicked almost every day back then and 2 out of 3 days in training camp in these blocks. I thought both guys have had productive days, but I thought Drew established himself. He was kicking it pure and clean. It is important for him to have the next two games where he gets all the kicks, all the moments. It was a good competition. I thought Drew earned it. Now we’re moving forward.” Our starting kicker: pic.twitter.com/5PT7ObsDrn — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 18, 2026 Stevens has put his best foot forward this camp. Per 106.7 The Fan host Grant Paulsen , Stevens was 43-of-48 in camp practices and 1-for-1 in the preseason. Then, per Commanders reporter Ben Standig , Stevens went 6-for-6 on Tuesday, in his first practice as the lone kicker, including a hit from 60 yards out. Stevens said Tuesday’s practice felt no different than any other. Why? His approach hasn’t changed. He believes in his technique and his approach to the craft. That’s unwavering. It got him through four standout years at Iowa, and he’s not veering from it now. Stevens has a word for it, and it’s a good one for kickers. Conviction. “I’m believing that what I do is going to be good enough.” Steadfast confidence has served him well to this point. His mental approach will help him in the NFL, where the pressure’s always sky-high. “It is the most important thing,” Stevens said. “How many kickers have you seen just bomb one dead straight? That means you’re physically capable of doing it every time. Then where’s the disconnect? It’s up here (pointing to his head). Getting your mind right is the most important thing in kicking. Being convicted is showing true belief in what it is you’re doing.” Stevens is always willing to listen, especially to those more experienced. He followed in Moody’s footsteps in terms of learning how to be a pro and operate well within an NFL organization. Stevens gave Moody credit for that, freely giving advice during a competition where the runner-up would lose his job. Stevens thanked Moody twice during his seven-minute presser, making sure everyone knew how gracious Moody was, even in defeat. “He’s a really good human,” Stevens said. “It’s all the things he doesn’t have to do that he does. Probably two hours after I found out – he had obviously found out – he still texted me and said, ‘Hey man, best of luck. I’m here if you need anything.’ He did not have to do that. He could’ve not said anything. I’m sure some other guys would have done that. It’s just a huge character thing when you do something like he did.”

title: Commanders transactions: Jerome Ford to IR among several roster moves
summary: Commanders running back Jerome Ford was active and available to start Friday’s preseason game against Miami. Somewhere during Washington’s 20-7 victory over the Dolphins, the veteran’s status changed.   He suffered a hamstring injury, head coach Dan Quinn said, that proved to be a serious one. It resulted in the Commanders placing him on injured […]
full_text: Commanders running back Jerome Ford was active and available to start Friday’s preseason game against Miami. Somewhere during Washington’s 20-7 victory over the Dolphins, the veteran’s status changed. He suffered a hamstring injury, head coach Dan Quinn said, that proved to be a serious one. It resulted in the Commanders placing him on injured reserve on Tuesday morning, effectively ending his season. A player placed on IR before the 53-man roster deadline makes a player ineligible to return, though he can be waived with an injury settlement and play for another team when healthy. Ford and receiver River Cracraft were moved to IR as part of a series of roster moves announced before Tuesday’s non-padded practice. We have made the following roster moves: – Signed LB Krys Barnes, DT Maurice Hurst II, TE Tre McKitty and RB Craig Reynolds – Released P Matt Haack and K Jake Moody – Placed WR River Cracraft and RB Jerome Ford on the Reserve/Injured List pic.twitter.com/O5G4v1erga — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 18, 2026 Most of them were reported on Monday, but a few were not. That includes the addition of veteran defensive tackle Maurice Hurst II, a Michigan product drafted in 2018 with stops in Oakland/Las Vegas, San Francisco and Cleveland. Tight end Tre’ McKitty was also signed. He played regular-season games for the Chargers from 2022-24. The signings of linebacker Krys Barnes and running back Craig Reynolds were also confirmed. Some of these signings make more sense when matched with those not practicing Tuesday due to injury. Don’t see LB Jordan Magee or DL Johnny Newton out here at Commanders practice. Told both are injury-related, but teams are not required to disclose injury specifics in camp/preseason. — Nicki Jhabvala (@NickiJhabvala) August 18, 2026 Hursts and Barnes will help in those areas, and Reynolds picks up some slack with Ford on IR. In addition, the Commanders make kicker Jake Moody’s release official and also cut reserve punter Matt Haack. Tress Way was active, but only held for field goals. He’ll return to full duty in training camp this week and on Saturday against the Lions.

Commanders links Articles Bullocks Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Review: Joshua Josephs vs Dolphins Coming out of college, Josephs profiled as a unique blend of size, length, athleticism with upside not just as a pass rusher and run defender, but in coverage too . New defensive coordinator Daronte Jones comes from a Vikings defense where they task edge rushers to not just be able to rush the passer and stop the run, but also be capable of dropping into coverage. They need edge rushers like Andrew Van Ginkel that can do all three facets because of the blitzing nature of the defense where anyone can rush and anyone can be asked to drop into coverage on any given play. Josephs has the profile to fit that role well, but he looked very raw coming out of college. In his first action in preseason. Josephs proved he was still raw with plenty to work on, but also that he could compete at this level and offer something in all three parts of what this defense asks from its edge rushers. Let’s start first with the pass rush. Against the Dolphins, you could see that Josephs still has a lot to work on to improve his pass rush technique, but despite that, he is still a real handful for offensive lineman. Commanders 5th rounder OLB Joshua Josephs might be a bit raw technically, but in the preseason opener against the Dolphins, he flashed his potential as a pass rusher, run defender AND in coverage. I broke it all down: https://t.co/0TkDy66iC6 pic.twitter.com/Rhdezzw5xr — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) August 18, 2026 The Athletic (paywall) Commanders to release K Jake Moody, give starting job to rookie Drew Stevens At Iowa, he broke or tied school records for most made field goals (76), 50-plus-yard field goals (12) and longest field goal (58 yards). He connected on 80 percent of his attempts in college (76 of 95) and missed only two of 126 extra-point attempts. During the spring, Stevens said his range stretched to about 63 to 65 yards, when not accounting for outside conditions. His long-time kicking trainer, Dan Orner, told The Athletic at the time that he believes Stevens’ range can actually stretch to 65 or 70 yards. Last season, 73 NFL games were decided by three points or fewer, tying the league’s all-time single-season record. What’s more, kickers made 12 of 22 field-goal attempts from at least 60 yards, shattering league records. “What the most important thing is gonna be is who’s making the kicks,” special teams coordinator Larry Izzo said in June. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Sports Illustrated Dan Quinn Reveals Next Stage of Commanders’ Center Competition When asked how important it is for Allegretti to get as many reps with quarterback Jayden Daniels as possible, he couldn’t answer fast enough. “Yeah, it’s for sure super important. Not just for he and Jay, but for the two guards next to him, the identification, the call,” said Quinn. “So, he’s been doing the walkthroughs in the evenings, but that’s just not the same.” Quinn continued about Allegretti’s ramp-up process: “And so those reps will be important. We won’t give him 50 plays right off the bat. We’ll work him back into a ramp-up as he’s returning to play. But it is super important just to make sure the communication, the calls, all of that comes together. So, that’s the goal, man. Now start stacking days with he and Jay together.” Quinn made sure to point out that the competition has now evolved: “So, over the next two weeks, or maybe two and a half weeks, we’ll call it,” Quinn said. “I’d like to see what that rotation looks like with the three of these guys.” That gives this competition an identifiable evaluation window through the rest of preseason, which it has lacked so far. Quinn’s little nugget at the end gives Gulbin another shot at the 53-man roster: “I’ll also probably work Matt at some guard at some point.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable RB Craig Reynolds returns to Commanders roster after 5 seasons in Detroit Reynolds, 30, arrives in Washington adding depth at the position given the news comes one day after head coach Dan Quinn said that veteran Jeremy McNichols is expected to be sidelined a few weeks due to a quad injury. Reynolds will now look to serve as a boost in preseason and play spoiler in his second stint with the team. The former undrafted free agent first arrived in Washington as part of rookie minicamp in May 2019 before being waived ahead of the final round of roster cuts, leading him to spend the 2019 season on the Atlanta Falcons’ practice squad. After the spending the 2020 season on the Jacksonville Jaguars practice squad along with appearing in two games, Reynolds made a name for himself with the Detroit Lions as part of the rotation where he’s totaled over 650 rushing yards and one touchdown in two starts and 55 appearances over the last five seasons. Barnes was one of four linebackers to work out for the team alongside Triston Newson, Brandon Smith and Kyzir White while a trio of tight ends — Brandon Frazier, Johnny Lumpkin, Tre McKitty — also arrived in Ashburn for workouts. The signing makes Barnes just the second free agent linebacker to sign with the Commanders this offseason with Leo Chenal, along with the third addition to the unit with rookie Sonny Styles anchoring the inside linebackers. Barnes spent the 2025 season with the Carolina Panthers where he tallied 23 total tackles and 0.5 sacks in seven games before becoming a free agent. He also started in six games and appeared in 32 games during his two seasons with the Arizona Cardinals where he tallied 90 total tackles, two sacks and an interception. He began his NFL career with the Green Bay Packers after inking a three year deal back in 2020 where he started in 24 games and appeared in 35 during the duration of his contract. Barnes recorded career-highs with 81 total tackles and 58 solo tackles in his second season with the Packers, along with 20 total tackles across three postseason appearances. title: How Commanders preseason win vs. Dolphins influenced key position battles
summary: The Commanders entered training camp with several key position battles needing resolution.   One has come early. Washington sided with Drew Stevens in the kicker competition, a point made clear by Jake Moody’s reported release on Monday afternoon. That made the undrafted rookie out of Iowa the choice, assuming Stevens continues playing well and no […]
full_text: The Commanders entered training camp with several key position battles needing resolution. One has come early. Washington sided with Drew Stevens in the kicker competition, a point made clear by Jake Moody’s reported release on Monday afternoon. That made the undrafted rookie out of Iowa the choice, assuming Stevens continues playing well and no other competition is added. There are several unsettled position battles on this roster, though Friday night’s preseason game had some influence on them. Let’s reexamine the state of a few roster spots following that 20-7 victory over the Miami Dolphins at Northwest Stadium. Running back The Commanders might have a tough time deciding how to round out their running back room. Bill Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White are obviously the top options, with sixth-rounder Kaytron Allen firmly in the mix. Veteran Jeremy McNichols will be out a few weeks dealing with a quadriceps injury , which kept him out of Friday’s game and a series of future practices. Jerome Ford returned the first kickoff, but didn’t play much. That created an opportunity for undrafted rookie Robert Henry Jr., who took full advantage . The former Texas-San Antonio back took full advantage, with 75 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries. He’s an explosive playmaker who quickly became a fan camp crush and is someone we need to see more of in the preseason. Can he protect the passer? Can he contribute well on special teams. The Commanders need all of that from a fourth running back. While McNichols is out a little while, he’s also a proven commodity. That will keep him firmly in the mix despite his injury. Center Nick Allegretti is set to return to practice on Tuesday. That’s a positive development for a position that has been without its starter since the first camp practice. Top reserve Julian Good-Jones has struggled some in camp, and there’s some video of him getting beat during Friday night’s game. Good-Jones gets completely BLOWN UP by a Dolphins LB on a blitz pic.twitter.com/nMh3sQWrbO — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 Our Mark Tyler also found evidence of Matt Gulbin playing well at center as a pass protector and a quality blocker in the second level. Quinn praised Gulbin’s performance during a Sunday press conference , and also said he’ll get some reps at guard to round out his versatility as a 2026 depth piece. Allegretti’s still your starter at center. His direct backup seems up in the air at this point, with Gulbin’s performance making it possible he could end up in the No. 2 spot on the depth chart. Safety Quan Martin had a solid game on Friday, parterning with Will Harris at the safety spot early in Friday’s game. He played a bit more than expected for someone who has played prominently over the past two seasons, but he’s locked in a position battle with veteran Jeremy Reaves. Quinn intimated that Reaves and three-down starter Nick Cross could be featured in a Week 2 preseason game at Detroit, allowing the staff to compare and contrast their options at safety. Quan coming downhill like a 🦇 out of HELL to make the big hit!!! pic.twitter.com/OKEHRODgA0 — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 Martin looked good on Friday, but he’ll have to maintain that level of play to fight off Reaves. Martin was often a liability last season — he had a 155 passer rating allowed when targeted in 2025 — and the Commanders need better from the safety position overall in 2026. Cross will provide that, but he needs a running mate that’s solid in coverage and playing deep. Martin’s game play was decent. Let’s see how Reaves responds when he’s given game reps. Quarterback Marcus Mariota suffered a right MCL sprain early in Friday’s game, leaving most of the work to Sam Hartman and Athan Kaliakmanis. Expect that trend to continue, with Mariota set to miss the entire preseason and Quinn stating the Commanders don’t anticiapte adding another quarterback. Jayden Daniels is the unquestioned starter and Mariota is his backup, but the Commanders will keep one developmental third quarterback. Which guy will win that spot? Kaliakmanis showed better on Friday, showcasing solid arm talent. Hartman was inefficient and had some big misses and an interception that showed lackluster decision making. Both quarterbacks must be better to take the lead in the race for QB3. The receivers need them on point as well, as they try to stand out and make the plays required to earn a roster spot. It will be interesting to see which quarterback takes second-team reps with Mariota out. That will be our first clue in who has the lead coming out of Friday. Based on that game, it should be Kaliakmanis. Wide Receiver Stefon Diggs complicated the receiver depth chart in the best possible way, adding proven, dynamic production to the No. 2 receiver spot. The Commanders have options with how to complete the group and the roles within it. Rookie Antonio Williams is expected to be the third option prominently featured in the slot, but it was mildly notable that he didn’t enter Friday’s game until the third quarter, well after others got their shot. Jaylin Lane caught some key passes. Treylon Burks was involved. Dyami Brown is sitting right there, and we haven’t even mentioned Luke McCaffrey yet. I just can’t see the Commanders keeping seven receivers, even with two of them as prominent returners and special teams players. Then there’s undrafted receiver Jaden Bradley. We need more time for these receivers to create separation and see which guy is performing in what role. Receivers made some nice plays, but it’s hard to say the first preseason game settled any arguments.

title: Countdown to the Super Bowl: Best teams ever to fall short
summary: ESPN is kicking off it's countdown to Super Bowl LXI series by ranking the best teams that didn't quite make the big game, including the 2023 Ravens.
full_text:
This February, ESPN will televise Super Bowl LXI for the first time. We will count down to the big game with Super Bowl stories every month. 

 Does the best team in the NFL always win at the end? Winning the Super Bowl is the goal, but the team that takes home the championship isn't always the best from start to finish. History is littered with teams that dominated in the regular season only to surprise with failures in the playoffs.

 Below, I took a look at some of the most elite teams to fall short of reaching the Super Bowl, according to my proprietary DVOA ratings ( explained further here ) which looks at efficiency on a play-by-play basis adjusted for situation and opponent. We've also included a couple of teams from before 1977 with estimated DVOA ratings.

 The top teams by DVOA to miss the Super Bowl are division rivals. One franchise saw its playoff failure very recently, blowing two straight dominant regular seasons. The other franchise saw its best regular-season team fall short 50 years ago.

 

 

 1. 2023 Baltimore Ravens (44.4% DVOA) 
 13-4, lost in AFC Championship Game 17-10 to Chiefs 

 

 4. 2024 Baltimore Ravens (40.9% DVOA) 
 12-5, lost in AFC divisional round 27-25 to Bills 

 By DVOA, the 2023 Ravens are the best team that didn't reach the Super Bowl, and the 2024 Ravens are right behind. The 2023 edition ranked fourth in the league in points scored and first in fewest points allowed. The 2024 edition had an even better offense, leading the league in DVOA by dominating the fifth-toughest schedule of opposing defenses.

 

 The 2023 Ravens weren't just winning in the regular season; they were blowing out other good teams. They beat the 12-5 Lions by the ridiculous score of 38-6. They beat the 12-5 49ers by two touchdowns on Christmas Day. They beat the 10-7 Texans twice, by 16 points in the regular season and then 24 points in the playoffs.

 The 2024 Ravens had some similar wins. They beat the 13-4 Bills by a score of 35-10 and the 10-7 Broncos by a score of 41-10. On Christmas Day, they beat the AFC South champion Texans 31-2.

 But the Ravens just couldn't get over the hump with two close playoff losses. Quarterback  Lamar Jackson struggled in 2023, but Baltimore lost to Kansas City in part because wide receiver  Zay Flowers fumbled the ball at the goal line. In 2024, Jackson played better in a battle of the previous two MVPs; the Ravens outgained quarterback Josh Allen  and the Bills 416-273 in total yards but turned the ball over three times. A last-minute comeback fell short when Mark Andrews dropped a 2-point conversion pass with 1:33 left.

 
 

 2. 1976 Pittsburgh Steelers (44.3% estimated DVOA) 
 10-4, lost in AFC Championship Game 24-7 to Raiders 

 The Steel Curtain of 1976 very well might have been the best defense in NFL history, especially from Week 6 onward. In the final nine games of the regular season, the Steelers had five shutouts. They won all nine games by a combined margin of 211-28. Then they blew out the Baltimore Colts 40-14 in the divisional round of the playoffs.

 Unfortunately, Steelers running backs Franco Harris and Rocky Bleier suffered injuries in the win over the Colts. The next week, the Oakland Raiders shut down the Pittsburgh offense except for a single touchdown drive in the second quarter. The Raiders ended the first half with a surprising play-action touchdown pass from 13 personnel at the goal line and then totally controlled the second half and went on to win Super Bowl XI.

 
 

 3. 2010 New England Patriots (42.4% DVOA) 
 14-2, lost in AFC divisional round 28-21 to Jets 

 Based on DVOA, the 2010 Patriots had the most efficient offense in NFL history, narrowly surpassing the 16-0 Pats from 2007 and the strike-shortened season of the 1982 San Diego Chargers. The Patriots and quarterback Tom Brady dominated with the help of two undrafted running backs (BenJarvus Green-Ellis and Danny Woodhead) and two rookie tight ends (Rob Gronkowski and Aaron Hernandez). They scored 32.4 points per game even though they traded wide receiver Randy Moss in early October. The Patriots scored at least 31 points in each of their final eight games of the regular season, all wins.

 The divisional-round rematch with their rivals from New York didn't seem like a big deal, especially since the Patriots had beaten the Jets a few weeks before by the absurd score of 45-3. But Brady threw his first interception since Week 6 on the Patriots' first drive, setting up the Jets for their first touchdown. A botched fake punt with a direct snap to safety Patrick Chung didn't help, as the Jets scored their second touchdown on the ensuing drive. The Patriots came back a bit late but couldn't recover an onside kick, and the Jets won.

 

 
 

 5. 1968 Dallas Cowboys (37.8% estimated DVOA) 
 12-2, lost in NFC divisional round 31-20 to Browns 

 The Cowboys opened the season by stomping the Lions 59-13 and never looked back. They finished the season with a league-best average of 30.8 points per game and were second in points allowed at 13.3. Don Meredith made the Pro Bowl at quarterback and wide receiver Bob Hayes was a first-team All-Pro with 909 receiving yards and 10 touchdowns. The defense was led by first-team All-Pro defensive tackle Bob Lilly and All-Pro linebacker Chuck Howley.

 But back then in the playoffs, home-field advantage was rotated instead of it being based on record, so the Cowboys had to travel to Cleveland to face the 10-4 Browns. It didn't seem like a cause for concern, since the Cowboys had won 28-7 over the Browns early in the season. But Meredith was terrible, going 3-for-9 with three interceptions before coach Tom Landry replaced him with Craig Morton. The Browns won the game, and Meredith went on to retire that offseason.

 
 

 6. 1973 Los Angeles Rams (37.6% estimated DVOA) 
 12-2, lost in NFC divisional round 27-16 to Cowboys 

 The Rams had a remarkable streak of coming close in the 1970s. They were 10-4 or better every single season from 1972 to 1978 but never made it to the Super Bowl until they went 9-7 and snuck through the playoffs in 1979. Of all those 1970s Rams teams, the 1973 edition was the best, leading the league with an average of 27.7 points scored and finishing fourth with just 12.7 points allowed. Quarterback John Hadl and wide receiver Harold Jackson were both first-team All-Pros, as was linebacker Isiah Robertson.

 But the Rams had to go to Texas to play the 10-4 Cowboys in the divisional round. Two Rams turnovers in the first quarter helped the Cowboys take a 14-0 lead. Three missed field goal attempts by David Ray did not help, but the Rams still came back and made the score 17-16 with 10 minutes left. Then Cowboys receiver Drew Pearson scored an 83-yard touchdown when Rams defensive backs Dave Elmendorf and Steve Preece ran into each other trying to tackle him.

 
 

 7. 1987 San Francisco 49ers (36.5% DVOA) 
 13-2 (but actually 10-2), lost in NFC divisional round 36-24 to Vikings 

 Minnesota's 1987 divisional-round upset of the 49ers is one of the greatest upsets in NFL history, but it becomes a bit murky once you filter through all the nonsense from the 1987 players' strike.

 

 The 49ers won all three of their games with replacement players, which suggests they weren't really as good as their 13-2 record. But they played the sixth-toughest schedule in the NFL that season in those games without replacement players, so DVOA suggests they were actually better than their "real" 10-2 record. The Niners ranked third in offensive DVOA and first in defensive DVOA. (I don't include the strike games in the 1987 DVOA ratings.)

 The Vikings, meanwhile, lost all three of their games with replacement players, which suggests they were better than their 8-7 record. But their "real" 8-4 record came against the third-easiest schedule in the league that season, so DVOA ranks them only No. 7.

 The wild-card Vikings blew out New Orleans (the No. 2 team in DVOA) 44-10. Then they…

title: How important is pass protection for a running back? Ask Jaxson Dart
summary: Dart was leveled after Tyrone Tracy missed a block, reflecting how important the underrated skill is for running backs.
full_text:
IT WAS SUPPOSED to be a routine dropback.

 In the  New York Giants ' preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings on Saturday, starting quarterback Jaxson Dart dropped back and was looking left at his downfield options. On his right, chaos was looming.

 Running back Tyrone Tracy Jr . drifted a bit too far right, tried to reverse course and slipped. Vikings safety Jay Ward sprinted toward Dart and leveled the quarterback. All Tracy could do was crane his neck backward while kneeling on the turf as Dart was crushed at the midfield logo.

 Dart went through the concussion sideline exam and later returned. That didn't stop Giants coach John Harbaugh from saying, "There's no way he should have been hit there. It just shouldn't have happened. It was a basic protection."

 The preseason play highlighted one of the most overlooked aspects of football: a running back's role in pass protection. Typically, the glory and grandeur for ball carriers depends on the number of yards and touchdowns they produce. But a running back who can block is invaluable, especially in the modern game. It's a skill that can secure a spot on the 53-player roster, earn offensive reps and even extend contracts.

 

 And at its core, it sums up the nature of football.

 "It's mano a mano," said Bengals running back Samaje Perine , who is one of the better backs at pass protection in the league. "Everybody else is covered up by linemen. It's just me and you, and may the best man win."

 

 IN 2014, PERINE set the NCAA single-game record with 427 rushing yards in Oklahoma's win over Kansas. While he hasn't been as prolific in his 10-year NFL career, he still has been effective, averaging 4.5 yards per carry or more in five of his past six seasons.

 But the primary reason he has earned nearly $14 million in his career is what he does when he isn't carrying the ball.

 "As a running back, you can't be one-dimensional," Perine said. "If you can only run the ball and if you're not that [No. 1] guy, then your chances of staying in the league go down a lot.

 "So I've learned that just the more you can do, the longer you can stay in."

 What Perine and other effective pass-blocking running backs excel at is typically referred to as a "jet" protection -- where the offensive line will slide to block any defenders and the running back picks up an extra blitzer.

 But here's what that actually looks like: a defender who weighs 200 pounds or more sprinting toward a player who is stationary and bracing for impact.

 After his rookie year in 2017, Aaron Jones was at a charity event during Super Bowl week and ran into Brian Westbrook, an All-Pro running back who played for the Philadelphia Eagles from 2002 to 2009. Jones had one question: How do you get better in pass protection?

 "He was like, 'That's your mom in the pocket,'" Jones recalled. "'Are you going to let him touch your mom? Are you going to let him hit your mom?'

 "I was like, 'When you think about it like that, you're right.'"

 

 Jones wasn't the only running back to gain counsel from a veteran during an early stage in his career. Before New England Patriots running back Rhamondre Stevenson went to the Senior Bowl in 2021, ex-Dallas Cowboy DeMarco Murray, then Stevenson's position coach at Oklahoma, told him that being a proficient pass blocker would generate more interest from teams.

 Murray was right. Stevenson was drafted in the fourth round and is set to enter his sixth season with the Patriots.

 And when Stevenson and other running backs execute a pass block to perfection, it can lead to big things from their offense.

 

 "The underrated part about pass blocking is picking up a pass block and watching [Patriots quarterback Drake Maye ] sit back there with time and throw a [deep ball]," Stevenson said.

 Zach Allen , the Denver Broncos ' 6-5, 285-pound defensive end who had seven sacks last season, has noticed something different about the 6-foot, 227-pound Stevenson.

 "We played the Patriots, we did a stunt and I wrapped, and Stevenson was right there," Allen said. "Usually, you just bull the running back, but I gave him that first contact and I was like, 'OK, I might have to work to a side against him.' Powerful guy.

 "A big body and he takes pride in it. It's easy to see when a guy doesn't."

 

 WHEN THE 2024 season opener was on the line, Baltimore Ravens running back Justice Hill had one of the most daunting tasks in football: blocking Kansas City Chiefs defensive lineman Chris Jones , one of the game's fiercest pass rushers.

 Hill, despite being 8 inches shorter and 115 pounds lighter than Jones, had to keep Jones off Lamar Jackson on back-to-back plays to give the Ravens a chance to win. And Hill did his job. Jackson nearly threw the game-tying pass at the end of regulation in a 27-20 loss.

 The clip went viral as Hill received praise for one of the game's unsung jobs.

 "Obviously I'm not the biggest guy, but it just takes a mindset of like, 'You're not going to get to my quarterback, and I don't care how big you are, how small you are,'" Hill said.

 What makes pass blocking as a running back unique is that it is one of the more teachable skills in football. The calculation is pretty simple.

 

 "It's probably 90% grit, 10% technique," Perine said. "Because at the end of the day, you just have to get in the way."

 That is always easier said than done, especially when facing someone like  Derwin James Jr ., the Los Angeles Chargers ' 6-2, 215-pound safety.

 "Most everybody else, they'll run at you, but then they'll break down at least a little bit to give you a chance to think what you're going to do," Perine said. "Him? He doesn't care. He's just going to run full speed straight into you, torpedo style."

 But a lot goes into that 10% of technique. At the beginning of each game week, Bengals assistant coach Justin Hill will spend considerable time identifying defensive fronts, patterns and what makes different players effective as a pass rusher. Any edge gleaned that can give the quarterback an extra split second is valuable.

 "It's not just about being physical at the point of attack," Justin Hill said. "It's also about you got to be smart enough to understand what the different looks are."

 And sometimes, looks can be deceiving. The Giants thought it was  Jamal Adams  who was going to be blitzing on the play that dropped Dart.

 "I didn't really think I would have a free rush, but our big nickel -- Jamal -- he sold it, so the protection slid to him," Ward said. "The back so happened to get ready to go into a route and ... he didn't think he had anyone [to block] and he seen me come late, and he couldn't adjust."

 Aaron Jones said pass blocking is a two-part process, with the first part being able to understand the protection scheme.

 

 "And then it comes to a want-to and a fight," he said. "So, I would say part of it is understanding protection, and the next part is having the willingness to do it.

 "Now we know every protection is not going to be perfect, but if you get in there and fight and you hit them first, that negates a lot of their charge. Now you're just hand fighting and standing in front instead of this guy hitting you. A lot of times when you get up there and you make that contact, it slows it down and it makes your job a lot easier."

 

 BEING A RELIABLE pass blocker and adding value to teams will be paramount across the NFL over the next couple of weeks. As teams prepare to trim their rosters from the 90-player limit in training camp down to the allotted 53 roster slots for the regular season, protecting the quarterback could prevent a running back from being cut.

 "It's crazy how long that can extend your career," Justice Hill said. "If you told me my second year when I felt like s---, 'You'll be playing here,' standing here at eight years, I wouldn't have believed it.

 "So yeah, just keep doing those little things, and it pays off long term."

 Hill didn't mean to minimize…

title: 2026 Buffalo Bills training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Follow our updates from Bills training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Bills reporter Alaina Getzenberg has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Bills camp. How will the transition to Jim Leonhard's defense go? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Bills' top camp performer and biggest lingering question.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Bills camp 
 
 New grass field held up well in opener, Bills president says 
 Bills' Phidarian Mathis banned 3 games for substance abuse violation 
 Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson carted off with leg injury 
 Josh Allen on Bills' alternate uniforms: 'Stop hating on the jerseys' 
 
 
 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 The Bills took to the field for the team's second open practice in the new Highmark Stadium early Tuesday morning, and the practice featured some developments on the injury front.

 Two expected starters -- safety Cole Bishop and cornerback Maxwell Hairston (groin) -- returned to practice after missing time over the past week. Hairston hadn't practiced since Aug. 6. Wide receiver DJ Moore also participated in practice after being looked at by athletic trainers during Saturday's preseason game against the  Carolina Panthers . He did not, however, participate in team drills.

 Players to keep an eye on in the wide receiver room include: Rookie Skyler Bell continues to miss time, while Khalil Shakir and Keon Coleman did not practice for the first time this camp. Coleman was wearing a walking boot on his right foot. The team is not sharing injury designations in the preseason.

 Other players not practicing include defensive tackle Ed Oliver , rookie safety Jalon Kilgore (wrap on right leg), safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson , running back Ty Johnson and center Connor McGovern  (McGovern said Saturday that his goal is to be back for the regular season).

 Next up for Buffalo is a joint practice at the  Cleveland Browns  on Thursday, which should serve as an extensive look at the first-team offense and defense.

 

 More observations: 

 
 A couple fights broke out late in practice among linemen. Overall, though, fights have been limited during camp and the skirmishes on Tuesday were relatively brief. 
 Rookie linebacker Kaleb Elarms-Orr almost intercepted a Josh Allen  pass and was visibly frustrated when he couldn't bring it in. He is competing with Dorian Williams for a starting inside linebacker job. 
 

 
 Thursday, Aug. 13 
 One key player the Bills are looking forward to having back on the field for the regular season is edge rusher  Michael Hoecht . Hoecht has been a full participant for much of training camp while working back from a torn right Achilles suffered in November.

 Coach Joe Brady said that the plan is for Hoecht to play in a preseason game, but did not want to disclose if that would be this week or in the future. Hoecht also said after practice that he believes it's a game-time decision.

 "[Hoecht's] way ahead of schedule, seeing what he's able to do," Brady said. "And so, if it's not this week, I do want to get him preseason football. Shoot, he's gonna want to do preseason season football."

 Other observations:  

 
 C Connor McGovern , RB Ty Johnson , WR Skyler Bell . CB Maxwell Hairston .and CB Kani Walker are all facing injuries, while S Cole Bishop and S C.J. Gardner-Johnson did not participate in practice. Hairston and Bishop did do some work inside the team's fieldhouse while the rest of the team was outside. 
 Offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael will be in the coaching booth instead of the sideline for Saturday's preseason game. Carmichael has traditionally coached on the sideline, but Brady wants to experiment with him in each place during the preseason. 
 Quarterback Shane Buechele threw interceptions on back-to-back plays during 11-on-11 drills. The first was a pick-six by defensive back Te'Cory Couch and the second was on an errant throw taken away by linebacker Jimmy Ciarlo . 
 

 

 Who is the Bills' top performer so far at camp? 
 Nickel corner Dee Alford . Quarterback Josh Allen put it best, "Dee Alford's been making a lot of plays." This could go to a couple of players, including receiver DJ Moore , but Alford has stood out on a defense that is undergoing major change. His training camp performance featured three interceptions off Allen.

 

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 
 Where does this defense stand? This is the part of the team that underwent the biggest change this offseason, going from a 4-3 base under Sean McDermott the last nine seasons to a 3-4 with new coordinator Jim Leonhard. Getting a look at this unit in game action will continue to help in seeing more and more of what to expect. Keep in mind, however, that multiple defensive secondary starters are dealing with injuries, including safeties Bishop and Gardner-Johnson and CB Hairston.

 
 Tuesday, Aug. 11 
 The Bills wide receivers room is a popular topic of conversation. While DJ Moore 's connection with quarterback Josh Allen has been a camp highlight, it was Joshua Palmer who stood out with a couple of nice grabs in Tuesday's practice.

 Palmer's first season with the Bills was disrupted by injuries, especially a left ankle injury, but the receiver said he is now feeling much more comfortable. Getting significant, and reliable, contributions from players such as Palmer would be big for Joe Brady's offense.

 "I don't have to question any of my movements," Palmer said. "I don't have to think before the route. I don't have to ... I'm not stressed before I go on the field. I just go out and play."

 Other observations: 

 
 Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said that he thinks the plan is for starters to play in the preseason opener Saturday but that it is TBD how much they will play. "It's gonna be exciting for guys to get out there and just kind of let it rip," Leonhard said. Leonhard said tackling is a big evaluation piece for the defense in the game, noting that getting offensive players to the ground and finishing plays was an "Achilles' heel" in Buffalo last year. 
 Rookie DT Zane Durant returned to practice, but a number of starters were still not participating. Among those not practicing are safeties C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Cole Bishop and center Connor McGovern . Cornerback Maxwell Hairston was doing some work on the side. The team has not disclosed injuries. 
 Nickel corner Dee Alford continues to be a camp standout. On Tuesday, he intercepted Allen for the third time in camp with a jump on a ball that was intended for receiver Keon Coleman . Alford said that he adjusted the call based on what they saw on film. "[Allen is] the best quarterback in the league, MVP. So ... any time you can catch an interception from him, man, it just shows what type of defender you are." 
 
 

 Monday, Aug. 10 
 Injuries were the theme of the day as the Buffalo Bills held their first training camp practice at the team's facility in Orchard Park, New York.

 Several starters did not participate, including safety Cole Bishop , cornerback Maxwell Hairston and center Connor McGovern . Also not taking part were running back Ty Johnson , wide receivers Skyler Bell and Ja'Mori Maclin , defensive tackle Zane Durant , defensive back D.J. Miller and punter Mitch Wishnowsky .

 The team did not disclose the nature of the injuries.

 Starting safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson , who missed two practices with a right calf strain, also left practice early after falling to the ground while making a pass breakup in the end zone. Athletic trainers looked at his right leg. He eventually walked to the locker room on his…

title: 2026 Dallas Cowboys training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Cowboys training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. Cowboys reporter Todd Archer has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and, of course, the quarterbacks room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at the Cowboys' camp. Will Dallas turn around the NFL's worst defense from 2025? Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Catch up on all the updates, including the Cowboys' top camp performer and biggest lingering question as preseason games begin.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Cowboys camp 
 
 Miller to play 15th season after getting 1-year deal from Cowboys 
 Sources: Cowboys, Quinnen Williams reach 3-year, $105.9M deal 
 Cowboys' Dak Prescott not shying away from setting lofty goals 
 Jones optimistic about Cowboys, likes 'what we put together' 
 Source: Ex-Cowboys QB Will Grier returns as offensive assistant 
 Quieter offseason has Cowboys focused on the right things 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 Amid the fights and skirmishes between the Cowboys and Saints, there was actually some practice, but not enough for coach Brian Schottenheimer's liking.

 On the first play between the offense and defense, there was a shoving match. On the fifth snap between the first-teamers, there was a fight. But let's stick to football, specifically the Cowboys' first-team offense against the Saints' defense.

 Unofficially,  Dak Prescott was 20-of-25 with one interception. On a crosser to CeeDee Lamb , the pass sailed over Lamb and right into the arms of safety Julian Blackmon . Prescott had a deep completion near the sideline to George Pickens that drew loud cheers from the fans.

 In red zone work, Prescott had touchdown passes to tight end  Jake Ferguson on a shovel pass, a quick throw to Pickens on a slant and a perfectly placed ball to the post that was high enough that only receiver  Ryan Flournoy could come down with the catch. Pickens was flagged for a celebration penalty by the officials when he flipped the ball in the direction of Saints cornerback  Kool-Aid McKinstry .

 "I think we're finding our rhythm," Schottenheimer said. "I'll go back to the preseason game. I think we kind of found our rhythm even in the second half against Seattle. And that's what training camp is for."

 

 Who is the Cowboys' top performer so far at camp? 

 George Pickens . He has essentially made a big play in every practice as he gets set to play on the $27.3 million franchise tag. Whatever disenchantment some might have expected from Pickens without a long-term deal has not materialized. Coaches have noted his attention in the meeting rooms since the start of training camp.

 He and Dak Prescott have picked up where they left off in 2025 when the receiver had career highs in catches, yards and touchdowns. Does that mean he will surpass those figures again in 2026? Not necessarily, but his performance so far has shown a focused player as the season inches closer.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 Because the Cowboys aren't going to play their starters in the preseason, it's impossible to completely answer anything about the defense. There have been encouraging signs there, but let's look to the offense for what can be answered in the preseason games: Who will back up Prescott?

 Joe Milton III and Sam Howell have alternated as Prescott's backup in practice and both have had good moments and not-so-good ones. The Cowboys believe they have line play and skill players to give both QBs a fair shot to perform in the preseason and not have them running for their lives. Read more below:

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 

 For the second time this month, the Cowboys will hold a joint practice, hosting the New Orleans Saints  on Tuesday after traveling to the Los Angeles Rams a week ago.

 The importance of the work isn't lost on tight end Jake Ferguson , who, like the rest of the Cowboys' starters and regulars, will not play in any of the three preseason games.

 "It's usually their starting defense going against our starting offense," Ferguson said. "That's where we get a good read of what we're looking like, what we're feeling like, what we need to clean up. We had that one against the Rams and came out firing. It was a lot of things we needed to clean up, but this is a good tell."

 The Saints will bring a familiar face with coach Kellen Moore. Ten years ago, Moore was Tony Romo 's backup for Dallas before breaking his ankle early in training camp. It helped pave the way for Dak Prescott to become the starter. Moore became a Cowboys assistant coach and served as offensive coordinator from 2019 to 2022. Moore also interviewed for the Cowboys head coaching vacancy that went to Brian Schottenheimer.

 "Kellen and I have kind of laid it out," Schottenheimer said. "It'll be similar to what we did with the Rams. A few less reps since they have another joint practice coming up [with the Rams], but you'll see a lot of the same situational work, some of the special teams stuff."

 More observations: 

 Monday's practice was conducted in helmets and jerseys, with no shells or pads, since the players were just two days removed from a preseason game. With the late return from Seattle, the Cowboys could not meet until late in the morning, and they held a practice that ran about 75 minutes.

 A sign the starters will get most of the work versus New Orleans: The backups had only 12 reps in practice; the starters had 30.

 Jaydon Blue was the only running back to not take any snaps during practice. He went through individual drills, but he is dealing with a shoulder injury. Phil Mafah (chest) did not get a carry, but he caught one pass. The bulk of the work went to Javonte Williams , Malik Davis and Israel Abinkanda .

 

 Friday, Aug. 14 

 Most of the regulars will not play in Saturday's preseason opener against the Seattle Seahawks , but there is one important position that could start to take shape: backup quarterback.

 Throughout training camp, Joe Milton III and Sam Howell have alternated days as Dak Prescott 's backup as they compete to be the No. 2.

 "It's been a very highly competitive contest," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I think Joe's talent and ability to throw the football and athleticism jumps off the practice field when you see it. I think Sam's doing a great job of moving the team. But at the end of the day, the preseason games, they're going to play really the entire preseason, and that's where the bulk of the evaluation will be."

 Schottenheimer said there has been a back and forth between the quarterbacks. Milton served as Prescott's backup last year, appearing in four games and completing 15 of 24 passes for 183 yards with a touchdown and two interceptions. Howell signed a one-year deal worth $2.5 million guaranteed in free agency.

 He has started 18 games in his career, including all 18 for the Washington Commanders in 2023.

 Milton said having a full year in the offense has "definitely made a huge difference. Shoot, coming in here last year at this time I probably knew 85% of the playbook, 75% of the playbook. Now it's pretty much everything and picking up all of the small stuff, the new stuff, so it's been great."

 Howell has liked what he has done in training camp.

 "We've both been doing a good job trying to make each other better," he said. "I think that's the main thing, coming out each and every day, trying to get better, trying to make the quarterback room better, trying to push each other."

title: 2026 Denver Broncos training camp: Latest intel, updates
summary: Catch up on our daily updates from Broncos training camp, including intel on QBs, position battles and potential breakouts.
full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action. The Denver Broncos camp is taking place in Englewood, Colorado, and Broncos reporter Jeff Legwold has the latest intel on standouts, highlights, position battles, depth chart movement, cut decisions and of course the quarterback room.

 What follows is everything we are seeing and hearing at Broncos camp. We will update this file often as we track the Broncos' push toward getting to the Super Bowl after falling one game short last season. Who are the breakout players to watch, especially for fantasy football? And which players on the roster bubble could make the final 53?

 Dive in to all the updates and be sure to check back for more information until the first full week of the preseason begins Aug. 13.

 
 Camp updates for all 32 NFL teams 

 
 

 

 Latest news from Broncos camp 
 
 Why 2026 is a crucial season for Nix and the Broncos 
 Payton to talk to Taysom Hill about interest in Broncos 
 Nix won't be afraid to run on repaired ankle 
 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 
 The Broncos might be a business-like, veteran team with aspirations that reach well beyond an August practice, but emotions finally boiled with several skirmishes during team periods. The emotional temperature rose, as some pushing and shoving later turned into celebrations after each play in a red zone period. That later turned into a full-blown mass of humanity during an 11-on-11 period.

 Among the incidents were quarterback Bo Nix firing a ball at a defender after Nix had been knocked to the ground. Nix and edge rusher Nik Bonitto got entangled, with offensive tackle Mike McGlinchey having to be restrained as coaches tried to separate the players.

 

 "I love it,'' Nix said. " ... It's a physical game played by physical people. ... Practice gets long and the intensity gets high."

 Coach Sean Payton is well known for his stance against practice fights, feeling that a loss of discipline in practice results in a similar loss of discipline in games. Tuesday's skirmishes were the most significant of this camp.

 "It's gonna happen, [but] it just can't cross the line," offensive coordinator Davis Webb said. " ... I'm glad we're fiery, I love the competition out here ... [but] we can't cross the line."

 Webb added that Payton will certainly have something to say to the team at the conclusion of practice.

 More observations: 

 
 McGlinchey, who had two penalties (ineligible player downfield and a holding flag) in his 25 snaps played in the preseason opener , was pulled out of the formation after a false start penalty. McGlinchey finished the 11-on-11 period with the second-team offense. "It's not our standard,'' Webb said. " ... If it's not up to our standard you can be taken out.'' 
 Linebacker Drew Sanders was held out of practice for the second consecutive day. Center/guard Calvin Throckmorton left practice after the big skirmish with what looked like a cut above his left eye. 
 

 

 Monday, Aug. 17 
 Rookie running back Jonah Coleman continues to work his way up the depth chart toward a spot in the regular-season rotation, so much so that coach Sean Payton gave Coleman a fairly quick hook from the preseason opener. Coleman played 12 snaps Friday night in Atlanta and had four carries for 24 yards, with his last carry coming with 47 seconds left in the first quarter. Payton said he's seen enough from Coleman on the practice field to get the rookie out of the preseason opener that early.

 "I kind of felt it ... and there was a point when he got like two or three carries and I'm like 'alright, I've seen enough,'" Payton said. "I didn't need additional evidence of what I've been seeing for three weeks.''

 Coleman continues to get practice snaps with the first- and second-team offenses in camp in a variety of situations.

 More observations: 

 
 Inside linebacker Levelle Bailey suffered a fractured leg in the win over the Falcons, so the Broncos might be on the hunt for depth to finish out the preseason. Seventh-round rookie Red Murdock played the most defensive snaps in Friday's game (47) and continues to close in on a roster spot. Karene Reid (28 snaps) tipped the pass that cornerback Jahdae Barron returned 97 yards for a touchdown and undrafted rookie Taurean York played 22 snaps. Payton said "we'll see" when asked if they would add an inside linebacker, adding it was too soon to know if Bailey would be able to return this season. 
 Linebacker Drew Sanders played in his first game Friday since the playoff loss in Buffalo to close out the 2024 season -- he finished with a sack in 13 snaps against the Falcons. Sanders was held out of Monday's practice and worked on a side field. 
 Wide receiver Jaylen Waddle return to practice Monday and worked in team drills. Wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr . also returned to practice but worked on a side field after individual drills. 
 

 

 Who has been the Broncos' top performer at camp so far? 

 It is a close race between two receivers, second-year man Pat Bryant and Marvin Mims Jr ., with Bryant getting the nod in part due to Mims being slowed recently by a leg injury suffered last Friday.

 Mims started camp with a flourish, creating impact plays until he was limited by a soft-tissue injury that knocked him out of practice for a couple days. Bryant swooped in to be the big-play creator in Mims' absence. Bryant continues to ascend with precise routes and a seemingly fanatical desire to win the ball in the air every time. And on a team where most of the depth chart is settled, his efforts have been the most noteworthy.

 What still needs to be answered over the course of preseason games? 

 The Broncos suddenly have an issue at center, as starter Luke Wattenberg and backup Alex Forsyth have missed significant practice time with injuries while the No. 3 center -- Michael Deiter -- suffered a season-ending thigh injury this past week. It has put Calvin Throckmorton , who has gotten far more work at guard in his time with Denver, as the starting center, with undrafted rookie Gavin Ortega backing him up. Until either Wattenberg or Forsyth return to practice, center is a spot that could significantly impact how effective the Broncos are upfront.

 

 Wednesday, Aug. 12 
 Since Bo Nix will not play in Friday's preseason opener in Atlanta, there will be a chance for Jarrett Stidham and Sam Ehlinger to continue what has been one of the most spirited position battles of camp. On a team that returns 20 of 22 starters on offense and defense from the AFC Championship Game and returns most of the backups, too, Stidham and Ehlinger have had a heated battle to be the No. 2 quarterback. And Friday might be their best chance to show what they can do given Nix is expected to play some snaps in the Broncos' two other preseason games.

 Coach Sean Payton said after Wednesday's practice that each of the quarterbacks will play a half against the Falcons. Stidham is expected to start the game and play the first half.

 "They're focused on like their best stuff, they're competing against the 31 other quarterbacks (in the league) like any other position," Payton said. "... It's a great room, they get along well."

 Ehlinger, who led the team with 412 yards passing last preseason, has been consistently lauded by Payton for his work in camp and has routinely moved the second- and third-team offenses in practices. Stidham led the quarterbacks in touchdown passes last preseason, with four in three games.

 More observations: 

 
 Payton expects most of the healthy starters to get about 15 plays against the Falcons and said some of the injured players will remain back in Denver to continue to rehab their injuries. Wide receivers Jaylen Waddle and Marvin Mims Jr ., who are both working back from leg injuries in camp, are expected to be among the group that remains in Denver. 
 When asked why he, unlike many other coaches, will likely have…

full_text:
The 2026 NFL training camps have kicked off around the league, and our team reporters are on the ground each day following all the action.  Latest news out of Packers camp 
 
 CB Keisean Nixon not guaranteed starting role with Packers 
 Aaron Rodgers wishes game at Lambeau, discusses retirement return 
 Packers QB Love expected to play in first preseason game 
 Micah Parsons: Playing vs. Cowboys in Week 6 'realistic' 
 Packers RT changes last name to Bako-Bewele to honor heritage 
 Packers star TE Tucker Kraft activated off PUP after ACL recovery 
 Packers CEO: Team needs financial bump to stay competitive 
 

 

 Tuesday, Aug. 18 

 One thing that was evident almost immediately in training camp was Zaire Franklin 's intensity. Coach Matt LaFleur noted within the first week that the veteran linebacker "brings it every day."

 That has gone to another level since tight end Tucker Kraft returned to 11-on-11 drills this week.

 
Franklin didn't even remember that he and Kraft got into a scuffle last summer, when the linebacker was with the Colts and they had a joint practice with the Packers, but it's safe to say the tight end brings out the competitiveness in him.

 
Franklin took it up a notch Tuesday. He snagged an interception off a deflection by Edgerrin Cooper in the two-minute drill and then in the next period, he and Kraft barked at each other after Kraft knocked Franklin back as he was trying to get yards after the catch in the right flat.

 
"He's a dog," Franklin said after practice. "That's how it's supposed to be. I feel like with Tuck being out there, I told him, 'I feel like that's what the team is missing.' Like, he brings that same energy, that same competitiveness, that same a--hole mentality that I feel like I bring on the defense. That's what Tuck can do for the offense. So it was great to have him out there, great to compete."

 
It's a different story off the field, though.

 
"We laugh about it," Franklin said. "I think me and Tuck eat breakfast together every morning. I think we could just decide that we're fighting that day, and we still going to eat breakfast together the next morning. So yeah, it's good to have them out there for sure."

 
The Packers traded for Franklin, 30, and then signed him to a restructured contract of two years for $18.01 million after they realized they would not be able to re-sign Quay Walker in free agency.

 
As for Kraft, who is returning from last season's torn ACL, he once again caught every pass thrown his way, including one he pulled in with one hand on the run for a 46-yard touchdown.

 More observations: 

 
 Before practice, LaFleur addressed the recent comments made by Keisean Nixon , who said he thought he was being punished by taking reps with the backups at times. LaFleur said before practice: "The way I look at it is this: then I guess our whole team is being punished because everybody's in competition. I'm a big believer that competition will bring the best out of people. I want everybody to play with the chip on their shoulder. If they feel like they have something to prove, you're probably going to get more out of them." Nixon started at left cornerback with the No. 1 defense, but Benjamin St-Juste and Carrington Valentine also rotated in at that spot. Meanwhile, rookie Brandon Cisse manned the right cornerback spot. 
 Several players did team (11-on-11) drills for either the first time in camp or after an extended absence: left guard Aaron Banks (knee), defensive tackle Javon Hargrave (knee), cornerback Domani Jackson (core) and Valentine (hamstring). Edge rusher Lukas Van Ness returned after missing one open practice because of a shoulder injury. 
 With Banks back, the Packers might have had their opening-day starting offensive line on the field for the first time in camp with (from left to right) Jordan Morgan , Banks, Sean Rhyan , Jacob Monk and Zach Bako-Bewele . 
 Hargrave gave rookie guard Jager Burton a little welcome-to-the-NFL moment during the one-on-one pass-rushing drill. The 11th-year veteran pushed his way through on consecutive reps against Burton, who has otherwise had a strong camp. 
 Running back Josh Jacobs practiced for the first time since his Aug. 6 groin injury but did only individual drills. 
 Trey Smack went 1-for-2 on field goals -- both at the end of two-minute drives -- making one from 42 yards and missing wide right from 47. He's 28-of-37 on all competitive kicks since training camp opened. 
 Edge rusher Brenton Cox Jr ., who figures to play significant snaps before Micah Parsons returns from his ACL rehab, had another strong pass-rushing day and afterward offered one of the best quotes of camp: "Nobody wants their face peeled off every play like that. So when I'm attacking, it's either I'm going to peel your face off or you might get me, but I'm coming back to you." 
 
 

 

 Sunday, Aug. 16 

 How eager was Tucker Kraft to get on the practice field Sunday? He was the first player out of the Don Hutson Center and onto the practice field. The reason? He was finally cleared to do 11-on-11 team drills. While Kraft had returned to practice on July 31, he had been limited only to individual drills as he continued his comeback from last year's ACL surgery.

 Kraft caught all five of the passes thrown his way in practice, including one touchdown that prompted an emphatic spike and his chest-bumping, starfish celebration.

 The fourth-year tight end who tore his ACL in Week 9 last season has made no secret of his desire for a contract extension. He's in the final year of his rookie contract. He said he never considered skipping any 11-on-11s until he got his deal.

 "Well, that's a whole part of this process, is me day in and day out, coming in and being consistent, stacking days without setbacks and accumulating these reps now in a team setting so that they can see my health and we can just keep taking the talks from there," Kraft said.

 However, he said he hopes to have a contract extension done before the Sept. 13 opener against the Vikings.

 "That's the goal," Kraft said. "I think we're a different team when I'm out on the field and I think that's obvious. I think everyone in this organization, every fan knows that, without sounding arrogant.

 "I've kinda gone through life, just taking things blow by blow, assuming things will always just work out in the end. So me, the preparation, the sacrifices I've made to be here right now, I'm just going to continue to assume that it's all going to work out for me."

 

 
 On more than one occasion, defensive players got too close to quarterback Jordan Love . Late in practice, coach Matt LaFleur had finally seen it one too many times. He tossed Barryn Sorrell from a team period after Sorrell bull-rushed tackle Anthony Belton right into Love. 
 Belton took some snaps at left tackle with the starters late in practice. So did John Williams after starter Jordan Morgan appeared to be limited. 
 The defense came up with three interceptions: Brandon Cisse undercut an out route by Matthew Golden that Love slightly underthrew, Kitan Oladapo picked off Love to end a two-minute period and Jaylin Simpson picked off Tyrod Taylor with an over-the-shoulder interception deep down the sideline.

title: Texans ready to feature David Montgomery's dual-threat ability
summary: Houston traded for the running back and hopes he will complement quarterback C.J. Stroud.
full_text:
HOUSTON -- Days before hosting the Los Angeles Chargers in their preseason opener, the Houston Texans transformed practice at NRG Stadium into a dress rehearsal as they ran through a game-day simulation, knowing most starters wouldn't play in the exhibition.

 So during a competitive back-and-forth for the starters, quarterback C.J. Stroud surveyed Houston's stifling defense, searching for the crack that could finally spring the offense loose.

 Then, running back David Montgomery caught a floating pass from Stroud down the sideline and burst untouched into the end zone for an 80-yard touchdown. A sea of teammates flooded the field behind him as their celebration echoed through the otherwise empty stadium.

 The reception offered a glimpse of what Montgomery plans to deliver on game day: being an all-around back.

 

 "[Texans offensive coordinator] Nick Caley let me know that I will be able to showcase [my dual-threat ability] because I know I can do it," Montgomery told ESPN. "So, I'm excited."

 When Houston acquired Montgomery from the Detroit Lions in March for offensive lineman Juice Scruggs , a 2026 fourth-round draft pick and a 2027 seventh-rounder, it was to be a lead back.

 But Montgomery wants to shed the label of being only a physical back while he's the lead back for Houston. That includes showing his multidimensional ability to run downhill, outside the tackles and catch passes out of the backfield. He scoffed at the notion of being solely a physical back, confirming his attempt to distance himself from the label.

 "I can do everything," Montgomery told ESPN. "I try not to categorize myself."

 During Montgomery's three years with the Lions, he had a running mate in All-Pro Jahmyr Gibbs as they sported the nickname "Sonic and Knuckles" after 1990s video game characters that ran together. But in Houston, Montgomery is expected to be the star of the show -- even though running back Woody Marks has received rave reviews.

 In terms of doing it all, Montgomery has been effective running outside the numbers. Since his rookie season with the Chicago Bears  in 2019, he has averaged 4.6 yards running outside zone, and that's in multiple schemes for different teams. While running inside, he averaged 4.1 yards. He has 1,890 receiving yards with four touchdowns, and he believes that he has more to offer as a receiver.

 Through the first offseason with Montgomery, Caley has been pleased with the new addition to the backfield. Montgomery had 2,506 rushing yards (17th) and 33 touchdowns (eighth) in the past three seasons with the Lions. The Texans are hoping he can bring that production to an offense that ranked 22nd in rushing yards per game (108) last season.

 "He's all business," Caley said. "He's a really, really good player. He's grounded as a runner, but he's a very good pass-game player, and he's tough as nails in protection. Those guys have really fed off each other and just really pushed the needle and helped each other improve. I'm excited about them."

 

 A team with Super Bowl hopes wants to take pressure off Stroud. Relying on Montgomery and a physical run game that matches coach DeMeco Ryans' identity should help the offense become more effective.

 But don't be fooled, Ryans loves seeing Montgomery show some finesse to his game, just as he did on that 80-yard score last week.

 "It was a huge play. A huge momentum boost for our offense," Ryans said. "What David has done a really good job of is route running. Him and linebacker [ Henry To'oTo'o ] have had a lot of battles thus far in camp. It was cool to see David make a big play for us.

 "That's the type of player he is. That's why he's here for us. He can spark an offense. He can lift us with just making those plays, or it's just by him being a leader, being vocal and encouraging the other guys."
